school-c12-cs-a.title: Class 12 Computer Science — Python & Data Structures (Part A)
school-c12-cs-a.description: Class 12 Computer Science with live Python code activities: Python revision and functions, exception handling, file handling, stack, queue, sorting and searching.

courses.title: Python Revision Tour & Functions
courses.summary: A fast revision of Class 11 Python (tokens, data types, operators, control flow, strings, lists, tuples, dictionaries) followed by functions — parameters, default and keyword arguments, return values, scope — and standard modules, as required in the CBSE Class 12 syllabus.
outcomes: Learners can predict output of Python expressions and control structures
Learners can manipulate strings, lists, tuples and dictionaries
Learners can define and call functions with positional, default and keyword arguments
Learners can explain local and global scope
Learners can use math, random and statistics modules

scenes.text: Aarav writes a cricket score program.
print(7/2) shows 3.5 but he expected 3.
He learns the difference between / and //.

steps.title: Tokens and data types
steps.body:
**Tokens:** keywords (if, for, def…), identifiers, literals, operators, punctuators.
**Data types:** int, float, complex, bool, str, list, tuple, dict, set, NoneType.
**Mutable:** list, dict, set. **Immutable:** int, float, str, tuple, bool.

steps.title: Operators
steps.body:
Arithmetic: + − * / (true division) // (floor division) % (remainder) ** (power)
Relational: == != < > <= >=
Logical: and, or, not
Membership: in, not in · Identity: is, is not
Precedence (high → low): ** → unary − → * / // % → + − → relational → not → and → or. Note ** is right-associative: 2**3**2 = 2**9 = 512.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: x = 5; print(x > 3 and x < 10) → True · print(not x == 5) → False · print(10 - 4 * 2 ** 2) → 10 − 16 = −6

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming // rounds toward zero (it floors: −7//2 = −4).
- Using = (assignment) instead of == (comparison).
- Forgetting that input() returns a string — convert with int() or float().

activity.prompt: Read two integers a and b (one per line). Print a//b, a%b and a**2 on three lines.
activity.starter:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
# print a//b, a%b, a**2
activity.solution:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
print(a // b)
print(a % b)
print(a ** 2)
activity.hint: Floor division rounds down, even for negatives.

quiz.why: The // operator floors the result. −9 ÷ 4 = −2.25, and the floor of −2.25 is −3, because floor goes down, not toward zero.
The ** operator is right-associative, so 2 ** 2 ** 3 = 2 ** (2 ** 3) = 2 ** 8 = 256, not (2 ** 2) ** 3 = 64.
A list can be changed after creation (append, item assignment), so it is mutable. int, tuple and str are immutable.
input() always returns what the user typed as a string (str). You must convert it with int() or float() for numbers.
10 % 4 gives the remainder 2, and 2 == 2 is True.

scenes.text: Meera wants to count vowels in her name.
A for loop over the string does it.
She stores results in a list.

steps.title: Control flow
steps.body: if / elif / else; for loops with range(start, stop, step); while loops; break (exit loop), continue (skip to next iteration), pass (do nothing). A loop's else runs if the loop ends without break.

steps.title: Strings
steps.body: Indexing s[0], negative s[−1]; slicing s[a:b:c]; immutable. Methods: len, upper, lower, title, capitalize, count, find (−1 if absent), index (error if absent), replace, split, join, strip, isalpha, isdigit, isalnum, startswith, endswith.

steps.title: Lists
steps.body: Mutable ordered collections. Methods: append, extend, insert, pop (by index, returns), remove (by value), sort, reverse, index, count, clear; functions len, max, min, sum, sorted. Slicing creates a new list.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: s = "COMPUTER"; s[1:5] → "OMPU"; s[::-1] → "RETUPMOC"; s[-3:] → "TER".

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting s.upper() to change s — strings are immutable; assign the result.
- Confusing append (adds one item) with extend (adds each item).
- Off-by-one with range: range(1, 5) gives 1..4.

activity.prompt: Read a word. Print the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u — any case) and then the word reversed.
activity.starter:
w = input()
# count vowels, then print reversed word
activity.solution:
w = input()
count = 0
for ch in w.lower():
    if ch in "aeiou":
        count += 1
print(count)
print(w[::-1])
activity.hint: Loop over w.lower() and check membership in "aeiou". Reverse with slicing [::-1].

quiz.why: Slicing [1:4] takes indices 1, 2 and 3, which are Y, T and H, and stops before index 4. So the result is YTH.
find() returns the index of the first match, or −1 when the substring is not found. It does not raise an error.
extend() adds each element of [3, 4] separately, so the list becomes [1, 2, 3, 4] with length 4.
range(2, 10, 3) starts at 2 and adds 3 each time while below 10: 2, 5, 8. The next value, 11, is beyond the stop value.
break ends the loop at once and control moves to the first statement after it. continue is the one that skips one iteration.

scenes.text: Ms. Iyer stores roll numbers and marks.
A dictionary maps names to marks.
She finds the topper in one line.

steps.title: Tuples
steps.body: Immutable ordered sequences: t = (1, 2, 3); single element needs a comma: (5,). Support indexing, slicing, count, index, len, max, min, sum. Packing/unpacking: a, b = b, a swaps values.

steps.title: Dictionaries
steps.body: Key–value pairs; keys must be immutable and unique. d[key] (KeyError if absent), d.get(key, default), d.keys(), d.values(), d.items(), d.update(), d.pop(key), del d[key], len(d). Iterating "for k in d" gives keys.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: marks = {"Asha": 88, "Ravi": 92}; marks["Zoya"] = 79 adds a key; max(marks, key=marks.get) → "Ravi".

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing (5) for a one-element tuple — that is just the int 5.
- Using a list as a dictionary key (unhashable).
- Using d[key] when key may be missing — prefer d.get(key, 0).

activity.prompt: Read a line of words separated by spaces. Print each distinct word and its frequency as "word:count", in order of first appearance, one per line.

tests.stdin: to be or not to be

activity.hint: Use d.get(w, 0) + 1. Dictionaries keep insertion order in Python 3.7+.

quiz.why: A one-element tuple needs a trailing comma, (5,). Without it, (5) is just the number 5 in brackets.
get() with a default returns that default when the key is missing, so d.get("x", 0) gives 0 and no KeyError is raised.

quiz.q: Which can be a dictionary key?
quiz.why: Dictionary keys must be immutable and hashable. A tuple of numbers qualifies, but lists, sets and dictionaries are mutable.

quiz.q: for k in d: iterates over:
quiz.why: A for loop over a dictionary goes through its keys. Use d.values() or d.items() for values or pairs.
Tuples are immutable, so item assignment such as t[0] = 9 raises a TypeError.

scenes.text: Kabir copies the same tax code five times.
His teacher shows him how to write a function.
One fix now updates every use.

steps.title: Defining and calling
steps.body:
def name(parameters):
    body
    return value
Types: built-in (len, print), from modules (math.sqrt), user-defined. A function without return returns **None**. Multiple values can be returned as a tuple: return a, b.

steps.title: Arguments
steps.body:
- **Positional:** matched by position
- **Default:** def f(a, b=10) — default parameters must come after non-default ones
- **Keyword:** f(b=5, a=2) — order does not matter
Parameters (in definition) vs arguments (in call). Mutable objects (lists) passed to a function can be changed inside it; immutable ones (int, str) cannot be changed in place.

steps.title: Scope (LEGB)
steps.body: **Local** variables exist only inside the function. **Global** variables are defined at top level. To modify a global inside a function, declare global x. Name lookup order: Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in.

steps.title: Solved example 1
Solved example 2
steps.body:
x = 10
def f():
    x = 5
    print(x)
f(); print(x) → prints 5 then 10 (local x does not change global x).
With "global x" inside f, the second print would also give 5.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- def f(a=1, b) → SyntaxError (non-default after default).
- Forgetting return → function gives None.
- Expecting an int argument changed inside a function to change outside.

activity.prompt: Write a function stats(nums) that returns (minimum, maximum, average rounded to 2 decimals) for a list. Read space-separated integers, call it and print the three values separated by spaces.
activity.starter:
def stats(nums):
    # return min, max, average
    pass

nums = list(map(int, input().split()))
activity.hint: Return a tuple and unpack it: lo, hi, avg = stats(nums).

quiz.q: A function with no return statement returns:
quiz.why: A function with no return statement returns None by default.

quiz.q: def f(a, b=3): return a*b; f(2) =
quiz.why: f(2) uses the default b = 3, so the function returns 2 * 3 = 6.
Parameters with default values must come after those without defaults. So def f(a=1, b) is a syntax error.

quiz.q: To modify a global variable inside a function use:
quiz.why: The global keyword inside the function tells Python to use the global variable, so assignments change it. Without it, an assignment creates a local variable.

quiz.q: Variables defined inside a function are:
quiz.why: Variables created inside a function are local and exist only while the function runs.

scenes.text: Riya needs a dice roller and averages for her game.
Python's standard library already has them.
import does the job.

steps.title: Importing
steps.body: import math · from math import sqrt · import math as m. Use math.sqrt(16) or sqrt(16) depending on import style.

steps.title: Useful functions
steps.body:
**math:** sqrt, pow (returns float), ceil, floor, fabs, factorial, gcd, pi, e
**random:** random() (0 ≤ x < 1), randint(a, b) (both inclusive), randrange(start, stop, step) (stop excluded), choice(seq), shuffle(list)
**statistics:** mean, median, mode

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
import math
print(math.ceil(4.1), math.floor(4.9), math.pow(2, 3)) → 5 4 8.0

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Possible outputs of random.randint(1, 3) are 1, 2, 3. random.randrange(1, 10, 3) can give 1, 4, 7 (never 10). Exam tip: for "possible output" questions, list min and max values first.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking randint(1, 6) excludes 6 — it includes it.
- Thinking randrange(1, 6) includes 6 — it does not.
- math.pow returns float (8.0), while ** with ints returns int.

activity.prompt: Read space-separated integers. Using the statistics module, print the mean, median and mode on three lines.
activity.starter:
import statistics
nums = list(map(int, input().split()))
activity.solution:
import statistics
nums = list(map(int, input().split()))
print(statistics.mean(nums))
print(statistics.median(nums))
print(statistics.mode(nums))
activity.hint: Median of an even-length list is the average of the two middle values (a float).

quiz.why: random.randint(a, b) includes both ends, so randint(2, 5) can return 2, 3, 4 or 5.
math.ceil rounds up to the next integer. For −2.3 the next higher integer is −2, not −3.
math.pow always returns a float, so math.pow(3, 2) is 9.0, unlike 3 ** 2 which gives the integer 9.
randrange(0, 10, 5) picks from 0, 5 in steps of 5 up to but not including 10. So only 0 or 5 are possible.
With an even number of values the median is the mean of the two middle values: (2 + 3)/2 = 2.5.

questions.q: Output of print(15 // 4)?
questions.why: // is floor division, and 15 ÷ 4 = 3.75, so the floor is 3. Both operands are ints, so the result is an int, 3.

questions.q: Which is immutable?
questions.why: A tuple cannot be changed after creation, so it is immutable. Lists, sets and dictionaries can be changed.

questions.q: len("Hello World") =
questions.why: len counts every character, including the space: Hello (5) + space (1) + World (5) = 11.

questions.q: Default parameters must come:
questions.why: Python needs parameters with defaults to come after non-default ones, otherwise the call would be ambiguous.
append([4]) adds the whole list as a single element, not its items. So the list becomes [1, 2, 3, [4]] with length 4.

questions.q: Assertion: A local variable cannot be accessed outside its function. Reason: Its scope is limited to the function body.
questions.why: Both are true. A local variable exists only within its function body, so using it outside raises a NameError; the scope explains this.

questions.q: Output of "abcdef"[::2]?
questions.why: The slice [::2] takes every second character from the start: a, c, e. So the output is ace.
Assigning d["b"] = 2 adds a new key to the dictionary, so it now has two items and len(d) is 2.

questions.q: def f(x, y=2): return x ** y; print(f(3), f(2, 3)) →
questions.why: f(3) uses y = 2, so 3 ** 2 = 9. f(2, 3) gives 2 ** 3 = 8. So it prints 9 8.

questions.q:
x = 5
def g():
    global x
    x = x + 1
g(); print(x) →
questions.why: global x lets g() change the global variable, so x becomes 5 + 1 = 6, and print(x) shows 6.

questions.q: Possible outputs of: import random; print(random.randint(1, 3) * 10)
questions.why: randint(1, 3) returns 1, 2 or 3, so the output times 10 can be 10, 20 or 30.

questions.q:
What does this print?
L = [3, 1, 2]
L2 = L
L2.sort()
print(L)
questions.why: L2 = L does not copy the list; both names refer to the same object. L2.sort() sorts it in place, so printing L shows [1, 2, 3].

questions.q:
def h(a, b): a = a + b; return a
x = 2; print(h(x, 3), x) →
questions.why: Integers are immutable and passed by value-like behaviour: a = a + b changes only the local name. So h returns 5 while x stays 2.

questions.q: Output: s = "banana"; print(s.count("an"), s.find("na"), s.replace("a", "o", 2))
questions.why: "banana" has "an" twice. find("na") is index 2. replace("a", "o", 2) changes only the first two a's, giving bonona. So 2 2 bonona.

questions.q: Which correctly swaps a and b?
questions.why: a, b = b, a swaps the two values at once using tuple packing and unpacking. a = b; b = a would lose the original value of a.

questions.q: math.floor(7.9) =
questions.why: math.floor rounds down to the nearest integer, so floor(7.9) = 7.

questions.q: Which statement creates an empty dictionary?
questions.why: {} creates an empty dictionary. [] is an empty list, () an empty tuple, and set() an empty set.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Exception Handling in Python
courses.summary: Syntax errors vs exceptions, built-in exceptions, raising exceptions with raise and assert, and handling them with try–except–else–finally, with live code activities.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish syntax errors from exceptions
Learners can name common built-in exceptions and their causes
Learners can raise exceptions using raise and assert
Learners can handle exceptions using try, except, else and finally

scenes.text: Sana's calculator app crashes when a user types "ten".
Python shows ValueError and stops.
She learns to handle exceptions.

steps.title: Two kinds of errors
steps.body:
**Syntax errors (parsing errors):** the code breaks Python's grammar — e.g. missing colon, unmatched bracket. The program does not run at all until fixed.
**Exceptions:** errors that occur **during execution** even when syntax is correct — e.g. dividing by zero, opening a missing file. An exception is a Python **object** that represents an error. If not handled, the program stops (abnormal termination) and Python prints a traceback.

steps.title: Common built-in exceptions
steps.body:
- **SyntaxError** — invalid syntax
- **ValueError** — right type, wrong value (int("abc"))
- **IOError** — input/output failure (e.g. file cannot be opened; in Python 3 it is an alias of OSError)
- **KeyboardInterrupt** — user presses Ctrl+C / Delete
- **ImportError** — module not found
- **EOFError** — input() hits end of file
- **ZeroDivisionError** — division by zero
- **IndexError** — index out of range
- **NameError** — name not defined
- **IndentationError** — wrong indentation
- **TypeError** — operation on incompatible types ("2" + 3)
- **OverflowError** — result too large to be represented

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: print(10/0) → **ZeroDivisionError**. L = [1, 2]; L[5] → **IndexError**. print(x) with x undefined → **NameError**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: "5" + 5 → **TypeError**. int("5.5") → **ValueError**. d = {}; d["a"] → **KeyError** (another built-in exception).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a missing colon an "exception" — it is a syntax error found before execution.
- Confusing TypeError (wrong type) with ValueError (right type, invalid value).

activity.prompt: Each input line is an expression name. For "zero" print the exception name raised by 1/0; for "index" by [1][3]; for "value" by int("x"); for "type" by "a"+1. Read 4 lines and print the exception class name for each.
activity.hint: Catch with "except Exception as e" and print type(e).__name__.

quiz.why: int("abc") has the right type (a string) but the value cannot be converted to a number, so Python raises ValueError.

quiz.q: A missing colon after "if x > 2" is a:
quiz.why: A missing colon breaks the grammar rules, so Python reports a syntax error before running the program.
"3" + 4 mixes a string and an integer, an unsupported operand type combination, so it raises TypeError.
Using a name that has not been defined raises NameError.

options: An object representing an error during execution
quiz.why: An exception is an object created when an error occurs during execution. It can be caught and handled, unlike a syntax error.

scenes.text: An age field receives −5.
Python itself sees nothing wrong.
The programmer raises an exception deliberately.

steps.title: raise
steps.body:
The **raise** statement forcefully throws an exception: raise ExceptionName("optional message"). Once raised, no further statements in the current block run.
Example: if age < 0: raise ValueError("Age cannot be negative")

steps.title: assert
steps.body: **assert** tests an expression; if it is False, an **AssertionError** is raised (with an optional message): assert age >= 0, "Negative age". Used for checking assumptions and input validation during development.

steps.title: Solved example 1
Solved example 2
steps.body:
n = -3
assert n >= 0, "Only non-negative numbers"
→ AssertionError: Only non-negative numbers

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing raise ValueError without parentheses message is fine, but writing raise "error" (a string) is invalid in Python 3.
- Using assert for user-facing validation in production — asserts can be disabled with optimisation flags.

activity.prompt: Write a function check_marks(m) that raises ValueError("Invalid marks") if m is not between 0 and 100 (inclusive), else returns m. Read 3 integers (one per line); for each, print the returned value or the error message.
activity.hint: print(e) prints the message passed to ValueError.

quiz.why: assert checks a condition. When it is False, Python raises AssertionError with the given message, "Stop".

quiz.q: After raise executes, the remaining statements in the block:
options: Are skipped only if in a loop
quiz.why: raise stops normal execution at that point, so the statements after it in the block do not run; control goes to a matching handler.
The raise statement is used to throw an exception deliberately. try, except and finally are for handling.
assert x > 0 passes silently when the condition is True. Here x = 5, so nothing happens.
The string given to the exception is its message, so the message here is "bad", while ZeroDivisionError is the type.

scenes.text: A billing app divides total by number of people.
Someone enters 0 people.
Instead of crashing, the app says "Enter at least 1 person".

steps.title: How handling works
Solved example 1
Solved example 2
steps.body: Multiple exceptions in one clause: except (ValueError, TypeError): ... Using "except Exception as e: print(e)" shows the error message.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing a bare except: before specific ones (SyntaxError: default except must be last).
- Putting too much code inside try, hiding unrelated bugs.

activity.prompt: Read two lines a and b. Print int(a)/int(b) rounded to 2 decimals. If b is 0 print "Cannot divide by zero"; if either is not an integer print "Invalid input".
activity.starter:
a = input()
b = input()
# handle ValueError and ZeroDivisionError
activity.hint: Two except blocks: one for ZeroDivisionError and one for ValueError.

quiz.q: A bare except: clause must be placed:
quiz.why: A bare except: catches every exception, so it must be placed last. If it were first, the more specific except blocks would never run.

quiz.q: Searching for a handler happens in the:
quiz.why: When an exception occurs, Python searches for a handler through the call stack, from the current function to the callers.
If no handler is found anywhere in the call stack, the program terminates and prints a traceback.
A tuple of exception types in except handles any one of them, so either ValueError or TypeError is caught.

quiz.q: Exception thrown → handler found → handler runs. This is called:
quiz.why: When an exception is thrown and a handler takes it, the exception is said to be caught.

scenes.text: A program opens a file and processes data.
An error may occur in the middle.
finally makes sure clean-up always happens.

steps.title: else and finally
steps.body:
**else:** runs only if **no exception** occurred in try.
**finally:** runs **always** — whether or not an exception occurred, even if it was not handled. Used for clean-up (closing files, releasing resources).
Order: try → except (if error) or else (if no error) → finally.

steps.title: Solved example 1
Solved example 2
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting else to run after an exception.
- Thinking finally is skipped when an exception is unhandled — it still runs before termination.

activity.prompt: Read an integer n per line for 2 lines. For each: try to print 100 // n; on ZeroDivisionError print "div error"; in else print "ok"; in finally print "next". (Output for each input in that order.)
activity.hint: else runs only when try succeeds; finally always runs.

quiz.why: The else block runs only if the try block finished without raising an exception.
The finally block runs whether or not an exception occurred, even when return or break is used.

quiz.q: Output of try: print("A") except: print("B") else: print("C") finally: print("D")
quiz.why: No exception occurs in try, so A is printed. The except block is skipped, else prints C, and finally prints D, giving A C D.
finally always runs, so it is typically used for clean-up such as closing files and releasing resources.
The standard order is try, then except, then else, then finally.

questions.q: Errors detected before execution are:
questions.why: Syntax errors are found by Python when it parses the code, before execution starts. Exceptions occur while the program runs.

questions.q: 10/0 raises:
questions.why: Dividing a number by zero raises ZeroDivisionError.

questions.q: The block that always executes:
questions.why: The finally block is executed in every case, whether or not an exception occurs.

questions.q: int("12a") raises:
questions.why: "12a" is a string but not a valid integer, so int() raises ValueError.

questions.q: Which keyword forcefully throws an exception?
questions.why: The raise keyword throws an exception deliberately. Python has no throw keyword.

questions.q: Assertion: else runs only when no exception occurs in try. Reason: else is meant for code that should run only after successful try.
questions.why: Both are true. else is designed for code that should run only after try succeeds, which is why it runs only when no exception occurs.

questions.q: L = [1, 2, 3]; print(L[3]) raises:
questions.why: The list has indices 0 to 2, so L[3] is out of range and raises IndexError.

questions.q:
What is printed?
try:
    x = 1/0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Z")
finally:
    print("F")
questions.why: 1/0 raises ZeroDivisionError, so Z is printed by the handler. finally then always runs and prints F, giving Z then F.

questions.q: Pressing Ctrl+C during input raises:
questions.why: Pressing Ctrl+C interrupts a running program, and Python raises KeyboardInterrupt.

questions.q:
What is printed?
try:
    print("1")
    raise ValueError
    print("2")
except ValueError:
    print("3")
questions.why: 1 is printed first. Then raise ValueError jumps to the handler, skipping print("2"), and 3 is printed. So the output is 1 then 3.

questions.q:
What is printed?
def f():
    try:
        return "T"
    finally:
        print("F")
print(f())
questions.why: The return value "T" is prepared first, but finally runs before the function actually returns, so F is printed first. Then print(f()) shows T.

questions.q: assert len("abc") == 4, "len" raises:
questions.why: len("abc") is 3, not 4, so the assertion fails and raises AssertionError with the message len.

questions.q: Which ordering is invalid?
questions.why: A bare except: catches everything, so putting it before except ValueError: is invalid, as the later handler could never run.

questions.q: Case: A program reads marks and must reject values above 100 and also handle non-numeric input. Best design:
options: raise ValueError for >100 inside try; catch ValueError for both
questions.why: Raising ValueError for marks above 100 inside try, and catching ValueError, handles both the range error and non-numeric input in one handler.

questions.q: import mathss raises:
questions.why: Importing a module that does not exist raises ModuleNotFoundError, which is a subclass of ImportError.

questions.q: "abc" * "2" raises:
questions.why: A string can be repeated only by an integer, so multiplying "abc" by the string "2" is an invalid operand combination and raises TypeError.

courses.title: Ch 2 · File Handling in Python
courses.summary: Text and binary files, opening and closing files (modes, with statement), reading and writing text files, seek() and tell(), binary files with pickle, and CSV files with the csv module. Code activities use in-memory files (io.StringIO / io.BytesIO) so they run safely in the browser; in your exam use open().
outcomes: Learners can distinguish text, binary and CSV files
Learners can open files in the correct mode and use the with statement
Learners can read and write text files and use seek() and tell()
Learners can store and retrieve objects with pickle
Learners can read and write CSV files with the csv module

scenes.text: Ravi's program stores marks in a list.
When the program closes, the data is gone.
Files keep data permanently.

steps.title: Why files?
steps.body:
Variables live in RAM and disappear when the program ends. **Files** store data permanently on secondary storage.
**Text files:** sequence of characters (human-readable), lines end with EOL (\n); e.g. .txt, .py, .csv.
**Binary files:** bytes representing images, audio, Python objects; not human-readable; no EOL translation; e.g. .dat, .jpg.

steps.title: Opening and closing
steps.body:
f = open("notes.txt", "r") ... f.close()
Better: with open("notes.txt", "r") as f: … — the file closes automatically.

**f.seek(offset, reference)** — moves the pointer. reference 0 = beginning (default), 1 = current position, 2 = end. In text mode, only seek(n, 0) with values from tell() (and seek(0, 2)) are reliably allowed; relative seeks are for binary mode.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Stack
courses.summary: The stack data structure (LIFO), PUSH and POP with overflow/underflow, implementing a stack with a Python list, applications, infix–prefix–postfix notations, converting infix to postfix and evaluating postfix expressions — with code activities.
outcomes: Learners can explain LIFO and stack operations
Learners can implement a stack using a Python list with functions
Learners can apply stacks to reverse data and check balanced brackets
Learners can convert infix to postfix and evaluate postfix expressions

scenes.text: In the canteen, clean plates are stacked one on top of another.
The last plate placed is the first one taken.
That is LIFO — a stack.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body:
A **stack** is a linear data structure in which insertion and deletion happen at **one end** called the **TOP**. It follows **LIFO** (Last In, First Out).
Operations: **PUSH** (insert at top), **POP** (remove from top), **PEEK/TOP** (read top without removing), **isEmpty**, **size**.
**Overflow:** PUSH on a full stack (fixed-size stacks). **Underflow:** POP/PEEK on an empty stack. With a Python list there is no fixed limit, so we mainly check underflow.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: Undo/redo in editors, browser back button, reversing a string, function-call stack, checking balanced parentheses, expression conversion and evaluation.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Start empty. PUSH 10, PUSH 20, PUSH 30, POP, PUSH 40, POP, POP → popped: 30, 40, 20; stack now [10] (top = 10).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Reverse "CODE" with a stack: push C, O, D, E; pop four times → E, D, O, C → "EDOC".

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Popping from the bottom (index 0) — the top is the **end** of the list (L[-1]).
- Forgetting to check for an empty stack before POP (underflow).

quiz.why: Trying to POP from an empty stack is called underflow. Overflow is pushing into a full stack.

quiz.q: In a Python list stack, the top is:
quiz.why: With append() and pop(), the end of the list is the top of the stack, so the last element is the top.
The back button returns to the most recently visited page first, which is LIFO behaviour, so it uses a stack.

quiz.why: PUSH 1, PUSH 2 gives [1, 2]. POP removes 2, leaving [1], and PUSH 3 makes it [1, 3], so the top is 3.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body:
Scan left to right.
- Opening bracket ( [ { → PUSH
- Closing bracket → if stack empty → **unbalanced**; else POP and check it matches
At the end: balanced only if the stack is **empty**.

- Forgetting to check the stack is empty at the end.

quiz.why: Every opening bracket should have been matched and popped, so the stack must be empty at the end for a balanced expression.
An opening bracket is pushed onto the stack, to be matched later with a closing bracket.

quiz.q: A closing bracket with an empty stack means:
quiz.why: A closing bracket with an empty stack has no opening bracket to match, so the expression is not balanced.

quiz.q: Equal number of opening and closing brackets guarantees balance?
quiz.why: Equal counts are not enough: the order and type must match. For example ")(" or "([)]" have equal counts but are not balanced.

lessons.title: Infix, prefix, postfix — conversion and evaluation

scenes.text: Humans write A + B * C (infix).
Computers prefer ABC*+ (postfix) — no brackets needed.
A stack does the conversion and evaluation.

steps.title: Notations
steps.body:
**Infix:** operator between operands (A + B). **Prefix (Polish):** operator before (+ A B). **Postfix (Reverse Polish):** operator after (A B +). Postfix and prefix need no parentheses and no precedence rules during evaluation.
Precedence: ^ (or **) highest, then * /, then + −; left-to-right for equal precedence (except ^ right-to-left).

steps.title: Infix → postfix (stack algorithm)
steps.body:
Scan left to right:
- Operand → output
- "(" → push
- ")" → pop to output until "(" (discard both)
- Operator → pop to output while top is an operator of higher or equal precedence; then push current
At end → pop all to output.

steps.title: Evaluating postfix
steps.body: Scan left to right: operand → push; operator → pop **two** (first popped = right operand B, second = left operand A), compute A op B, push result. Final stack item = answer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing operands for − and / (A − B, not B − A).
- Popping operators of lower precedence during conversion.

The brackets force A + B first, giving A B +, then multiply by C: A B + C *.

quiz.why: A binary operator needs two operands, so on reading an operator we pop two values, apply it, and push the result.
In prefix notation the operator comes before its operands, so A + B becomes + A B.

questions.why: append() adds at the end of a list, which acts as the top, so it implements PUSH.

questions.q: Postfix of A * B + C:
questions.why: A * B is done first (higher precedence), giving A B *. Then add C: A B * C +.

questions.q: Assertion: Postfix expressions do not need parentheses. Reason: The order of operators itself defines the evaluation order.

questions.why: Each bracket group becomes its own postfix: A B + and C D −. Then multiply: A B + C D − *.

questions.why: By precedence: B * C → B C *; A + that → A B C * +; D / E → D E /; and the subtraction last gives A B C * + D E / −.

questions.why: The top of a stack is its last element, so top() on [2, 4, 6] returns 6.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Queue
courses.summary: The queue data structure (FIFO), enqueue and dequeue, implementing a queue with a Python list and collections.deque, applications, and the double-ended queue (deque) with a palindrome-checking application.
outcomes: Learners can explain FIFO and queue operations

scenes.text: People line up at a cinema counter.

from collections import deque
q = int(input())
tasks = deque()
for item in input().split():
    name, t = item.split(":")
    tasks.append([name, int(t)])

    task = tasks.popleft()

scenes.text: In a glass of soda, big bubbles rise to the top.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body:
**Sorting** = arranging elements in a particular order (ascending/descending).
**Bubble sort:** repeatedly compare **adjacent** elements and swap them if they are in the wrong order. After pass 1 the largest element is at the end; after pass i the last i elements are in place. Total **n − 1 passes**.
Optimisation: if no swap happens in a pass, the list is already sorted — stop early.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Treat the first element as a sorted part. For each next element (the **key**), shift larger elements of the sorted part one position right and **insert** the key at the right place. n − 1 passes.

activity.prompt: Read space-separated integers. Perform insertion sort (ascending) and print the list after each pass (i = 1 to n−1), space-separated.
activity.starter:

# insertion sort; print after each pass
activity.solution:
L = list(map(int, input().split()))
n = len(L)
for i in range(1, n):
    key = L[i]
    j = i - 1
    while j >= 0 and L[j] > key:
        L[j + 1] = L[j]
        j -= 1
    L[j + 1] = key
    print(" ".join(map(str, L)))

steps.title: Time complexity
steps.body:
**Time complexity** describes how the running time grows with input size n, ignoring constants (Big-O notation).
- **Constant O(1):** no loop (e.g. accessing L[i])
- **Linear O(n):** single loop over n items
- **Quadratic O(n²):** nested loops over n items

steps.title: Comparison of the three sorts
steps.body:
All three use nested loops → **O(n²)** in the worst case.
- Bubble: many swaps; with early-exit flag, best case (already sorted) O(n)
- Selection: always O(n²) comparisons, but at most n − 1 swaps
- Insertion: best case O(n) for nearly sorted data; good for small or almost-sorted lists
Comparisons in bubble/selection = n(n−1)/2 (e.g. n = 6 → 15).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: n = 10: maximum comparisons for bubble sort without early exit = 10 × 9 / 2 = **45**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Count comparisons in selection sort for [3, 1, 2]: pass 1 compares 2 times, pass 2 compares 1 time → **3** = 3 × 2 / 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying selection sort is O(n) in the best case — it always does n(n−1)/2 comparisons.
- Confusing number of passes (n − 1) with number of comparisons.

activity.prompt: Read space-separated integers. Run bubble sort WITH the early-exit optimisation and print two numbers: the number of passes actually performed and the number of swaps made.
activity.starter:
L = list(map(int, input().split()))
n = len(L)
passes = swaps = 0
# bubble sort with early exit
activity.solution:
L = list(map(int, input().split()))
n = len(L)
passes = swaps = 0
for i in range(n - 1):
    passes += 1
    swapped = False
    for j in range(n - 1 - i):
        if L[j] > L[j + 1]:
            L[j], L[j + 1] = L[j + 1], L[j]
            swaps += 1
            swapped = True
    if not swapped:
        break
print(passes, swaps)
activity.hint: Count a pass at the start of each outer iteration; break if no swap happened.

steps.body:
first = 0, last = n − 1
while first <= last:
    mid = (first + last) // 2
    if L[mid] == key: found
    elif key < L[mid]: last = mid − 1
    else: first = mid + 1
If the loop ends, the key is absent. Complexity **O(log n)** — at most about log₂(n) + 1 comparisons.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — dry run
steps.body:
L = [2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 11, 12, 17, 19, 23, 29, 31, 37, 41, 43], key = 2
1) first 0, last 14, mid 7 → 17 > 2 → last 6
2) mid 3 → 7 > 2 → last 2
3) mid 1 → 3 > 2 → last 0
4) mid 0 → 2 = key → **found at index 0 in 4 iterations**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Same list, key = 31: mid 7 (17) → first 8; mid 11 (31) → **found in 2 iterations**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying binary search to an unsorted list.
- Using while first < last (misses the last single element).
- Forgetting mid ± 1 (can cause an infinite loop).

activity.prompt: First line: sorted space-separated integers. Second line: key. Perform iterative binary search and print the index and the number of iterations (space-separated), or "Not found" and the iterations.
activity.starter:
L = list(map(int, input().split()))
key = int(input())
first, last, steps = 0, len(L) - 1, 0
# binary search
activity.solution:
L = list(map(int, input().split()))
key = int(input())
first, last, steps = 0, len(L) - 1, 0
pos = -1
while first <= last:
    steps += 1
    mid = (first + last) // 2
    if L[mid] == key:
        pos = mid
        break
    elif key < L[mid]:
        last = mid - 1
    else:
        first = mid + 1
print(pos if pos >= 0 else "Not found", steps)
activity.hint: mid = (first + last) // 2; move first or last past mid.

quiz.q: Binary search requires the list to be:
quiz.why: Binary search decides which half to discard by comparing with the middle element, which only works if the list is sorted.
Each step halves the search range, so binary search takes O(log n) time.

quiz.q: For L of 15 elements, first mid index is:
quiz.why: With indices 0 to 14, mid = (0 + 14)//2 = 7.
If the key is smaller than the middle element, it can only be in the left half, so last = mid − 1.

quiz.q: Max iterations to search 1,000 sorted items (approx.):
quiz.why: Each step halves the list, and 2¹⁰ = 1024 ≥ 1000. So about 10 iterations are enough.

scenes.text: A shop with 20 items in a jumbled box.
A library with 1 lakh books sorted by number.
Which search where?

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
- **Precondition:** linear — none; binary — sorted list
- **Complexity:** linear O(n); binary O(log n)
- **Best for:** linear — small or unsorted lists, or when sorting cost is not worth it; binary — large sorted lists searched often
- **Data structure:** binary needs random access by index (lists/arrays)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: n = 1,024: linear worst case = **1,024** comparisons; binary ≈ **11** (log₂1024 = 10, plus one).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A list of 10 unsorted phone numbers searched once → **linear** search (sorting first would cost more).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying binary search is always better — not on unsorted or tiny lists.

activity.prompt: Linear or binary search is the better choice?

items.text: Unsorted list of 12 names, searched once
Sorted list of 1 million IDs searched many times

quiz.q: Binary search on an unsorted list:
quiz.why: Binary search assumes sorted order. On an unsorted list, discarding half the list can throw away the key, so results may be wrong.

quiz.q: For n = 64, binary search needs at most about:
quiz.why: 2⁶ = 64, so about log₂64 = 6 halvings plus one final check, giving at most 7 comparisons.

options: The list is small or unsorted
The list is huge and sorted
quiz.why: For a small or unsorted list, linear search is simple and needs no sorting, so it is the better choice.
log n grows much more slowly than n, so O(log n) algorithms stay fast as the data gets large.

options: Index-based access to a sorted list
quiz.why: Binary search jumps to the middle by index, so it needs a sorted list with direct (index-based) access to elements.

scenes.text: A school has 10 lockers numbered 0–9.
Locker = roll number % 10.
Find any student's locker in one step.

steps.title: Hashing
steps.body:
**Hashing** computes the position of an element directly using a **hash function**, giving (ideally) **O(1)** search.
A **hash table** is a list of slots indexed by hash values. **Remainder (modulo division) method:** h(element) = element % size_of_table.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Table size 10; elements 34, 16, 2, 93, 80, 77, 51 → slots: 34→4, 16→6, 2→2, 93→3, 80→0, 77→7, 51→1. Search 16 → compute 16 % 10 = 6 → check slot 6 → **found in one step**.

steps.title: Collision
steps.body: When two elements map to the same slot (e.g. 43 and 93 with size 10 → slot 3), it is a **collision**. It must be resolved by a **collision resolution** technique (e.g. placing in the next free slot — linear probing, or keeping a list in each slot — chaining). A **perfect hash function** maps every element to a unique slot.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Python dictionaries and sets use hashing internally — that is why "x in my_set" is fast on average.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that hashing needs collision handling.
- Using a table size smaller than the number of elements without chaining.

activity.prompt: First line: table size m. Second line: space-separated integers to insert into a hash table using h(x) = x % m with LINEAR PROBING (if a slot is taken, try the next slot, wrapping around). Print the final table as space-separated values with "-" for empty slots.
activity.starter:
m = int(input())
items = list(map(int, input().split()))
table = [None] * m
# insert with linear probing
activity.solution:
m = int(input())
items = list(map(int, input().split()))
table = [None] * m
for x in items:
    i = x % m
    while table[i] is not None:
        i = (i + 1) % m
    table[i] = x
print(" ".join("-" if v is None else str(v) for v in table))
activity.hint: Compute x % m; while the slot is occupied, move to (i + 1) % m.

quiz.why: The remainder method hashes a key by taking x % size, which gives a slot between 0 and size − 1.

quiz.q: With table size 10, 47 goes to slot:
quiz.why: 47 % 10 = 7, so the key goes to slot 7.

quiz.q: Two keys mapping to the same slot is called a:
quiz.why: When two different keys hash to the same slot, it is a collision.
With a good hash function, the slot of a key is computed directly, so search takes constant time, O(1).

options: Maps each element to a unique slot
quiz.why: A perfect hash function gives every element its own unique slot, so there are no collisions.

questions.q: Binary search works only on:
questions.why: Binary search can only be applied to a sorted list, because it relies on the order to discard half the items.

questions.q: Linear search complexity:
questions.why: Linear search may have to check all n elements, so its complexity is O(n).

questions.q: Hash function by remainder method uses:
questions.why: The remainder method uses the modulus operator %, so slot = key % table size.

questions.q: For n = 32, binary search worst case is about:
questions.why: 2⁵ = 32, so about 5 halvings plus a final check give at most 6 comparisons.

questions.q: Assertion: Binary search is faster than linear search on large sorted lists. Reason: It halves the search space each step.
questions.why: Both are true. Halving the search space at each step gives O(log n), far fewer steps than O(n) for large sorted lists.

questions.q: Collision means:
options: Two keys hash to the same slot
questions.why: A collision occurs when two different keys give the same hash value, so they map to the same slot.

questions.q: Linear search for 7 in [3, 7, 9, 7]: comparisons made:
questions.why: Linear search compares 3 (no), then 7 (match), and stops. That is 2 comparisons.

questions.q: Binary search for 9 in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]: first mid value is
questions.why: With 7 items at indices 0–6, mid = 3, which holds 7.

questions.q: Table size 11: slot for 25:
questions.why: 25 % 11 = 3, since 22 is the nearest multiple of 11 below 25.

questions.q: Binary search for 13 in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]: number of iterations:
questions.why: Iteration 1: mid = 3 (7) < 13, so first = 4. Iteration 2: mid = 5 (11) < 13, so first = 6. Iteration 3: mid = 6 (13), found. So 3 iterations.

questions.q: Table size 5, linear probing; insert 10, 15, 7: slots of 10, 15, 7 are
questions.why: 10 % 5 = 0 goes to slot 0. 15 % 5 = 0 is taken, so probing moves to slot 1. 7 % 5 = 2 goes to slot 2.

questions.q: Which search suits a small unsorted list searched once?
questions.why: For a small unsorted list that is searched once, sorting or hashing is not worth the cost. A simple linear search is best.

questions.q: Binary search for 4 in [1, 3, 5, 7]: iterations before concluding "not found":
questions.why: Iteration 1: mid = (0 + 3)//2 = 1, value 3 < 4, so first = 2. Iteration 2: mid = (2 + 3)//2 = 2, value 5 > 4, so last = 1; now first > last, so the search ends after 2 iterations.

questions.q: Table size 7, linear probing; insert 14, 21, 28: final slots
questions.why: 14 % 7 = 0, so slot 0. 21 % 7 = 0 collides, so linear probing puts it in slot 1. 28 % 7 = 0 collides twice, so slot 2.

questions.q: Python dictionary lookup is fast because of:
questions.why: Dictionaries use hashing to compute where a key is stored, so lookup is very fast, about O(1).

questions.q: Linear search best case comparisons:
questions.why: The best case is when the key is the first element, so only 1 comparison is needed.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Understanding Data
courses.summary: What data is and why it matters, structured and unstructured data, data collection, storage and processing, and statistical techniques — mean, median, mode, range and standard deviation — computed in Python.
outcomes: Learners can classify data as structured or unstructured
Learners can describe data collection, storage and processing
Learners can compute measures of central tendency
Learners can compute range and standard deviation and interpret variability

scenes.text: The canteen records every sale on a tablet.
At month-end the manager sees which snacks sell most.
Raw data became useful information.

steps.title: Data and information
steps.body: **Data** = raw facts and figures (numbers, text, images, audio). After processing, it becomes **information** that supports decisions. Organisations use data for planning, forecasting and improving services (e.g. banks detecting fraud, hospitals tracking patient trends).

steps.title: Types of data
steps.body:
- **Structured data:** organised in a fixed format, usually rows and columns (tables, spreadsheets, databases) — e.g. a marks register, bank transactions
- **Unstructured data:** no predefined format — e.g. emails, social-media posts, images, audio, video, web pages
(Semi-structured data such as JSON/XML has tags but no rigid table structure.)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Classify: attendance table → structured; WhatsApp voice notes → unstructured; product reviews (free text) → unstructured; railway reservation records → structured.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A school records "Name, Class, Date, Present/Absent" each day → structured data from which information like "attendance % per student" is derived.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling images "structured" because they are stored in folders — their content is unstructured.
- Using "data" and "information" interchangeably.

activity.prompt: Structured or unstructured data?

quiz.q: Raw facts and figures are called:
quiz.why: Raw facts and figures that have not been processed are called data. Information is data that has been processed to be meaningful.

quiz.q: A table of student marks is:
quiz.why: Marks arranged in rows and columns follow a fixed format, so they are structured data.
Posts mix text, images, emojis and videos with no fixed format, so they are mostly unstructured.

quiz.q: Processed data that is meaningful is:
quiz.why: Data that has been processed and organised so that it has meaning is information.
JSON has tags or keys giving some structure but not a rigid table format, so it is semi-structured data.

scenes.text: Students survey 200 people about screen time.
Responses are stored in a spreadsheet.
They clean, sort and summarise the data.

steps.title: Collection
steps.body: Sources: surveys/questionnaires, sensors and IoT devices, transactions (billing), websites and apps, existing records. **Primary data** is collected first-hand; **secondary data** is taken from existing sources (reports, government statistics).

steps.title: Storage
steps.body: Files (text, CSV), spreadsheets, **databases** (organised, multi-user, secure), cloud storage. Storage devices: HDD, SSD, pen drives, memory cards, cloud servers.

steps.title: Processing
steps.body: Steps: input → **cleaning** (remove duplicates/errors, handle missing values) → organising (sort, classify) → calculation/summarisation → output (reports, charts). Can be manual, mechanical or electronic (computer-based — fastest and most accurate).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A survey response has age "−3" and another is duplicated → **cleaning** removes/corrects them before analysis.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A census is a source of **secondary** data for a student project; the student's own questionnaire is **primary** data.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Skipping cleaning — wrong data leads to wrong conclusions ("garbage in, garbage out").

activity.prompt: Data cleaning: read comma-separated ages (some may be empty, non-numeric, negative or above 120). Keep only valid integers 0–120, remove duplicates while keeping first occurrence, then print the cleaned values space-separated and their count on the next line.
activity.starter:
raw = input().split(",")
clean = []
# validate and de-duplicate
activity.hint: str.isdigit() rejects "", "abc" and "-3"; then check the range and duplicates.

quiz.why: Data that you collect yourself first-hand, such as through your own survey, is primary data.
Data cleaning removes duplicates, errors and inconsistencies so the data is accurate and ready for analysis.

quiz.q: Government census data used in a project is:
quiz.why: Census data was collected by someone else and reused in your project, so it is secondary data.
The result of any process depends on the quality of its input. If the input data is wrong, the output will be wrong too.
A database is a way to store data. Surveys, interviews and questionnaires are ways of collecting data.

scenes.text: A class of 10 students has marks from 35 to 98.
What is the "typical" mark?
Mean, median and mode answer differently.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Mean** = sum of values ÷ number of values
- **Median** = middle value after sorting (average of two middle values if n is even)
- **Mode** = most frequent value
The median is less affected by extreme values (outliers) than the mean.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Salaries (₹ thousand): 20, 22, 25, 28, 300 → mean = 79 but median = **25** → the median better represents a "typical" salary because of the outlier 300.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to sort before finding the median.
- For even n, picking one middle value instead of averaging two.

activity.prompt: Read space-separated integers. Without using the statistics module, print the mean (rounded to 2 decimals), the median, and the mode (if several values tie, print the smallest) on three lines.
activity.starter:
data = list(map(int, input().split()))
# compute mean, median, mode
activity.solution:
data = list(map(int, input().split()))
n = len(data)
mean = round(sum(data) / n, 2)
s = sorted(data)
if n % 2:
    median = s[n // 2]
else:
    median = (s[n // 2 - 1] + s[n // 2]) / 2
freq = {}
for x in data:
    freq[x] = freq.get(x, 0) + 1
best = max(freq.values())
mode = min(k for k, v in freq.items() if v == best)
print(mean)
print(median)
print(mode)
activity.hint: Sort for the median; use a dictionary of counts for the mode.

quiz.why: Sorted: 1, 3, 7. The middle value is 3, so the median is 3.
The mode is the most frequent value. 5 occurs three times, more than 3 (twice) or 2 (once).
With four values the median is the average of the two middle ones: (2 + 3)/2 = 2.5.

quiz.q: Which is least affected by outliers?
quiz.why: The median depends only on the middle position, so one extreme value barely changes it. The mean and sum are pulled by outliers.

lessons.title: Measures of variability: range and standard deviation

scenes.text: Two batters both average 40 runs.
One scores 38–42; the other 0–100.
Spread tells who is consistent.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Range** = maximum − minimum
- **Standard deviation (σ)** = square root of the mean of squared deviations from the mean: σ = √( Σ(x − x̄)² / n )
A small σ means values are close to the mean (consistent); a large σ means they are spread out. (Python's statistics.pstdev gives the population σ; statistics.stdev gives the sample version with n − 1.)

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Batter A: 38, 40, 42 → σ ≈ 1.63; Batter B: 0, 20, 100 → mean 40, σ ≈ 43.2 → A is far more **consistent**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the square root.
- Mixing population (÷ n) and sample (÷ n − 1) formulas — follow the question.

activity.prompt: Read space-separated numbers. Print the range and the population standard deviation (rounded to 2 decimals) on two lines. Do not use the statistics module.
activity.starter:
import math
data = list(map(float, input().split()))
# range and standard deviation
activity.solution:
import math
data = list(map(float, input().split()))
n = len(data)
mean = sum(data) / n
var = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in data) / n
print(max(data) - min(data))
print(round(math.sqrt(var), 2))
activity.hint: Variance = mean of squared deviations; σ = √variance.

quiz.why: Range = maximum − minimum = 12 − 3 = 9.

quiz.q: Smaller standard deviation means data are:
quiz.why: A small standard deviation means values lie close to the mean, so the data are more consistent.

quiz.q: σ is the square root of:
quiz.why: Standard deviation σ is the square root of the variance.

quiz.q: If all values are equal, σ is:
quiz.why: If all values are equal, every value equals the mean, so deviations are zero and σ = 0.

quiz.q: Population σ divides squared deviations by:
quiz.why: For a population, the sum of squared deviations is divided by n. The n − 1 divisor is for a sample.

questions.q: Data in rows and columns is:
questions.why: Data arranged in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet or table, is structured data.

questions.q: Most frequent value is the:
questions.why: The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data.

questions.q: Range =
questions.why: Range is the difference between the largest and smallest values: Max − Min.

questions.q: Primary data is:
questions.why: Primary data is collected first-hand by the person or team doing the study, for example through a survey.

questions.q: Median of 5, 1, 9, 3, 7:
questions.why: Sorted: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. The middle (third) value is 5.

questions.q: Assertion: Median is preferred over mean for skewed income data. Reason: Median is not affected much by extreme values.
questions.why: Both are true. A few very high incomes drag the mean up, but the median stays near the typical value, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Median of 8, 2, 6, 4:
questions.why: Sorted: 2, 4, 6, 8. The median is the average of the middle two: (4 + 6)/2 = 5.
All values equal the mean (5), so all deviations are zero and σ = 0.

questions.q: Case: Test A marks 60, 61, 59; Test B marks 20, 60, 100. Same mean 60. Which is more consistent?
questions.why: Both tests have mean 60, but Test A's marks lie close to 60 while Test B's are widely spread. Smaller spread (standard deviation) means Test A is more consistent.

questions.q: Population σ of 1, 3, 5:
questions.why: Mean = 3. Squared deviations are 4, 0, 4, sum 8. Variance = 8/3 ≈ 2.67, so σ = √2.67 ≈ 1.63.

questions.q:
What is printed?
import statistics as s
print(s.median([3, 1, 4, 1, 5]))
questions.why: Sorted values: 1, 1, 3, 4, 5. The middle (third) value is 3, so median prints 3.

questions.q: Case: Data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9. Population σ:
questions.why: Mean = 40/8 = 5. Squared deviations: 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16 sum to 32. Variance = 32/8 = 4, so σ = 2.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: Emails are free-form text, so they are unstructured, while a sales table has rows and columns, so it is structured. The other pairs are mismatched.

questions.q: Cleaning data includes:
questions.why: Data cleaning means fixing or removing duplicates, errors and invalid values, not encrypting, printing or deleting everything.

questions.q: Information is:
questions.why: Information is data that has been processed and organised so that it is meaningful and useful.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Database Concepts
courses.summary: Limitations of file systems, database and DBMS, the relational data model (relation, attribute, tuple, domain, degree, cardinality) and keys — candidate, primary, alternate and foreign keys — with SQL activities on a sample table.
outcomes: Learners can state limitations of the file system
Learners can explain DBMS and its advantages
Learners can use relational model terminology correctly
Learners can identify candidate, primary, alternate and foreign keys

scenes.text: The school office keeps fee records in one file and exam records in another.
A student's address is updated in one file but not the other.
A database avoids such problems.

steps.title: Limitations of a file system
steps.body:
- **Difficulty in access** (writing a new program for each query)
- **Data redundancy** (same data in many files)
- **Data inconsistency** (copies don't match)
- **Data isolation** (data scattered in different formats)
- **Data dependence** (programs depend on file structure)
- **Controlled data sharing** is difficult (security)

steps.title: Database and DBMS
steps.body:
A **database** is an organised collection of logically related data. A **DBMS** (Database Management System) is software to create, manage and query databases — e.g. MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Microsoft SQL Server.
Key ideas: **database schema** (design/structure), **data constraint** (rules like NOT NULL, UNIQUE), **meta-data / data dictionary** (data about data), **database instance** (data at a point of time), **query** (request for data), **data manipulation** (insert, update, delete), **database engine**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Address changed in "Fees" file but not "Exams" file → **inconsistency**, caused by **redundancy**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: In a DBMS, one table STUDENT is shared by fees and exam modules; updating the address once updates it for all → redundancy and inconsistency are controlled.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling MS Excel a DBMS — it is a spreadsheet.
- Confusing schema (structure) with instance (current data).

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Same data stored in many places
Copies of the same data do not match
Data in the database at a moment
Software to create and manage databases

quiz.why: Storing the same data in several places is called redundancy, and it wastes space and can lead to inconsistency.
MySQL is a database management system (DBMS), software used to create and manage databases.
A data dictionary holds meta-data, which is data about data such as table names, column types and constraints.

quiz.q: The state of a database at a given time is its:
quiz.why: The data stored in a database at a particular moment is its instance. The schema is the design and stays the same.
In a file system the same data is stored in many files, and updating only one copy gives inconsistent data. This is a limitation of file systems.

scenes.text: STUDENT(RollNo, Name, Class, Marks, City).
Each row is a student; each column a property.
That is a relation.

steps.title: Terminology
steps.body:
- **Relation:** a table
- **Attribute:** a column (field)
- **Tuple:** a row (record)
- **Domain:** set of allowed values for an attribute
- **Degree:** number of attributes (columns)
- **Cardinality:** number of tuples (rows)

steps.title: Properties of a relation
steps.body: Each attribute has a unique name; order of attributes and of tuples does not matter; each tuple is distinct (no two identical rows); each value is atomic (single value); a missing value is represented as **NULL**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: STUDENT has 5 columns and 6 rows → **degree 5, cardinality 6**. If 2 rows are added → cardinality 8, degree unchanged.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Domain of Class = {"12A", "12B", "12C"}; domain of Marks = integers 0–100.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping degree (columns) and cardinality (rows).
- Treating NULL as zero — NULL means unknown/missing.

activity.prompt: Write a query that counts the rows (cardinality) of STUDENT. Output the count only.
activity.starter:
-- STUDENT(RollNo, Name, Class, Marks, City)
SELECT ...
activity.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT;
activity.hint: COUNT(*) counts all rows, including those with NULLs.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE STUDENT(RollNo INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name TEXT NOT NULL, Class TEXT, Marks INTEGER, City TEXT);INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(1,'Asha','12A',88,'Delhi');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(2,'Ravi','12B',72,'Pune');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(3,'Zoya','12A',95,'Delhi');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(4,'Kabir','12C',64,'Jaipur');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(5,'Meera','12B',81,'Pune');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(6,'Arjun','12A',NULL,'Agra');

quiz.q: A row in a relation is called a:
quiz.why: In relational terms a row is a tuple (record). A column is an attribute.
The number of columns (attributes) in a relation is its degree.
The number of rows (tuples) in a relation is its cardinality.

quiz.q: A table with 7 rows and 4 columns: degree, cardinality =
quiz.why: Degree is the number of columns (4) and cardinality the number of rows (7), so degree 4, cardinality 7.
NULL means a value is unknown or missing. It is not zero and not an empty string.

scenes.text: Two students can share a name — but not a roll number.
A key uniquely identifies each row.
A foreign key links two tables.

steps.title: Types of keys
steps.body:
- **Candidate key:** a minimal set of attributes that can uniquely identify each tuple (a table can have several)
- **Primary key:** the candidate key chosen to identify tuples; cannot be NULL and must be unique
- **Alternate key:** candidate keys not chosen as primary key
- **Composite primary key:** primary key made of two or more attributes
- **Foreign key:** an attribute in one table whose values must come from the primary key of another (or the same) table; maintains **referential integrity**; may be NULL

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: STUDENT(RollNo, AadhaarNo, Name, Class) — RollNo and AadhaarNo are both unique → **candidate keys**. RollNo chosen → **primary key**; AadhaarNo → **alternate key**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: RESULT(RollNo, Subject, Marks): neither RollNo nor Subject alone is unique, but (RollNo, Subject) together is → **composite primary key**. RESULT.RollNo referring to STUDENT.RollNo is a **foreign key**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a foreign key must be unique in its own table (it need not be).
- Allowing NULL in a primary key.

activity.prompt: The STUDENT table has a NULL in Marks for one student. Write a query listing Name of students whose Marks IS NULL.
activity.starter: SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE ...;
activity.solution: SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks IS NULL;
activity.hint: Use IS NULL, not = NULL.

quiz.q: A primary key value can be NULL?
quiz.why: A primary key identifies each row uniquely, so it can never be NULL.

quiz.q: Candidate keys not chosen as primary key are:
quiz.why: Candidate keys that are not chosen as the primary key are called alternate keys.

quiz.q: A key made of two or more attributes:
quiz.why: A key formed by combining two or more attributes is a composite key.
A foreign key must match a primary key value in another table, which keeps data consistent between tables (referential integrity).
A foreign key value can be NULL when the row has no related row in the other table. A primary key value can never be NULL.

scenes.text: Thousands of people book tickets at the same time.
No two can get the same berth.
A DBMS handles concurrency and security.

steps.title: Advantages of DBMS
steps.body: Controls redundancy and inconsistency; easy data sharing among many users; security (access control); data integrity (constraints); backup and recovery; concurrent access; standardised query language (SQL).

steps.title: Real-world applications
steps.body: Banking (accounts, transactions), railway/airline reservation, school management, hospital records, e-commerce inventory and orders, library management, social media.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A bank DBMS ensures that two ATMs withdrawing from the same account at once do not both succeed beyond the balance → **concurrency control** and integrity.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A school gives teachers permission to update marks but students only to view → **security / controlled access**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying a DBMS removes all redundancy — it **controls** (minimises) it.

activity.prompt: Write a query to display Name and City of students from Delhi, sorted by Name.
activity.starter: SELECT Name, City FROM STUDENT WHERE ... ORDER BY ...;
activity.solution: SELECT Name, City FROM STUDENT WHERE City = 'Delhi' ORDER BY Name;
activity.hint: Use WHERE City = 'Delhi' and ORDER BY Name.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE STUDENT(RollNo INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name TEXT NOT NULL, Class TEXT, Marks INTEGER, City TEXT);INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(1,'Asha','12A',88,'Delhi');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(2,'Ravi','12B',72,'Pune');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(3,'Zoya','12A',95,'Delhi');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(4,'Kabir','12C',64,'Jaipur');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(5,'Meera','12B',81,'Pune');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(6,'Arjun','12A',NULL,'Agra');

quiz.why: A DBMS reduces redundancy and keeps it under control, so one change is made in one place and data stays consistent.

quiz.q: Simultaneous access by many users is:
quiz.why: Many users using the database at the same time is concurrency, which a DBMS manages safely.

quiz.q: Constraints in a DBMS help maintain:
quiz.why: Constraints such as primary key, NOT NULL and foreign key keep the stored data correct and consistent, which is data integrity.
Railway reservation systems keep large shared data used by many users, so they use a DBMS.
SQL, Structured Query Language, is the standard language for relational databases.

questions.q: A table in the relational model is a:
questions.why: In the relational model data is stored in tables called relations.

questions.q: Columns are called:
questions.why: Columns of a table are called attributes. Rows are tuples.

questions.q: Software for managing databases:
questions.why: A DBMS (database management system) is software that creates and manages databases.

questions.q: Degree of a table with columns (ID, Name, Age) and 10 rows:
questions.why: Degree is the number of columns, and the table has 3 (ID, Name, Age). The 10 rows give its cardinality.

questions.q: A primary key must be:
questions.why: A primary key must identify each row uniquely, so it must be unique and cannot be NULL.

questions.q: Assertion: A table can have many candidate keys but only one primary key. Reason: The primary key is chosen from the candidate keys.
questions.why: Both are true. Several columns may be candidate keys, and the table designer picks one of them as the primary key.

questions.q: In EMP(EmpID, PAN, Name, DeptID), with DEPT(DeptID, DName): DeptID in EMP is a:
questions.why: DeptID in EMP refers to the primary key of DEPT, so it is a foreign key.

questions.q: In EMP above, if EmpID is primary key, PAN is a/an:
questions.why: PAN is unique, so it is a candidate key, but EmpID was chosen as the primary key. So PAN is an alternate key.

questions.q: Same data stored in several files leads to:
questions.why: Keeping the same data in several files is redundancy. If one copy is changed and others are not, the data becomes inconsistent.

questions.q: A table has degree 5 and cardinality 8. After adding 2 columns and deleting 3 rows:
questions.why: Adding 2 columns makes the degree 5 + 2 = 7. Deleting 3 rows makes the cardinality 8 − 3 = 5.

questions.q: ATTENDANCE(RollNo, Date, Status): best primary key:
questions.why: One student has many attendance rows, but a student has one row per date. The combination (RollNo, Date) is unique, so it is the best primary key.

questions.q: Which statement about foreign keys is TRUE?
options: Values must match a primary key in the referenced table or be NULL
questions.why: A foreign key value must either match a primary key value in the referenced table or be NULL. It need not be unique.

questions.q: Case: A school stores fees and exam data in separate Excel files; an address change is updated in only one. Problems illustrated:
questions.why: The address is stored in two files (redundancy), and updating only one leaves different values (inconsistency).

questions.q: Case: Each order in ORDERS references CUSTOMER(CustID). Deleting a customer who still has orders is blocked. Concept:
questions.why: A foreign key in ORDERS refers to CUSTOMER, so the DBMS blocks deletion of a customer who still has orders. This is referential integrity.

questions.q: Set of permitted values of an attribute:
questions.why: The domain of an attribute is the set of values it is allowed to take.

questions.q: Data about data is:
questions.why: Data about data, such as table names and column types, is called meta-data.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Structured Query Language (SQL)
courses.summary: SQL with MySQL syntax: data types and constraints, DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), SELECT with WHERE, DISTINCT, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, NULL and ORDER BY, single-row functions, aggregate functions with GROUP BY and HAVING, and operations on relations and joins — with live SQL activities. Our live SQL activities run on SQLite in your browser; the syntax used is common to MySQL. MySQL-only functions are explained in the steps.
