Learners can insert, update and delete records
Learners can write SELECT queries with filters and sorting
Learners can use single-row and aggregate functions with GROUP BY/HAVING
Learners can perform joins and set operations on two tables

scenes.text: The school wants a STUDENT table in MySQL.
Each column needs a data type and rules.
DDL commands build the structure.

steps.title: Data types (MySQL)
steps.body: CHAR(n) — fixed length (pads with spaces) · VARCHAR(n) — variable length · INT · FLOAT · DATE ("YYYY-MM-DD").

steps.title: Constraints
steps.body: NOT NULL · UNIQUE · DEFAULT · PRIMARY KEY (unique + not null) · FOREIGN KEY (references a primary key in another table).

steps.title: DDL commands
Solved example 1
steps.body: CHAR(10) storing "Ravi" occupies 10 characters (padded); VARCHAR(10) storing "Ravi" occupies 4 (+ length info).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Create a foreign key:
CREATE TABLE RESULT(RollNo INT, Subject VARCHAR(20), Marks INT, PRIMARY KEY (RollNo, Subject), FOREIGN KEY (RollNo) REFERENCES STUDENT(RollNo));

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing DROP (removes table) with DELETE (removes rows).
- Using double quotes for identifiers in MySQL — use backticks if needed; strings use single quotes.

activity.prompt: Create a table BOOK(BookID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Title VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, Price INTEGER), insert (1,'Python Basics',350) and (2,'SQL Made Easy',420), then select Title and Price of books costing more than 400.
activity.hint: Separate statements with semicolons; strings in single quotes.

quiz.why: DROP TABLE deletes the table, structure and data. DELETE FROM removes only rows.

quiz.q: Adds a column to an existing table:
quiz.why: ALTER TABLE ... ADD adds a new column to an existing table. UPDATE changes values.
CHAR stores a fixed-length string. VARCHAR is variable length.
DESCRIBE (or DESC) shows the structure of a table: column names, types and keys.

quiz.q: A constraint that ensures values are never missing:
quiz.why: The NOT NULL constraint does not allow a missing value in that column.

scenes.text: A new student joins.
Another's marks are re-evaluated.
A third leaves the school.

steps.title: Commands
Solved example 1
steps.body: UPDATE STUDENT SET City = 'Mumbai' WHERE Name = 'Ravi'; → only Ravi's row changes.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: DELETE FROM STUDENT; → removes all rows but keeps the table structure (unlike DROP TABLE).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting WHERE in UPDATE/DELETE.
- Inserting values in the wrong column order — list columns explicitly when unsure.
- Writing UPDATE … WHERE Marks = NULL — use IS NULL.

activity.prompt: Give a grace of 5 marks to every student of class 12B, then display Name and Marks of 12B students ordered by Name.
activity.starter:
UPDATE STUDENT SET ... WHERE ...;
SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE ... ORDER BY Name;
activity.solution:
UPDATE STUDENT SET Marks = Marks + 5 WHERE Class = '12B';
SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE Class = '12B' ORDER BY Name;
activity.hint: UPDATE … SET Marks = Marks + 5 WHERE Class = '12B'.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE STUDENT(RollNo INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name TEXT NOT NULL, Class TEXT, Marks INTEGER, City TEXT);INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(1,'Asha','12A',88,'Delhi');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(2,'Ravi','12B',72,'Pune');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(3,'Zoya','12A',95,'Delhi');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(4,'Kabir','12C',64,'Jaipur');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(5,'Meera','12B',81,'Pune');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(6,'Arjun','12A',NULL,'Agra');

quiz.why: With no WHERE condition, DELETE FROM T removes every row but keeps the table structure.
UPDATE changes existing values in a table. INSERT adds new rows and ALTER changes structure.
INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE work on the data in tables, so they are Data Manipulation Language (DML) commands.
CREATE, ALTER and DROP define or change the structure of database objects, so they are DDL commands.
With no WHERE clause, UPDATE applies to every row, so all rows get Marks = 0.

scenes.text: Which students from Pune scored above 75?
SELECT with WHERE answers it.
ORDER BY sorts the answer.

steps.title: Clauses and operators
steps.body:
SELECT [DISTINCT] col1, col2 AS alias FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY col [ASC|DESC];
Relational: = <> != < > <= >= · Logical: AND OR NOT · Range: BETWEEN a AND b (inclusive) · Membership: IN (…) / NOT IN · Pattern: LIKE with % (any number of characters) and _ (exactly one) · Null: IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90; → Asha (88), Ravi (72), Meera (81).
SELECT DISTINCT City FROM STUDENT; → Delhi, Pune, Jaipur, Agra.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Name LIKE 'A%'; → Asha, Arjun.
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Name LIKE '_a%'; → second letter "a": Ravi, Kabir.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing WHERE Marks = NULL (always unknown) — use IS NULL.
- Forgetting that BETWEEN includes both ends.
- Using * when only some columns are needed (fine, but read the question).

activity.prompt: Display Name and Marks of students whose City is Delhi or Pune and Marks are at least 80, sorted by Marks in descending order.
activity.solution: SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE City IN ('Delhi', 'Pune') AND Marks >= 80 ORDER BY Marks DESC;
activity.hint: Combine IN (…) with AND; sort with ORDER BY Marks DESC.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE STUDENT(RollNo INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name TEXT NOT NULL, Class TEXT, Marks INTEGER, City TEXT);INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(1,'Asha','12A',88,'Delhi');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(2,'Ravi','12B',72,'Pune');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(3,'Zoya','12A',95,'Delhi');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(4,'Kabir','12C',64,'Jaipur');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(5,'Meera','12B',81,'Pune');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(6,'Arjun','12A',NULL,'Agra');

quiz.why: In LIKE, % stands for any number of characters. '%a' means anything that ends with a.
BETWEEN includes both end values, so 20 is included.
SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result.
ORDER BY sorts in ascending order (ASC) by default. Use DESC for descending.
NULL cannot be compared with =. The correct test is IS NULL (or IS NOT NULL).

scenes.text: Names must be shown in capitals.
Average marks should be rounded.
Dates need month names.

steps.title: Math functions (MySQL)
steps.body: POWER(x, y) / POW · ROUND(x, d) · MOD(a, b) · (also ABS, SQRT, CEIL, FLOOR). ROUND(25.678, 1) = 25.7; ROUND(25.678, −1) = 30; MOD(17, 5) = 2.

steps.title: String functions (MySQL)
steps.body: UCASE()/UPPER() · LCASE()/LOWER() · MID(s, pos, n)/SUBSTRING()/SUBSTR() · LENGTH() · LEFT(s, n) · RIGHT(s, n) · INSTR(s, sub) · LTRIM() · RTRIM() · TRIM(). Positions start at **1**. Example: MID('COMPUTER', 4, 3) = 'PUT'; INSTR('COMPUTER', 'P') = 4.

steps.title: Date functions (MySQL)
steps.body: NOW() · DATE() · MONTH() · MONTHNAME() · YEAR() · DAY() · DAYNAME(). Example: MONTHNAME('2025-08-15') = 'August'; DAYNAME('2025-08-15') = 'Friday'.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: SELECT UPPER(Name), LENGTH(Name) FROM STUDENT WHERE RollNo = 3; → ZOYA, 4.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: SELECT LEFT('INFORMATICS', 4), RIGHT('INFORMATICS', 3), SUBSTR('INFORMATICS', 3, 4); → INFO, ICS, FORM.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting string positions at 0 (SQL starts at 1).
- Expecting ROUND(2.5) and similar edge cases to behave identically in every DBMS.
- LEFT/RIGHT, MID, MONTHNAME, DAYNAME are MySQL functions and may not exist in other DBMSs such as SQLite.

activity.prompt: Display each student's name in uppercase along with the first three letters of the name and the length of the name, for students of class 12A, ordered by RollNo. (Use UPPER, SUBSTR and LENGTH.)
activity.solution: SELECT UPPER(Name), SUBSTR(Name, 1, 3), LENGTH(Name) FROM STUDENT WHERE Class = '12A' ORDER BY RollNo;
activity.hint: SUBSTR(Name, 1, 3) takes 3 characters starting at position 1.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE STUDENT(RollNo INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name TEXT NOT NULL, Class TEXT, Marks INTEGER, City TEXT);INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(1,'Asha','12A',88,'Delhi');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(2,'Ravi','12B',72,'Pune');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(3,'Zoya','12A',95,'Delhi');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(4,'Kabir','12C',64,'Jaipur');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(5,'Meera','12B',81,'Pune');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(6,'Arjun','12A',NULL,'Agra');

quiz.why: MID(string, start, length) takes 3 characters starting at position 2 of SCIENCE: C, I, E, so CIE.
ROUND(45.678, 1) keeps one decimal place. Since the next digit is 7, it rounds up to 45.7.
MOD gives the remainder: 23 = 3 × 6 + 5, so the remainder is 5.
LENGTH counts every character, and the space counts too: SQL (3) + space (1) + Server (6) = 10.
INSTR gives the position of the first match, starting at 1. In B-A-N-A-N-A, the first N is at position 3.

lessons.title: Aggregate functions, GROUP BY and HAVING

scenes.text: The principal wants the highest marks in each section.
Aggregate functions summarise many rows.
GROUP BY makes one row per section.

steps.title: Aggregate (multi-row) functions
steps.body: MAX(), MIN(), AVG(), SUM(), COUNT(column), COUNT(*). Aggregates **ignore NULLs** except COUNT(*). COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique values.

steps.title: GROUP BY and HAVING
Solved example 1
steps.body: On STUDENT (Arjun's Marks NULL): COUNT(*) = 6; COUNT(Marks) = 5; SUM(Marks) = 400; MAX(Marks) = 95.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: SELECT City, COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT GROUP BY City HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2; → Delhi 2, Pune 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using an aggregate in WHERE (use HAVING).
- Selecting a non-grouped column with GROUP BY (not allowed in standard SQL).
- Forgetting that AVG ignores NULL (it is not counted as 0).

activity.prompt: For each Class, display Class, number of students, and highest Marks, sorted by Class.
activity.starter:
SELECT Class, COUNT(*), MAX(Marks)
FROM STUDENT
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
activity.solution: SELECT Class, COUNT(*), MAX(Marks) FROM STUDENT GROUP BY Class ORDER BY Class;
activity.hint: GROUP BY Class, then ORDER BY Class.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE STUDENT(RollNo INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name TEXT NOT NULL, Class TEXT, Marks INTEGER, City TEXT);INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(1,'Asha','12A',88,'Delhi');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(2,'Ravi','12B',72,'Pune');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(3,'Zoya','12A',95,'Delhi');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(4,'Kabir','12C',64,'Jaipur');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(5,'Meera','12B',81,'Pune');INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES(6,'Arjun','12A',NULL,'Agra');

quiz.q: Which counts all rows including NULLs?
quiz.why: COUNT(*) counts all rows, including those with NULLs, while COUNT(column) skips NULLs.
HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.
AVG ignores NULLs, so it averages 10 and 20: 30/2 = 15.

quiz.q: SUM, MAX, MIN, AVG, COUNT are:
quiz.why: SUM, MAX, MIN, AVG and COUNT take many rows and give a single value, so they are aggregate functions.
WHERE filters rows first, then GROUP BY groups the remaining ones, so WHERE is applied before grouping.

scenes.text: EMP has DeptID; DEPT has department names.
To show each employee with department name, join them.
Match rows on DeptID.

steps.title: Operations on relations
steps.body:
- **UNION:** rows in either table (duplicates removed) — tables must be union-compatible (same number and type of columns)
- **INTERSECT:** rows common to both
- **MINUS (EXCEPT):** rows in the first but not the second
- **Cartesian product:** every row of A with every row of B → degree = d₁ + d₂, cardinality = c₁ × c₂

steps.title: Joins
Solved example 1
steps.body: EMP has 5 rows and 4 columns; DEPT has 3 rows and 2 columns. Cartesian product: degree **6**, cardinality **15**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Department-wise total salary:
SELECT DName, SUM(Salary) FROM EMP E, DEPT D WHERE E.DeptID = D.DeptID GROUP BY DName; → HR 58000, IT 136000, Sales 97000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the join condition → Cartesian product with wrong, repeated rows.
- Ambiguous column names (DeptID) without table prefix in an equi-join.

activity.prompt: Display each employee's Name and their department name (DName) for employees earning more than 55000, sorted by Name.
activity.starter:
SELECT E.Name, D.DName
FROM EMP E, DEPT D
WHERE ... AND ...
ORDER BY E.Name;
activity.solution: SELECT E.Name, D.DName FROM EMP E, DEPT D WHERE E.DeptID = D.DeptID AND E.Salary > 55000 ORDER BY E.Name;
activity.hint: Join on E.DeptID = D.DeptID and add the salary condition with AND.

quiz.q: Cartesian product of tables with 4 and 3 rows has ___ rows.
quiz.why: The Cartesian product pairs every row of one table with every row of the other, so 4 × 3 = 12 rows.

quiz.q: Natural join shows the common column:
quiz.why: In a natural join the common column appears only once in the result.

quiz.q: Rows in A but not in B:
quiz.why: MINUS (set difference) gives rows present in A but not in B.
An equi-join joins tables on equality of values in columns, so it uses the = operator.

quiz.q: Degree of Cartesian product of tables with 3 and 2 columns:
quiz.why: The degree of a Cartesian product is the sum of the columns: 3 + 2 = 5.

questions.q: SQL command to remove all rows but keep structure:
questions.why: DELETE FROM T removes all rows but keeps the table structure. DROP TABLE would remove the table itself.

questions.q: Which is a DDL command?
questions.why: ALTER changes the structure of a table, so it is a DDL command. SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE work on data.

questions.q: Wildcard for exactly one character in LIKE:
questions.why: In LIKE, the underscore _ matches exactly one character, and % matches any number of characters.

questions.q: COUNT(Marks) ignores:
questions.why: COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values in that column.

questions.q: HAVING is used with:
questions.why: HAVING puts a condition on groups, so it is used together with GROUP BY.

questions.q: Assertion: A primary key column cannot have NULL values. Reason: A primary key must uniquely identify every row.
questions.why: Both are true. A primary key must identify each row uniquely, and a NULL value cannot identify anything, so NULLs are not allowed.

questions.q: On STUDENT (marks 88, 72, 95, 64, 81, NULL), SELECT AVG(Marks) gives:
questions.why: AVG ignores NULL. The five values sum to 400, so the average is 400/5 = 80.

questions.q: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT City) FROM STUDENT (Delhi, Pune, Delhi, Jaipur, Pune, Agra) →
questions.why: COUNT(DISTINCT City) counts different non-NULL cities: Delhi, Pune, Jaipur and Agra, which is 4.

questions.q: UCASE(MID('database', 5, 4)) returns:
questions.why: MID('database', 5, 4) takes 4 characters from position 5: b, a, s, e, giving 'base'. UCASE makes it BASE.

questions.q: Output of SELECT ROUND(1234.567, -2);
questions.why: A negative second argument rounds to the left of the decimal point. ROUND(1234.567, −2) rounds to the nearest hundred, giving 1200.

questions.q: Query to find classes having more than 2 students:
options: SELECT Class FROM STUDENT GROUP BY Class HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
SELECT Class FROM STUDENT WHERE COUNT(*) > 2;
SELECT Class FROM STUDENT HAVING Class > 2;
questions.why: Group the rows by class and then filter groups with HAVING COUNT(*) > 2. WHERE cannot use aggregate functions.

questions.q: EMP(5 rows, 4 cols) × DEPT(3 rows, 2 cols): degree and cardinality:
questions.why: Degree is 4 + 2 = 6 (columns add up). Cardinality is 5 × 3 = 15 (rows multiply).

questions.q: Which query gives employees with no department assigned (DeptID missing)?
options: SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE DeptID IS NULL;
SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE DeptID = NULL;
questions.why: NULL cannot be tested with = or by comparing with 0. Use DeptID IS NULL to find missing values.

questions.q: Case: SELECT Class, MAX(Marks) FROM STUDENT WHERE City <> 'Delhi' GROUP BY Class HAVING MAX(Marks) > 70; on the sample table returns:
questions.why: Non-Delhi rows: Ravi 12B 72, Kabir 12C 64, Meera 12B 81, Arjun 12A NULL. 12B max 81 > 70; 12C 64 fails; 12A max NULL fails.

questions.q: MONTHNAME('2024-03-15') in MySQL returns:
questions.why: MONTHNAME returns the full name of the month, so for 15 March it returns March.

questions.q: Which is NOT an aggregate function?
questions.why: UPPER() works on each value separately (a single-row function). AVG, SUM and COUNT are aggregate functions.

questions.q: ALTER TABLE STUDENT DROP Email; removes:
options: Email values only in one row
questions.why: ALTER TABLE ... DROP removes the named column, here Email, from the table structure and all its data.

courses.title: Interface Python with SQL
courses.summary: Connecting a Python program to a MySQL database with mysql.connector: connect(), cursor(), execute(), fetchone()/fetchmany()/fetchall(), rowcount, commit(), and parameterised queries using %s and format() — with practice on a built-in stand-in cursor that runs in the browser.
outcomes: Learners can write the steps to connect Python with MySQL
Learners can execute queries and fetch results with fetchone, fetchmany and fetchall
Learners can use rowcount and commit correctly
Learners can write safe parameterised queries and complete menu-driven programs

scenes.text: The school wants a Python app that reads marks from MySQL.
First, the app must connect to the database server.
It needs host, user, password and database name.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. Install the connector (pip install mysql-connector-python) and import it: import mysql.connector as mc
2. Create a connection: con = mc.connect(host="localhost", user="root", passwd="your_password", database="school")
3. Check: con.is_connected() → True
4. Create a cursor: cur = con.cursor()
5. Execute SQL: cur.execute("SELECT * FROM STUDENT")
6. Fetch / commit as needed
7. Close: con.close()

steps.title: Key objects
steps.body: **Connection object** — represents the session with the database. **Cursor object** — executes queries and holds results (result set). **Result set** — rows returned by a SELECT.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
import mysql.connector as mc
con = mc.connect(host="localhost", user="root", passwd="tiger", database="school")
if con.is_connected():
    print("Connected")

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: The module may be imported with alias; "passwd" and "password" are both accepted keyword names for the password in mysql.connector.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to create a cursor before execute().
- Hard-coding real passwords in shared code.
- Not closing the connection.

activity.prompt: Arrange the steps of connecting Python with MySQL
items: import mysql.connector
Create connection with connect(host, user, passwd, database)
Create a cursor with con.cursor()
Execute a query with cur.execute()
Fetch results (or commit for DML)
Close the connection

quiz.why: connect() of mysql.connector creates the connection to the database. cursor() is called on the connection.

quiz.q: Object used to execute SQL queries:
quiz.why: A cursor object is created from the connection and is used to execute SQL queries and fetch results.
is_connected() returns True if the connection is open and False otherwise.
The module mysql.connector is commonly used to connect Python to MySQL. csv, math and pickle do other jobs.

quiz.why: The rows returned by a SELECT query are called the result set.

steps.title: Fetch methods
steps.body:
- **fetchone()** — next row as a tuple, or None when no rows remain
- **fetchmany(n)** — list of the next n rows (fewer if not enough)
- **fetchall()** — list of all remaining rows
- **rowcount** — for SELECT, number of rows fetched so far; for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, number of rows affected

steps.body:

r = cur.fetchone()      # (1, "Asha", "12A", 88)
rows = cur.fetchmany(2) # next 2 rows
print(cur.rowcount)     # 3
rest = cur.fetchall()   # remaining rows
print(cur.rowcount)     # 4

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting fetchall() to return all rows again after some were fetched — it returns only the remaining ones.
- Treating a fetched row as a list and trying to modify it — it is a tuple.

activity.starter:
class FakeCursor:
    """Stands in for a MySQL cursor so this runs in the browser."""
    def __init__(self, rows):
        self._rows = list(rows)
        self.rowcount = 0
    def execute(self, query, params=None):
        self.last = query if params is None else query % tuple(repr(p) for p in params)
        self._pos = 0
    def fetchone(self):
        if self._pos < len(self._rows):
            self._pos += 1
            self.rowcount = self._pos
            return self._rows[self._pos - 1]
        return None
    def fetchall(self):
        rest = self._rows[self._pos:]
        self._pos = len(self._rows)
        self.rowcount = self._pos
        return rest
    def fetchmany(self, n):
        rest = self._rows[self._pos:self._pos + n]
        self._pos += len(rest)
        self.rowcount = self._pos
        return rest

steps.title: Two styles
steps.body:
**%s placeholders (recommended):**
q = "SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks > %s AND Class = %s"
cur.execute(q, (75, "12A"))
**format():**
q = "SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks > {} AND Class = '{}'".format(75, "12A")
cur.execute(q)
Placeholders let the connector quote values safely (protecting against SQL injection).

steps.title: commit()
steps.body: After **INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE**, call **con.commit()** to make changes permanent. Without commit, changes may be lost when the connection closes. (SELECT needs no commit.)

con.commit()
print(cur.rowcount, "record inserted")

con.commit()

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting commit() after DML.
- Passing a single value as (5) instead of the tuple (5,).
- Building queries by string concatenation with raw user input (unsafe).

courses.title: Ch 10 · Computer Networks
courses.summary: Introduction and evolution of networking, types of networks (PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN), network devices, topologies, identifying nodes with MAC and IP addresses, and the Internet, WWW and DNS — with Python activities that validate IP and MAC addresses and parse URLs.
outcomes: Learners can describe the evolution of networking and the Internet
Learners can classify networks by area
Learners can explain the role of each network device
Learners can compare network topologies
Learners can explain MAC and IP addresses, WWW, URLs and DNS

scenes.text: The computer lab shares one printer and the Internet.
All computers are linked — a network.
The same idea, scaled up, is the Internet.

steps.title: What is a computer network?
steps.body: A **computer network** is an interconnection of two or more computing devices (nodes/hosts) that can share data and resources (printers, Internet connection, files). Benefits: resource sharing, communication (email, chat), centralised data, cost saving, reliability.

steps.title: Evolution (key milestones)
steps.body:
- **1969:** ARPANET — a network funded by the US Department of Defense, connecting a few university computers
- **1971:** first network email sent (Ray Tomlinson)
- **1983:** ARPANET adopts the TCP/IP protocol suite
- **1986:** NSFNET — backbone linking universities (USA)
- **1989–1991:** World Wide Web proposed and released by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN
- 1990s onward: commercial Internet spreads worldwide

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A school lab with 30 PCs sharing one printer → **resource sharing**; teachers sending circulars by email → **communication**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Difference between the Internet and WWW: the **Internet** is the global network of networks (infrastructure); the **WWW** is a service on it — linked web pages accessed with HTTP.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating "Internet" and "WWW" as the same thing.
- Dating WWW to 1969 (that is ARPANET).

activity.prompt: Arrange the networking milestones in order

quiz.why: ARPANET, the forerunner of the Internet, began in 1969.
Tim Berners-Lee created the World Wide Web in 1989–1991.
A computer network lets devices share resources such as files, printers and an Internet connection.
The Internet is a global network of interconnected networks.

quiz.q: Each device in a network is called a:
quiz.why: Each device connected in a network, such as a computer or printer, is a node.

scenes.text: Your phone connects to wireless earbuds.
Your school computers share a printer.
Bank branches across India share one database.

steps.title: By geographical area
steps.body:
- **PAN (Personal Area Network):** devices of one person within a few metres — phone, earbuds, smartwatch (Bluetooth, USB)
- **LAN (Local Area Network):** a room, building or campus; high speed; owned by one organisation (Ethernet, Wi-Fi)
- **MAN (Metropolitan Area Network):** a city — e.g. cable TV network, city-wide Wi-Fi
- **WAN (Wide Area Network):** across cities/countries — the Internet is the largest WAN; bank networks

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A company connects its Delhi and Chennai offices → **WAN**. The Delhi office floor network → **LAN**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Smartphone hotspot shared with your own laptop → **PAN**. A city's traffic-camera network → **MAN**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Calling a campus network a MAN — a campus is usually a LAN.

activity.prompt: Classify the network

quiz.why: The Internet connects networks across the world, so it is the largest WAN.
A LAN (local area network) covers a small area such as one building or campus.
A MAN (metropolitan area network) covers a city, larger than a LAN and smaller than a WAN.
Earbuds linked to a phone cover only a person's own small space, a few metres around, which is a Personal Area Network (PAN).

quiz.q: LANs usually have ___ speed than WANs.
quiz.why: LANs cover a small area with short, good-quality cables, so they usually give higher speed than WANs, which cross long distances.

story.title: Who does what in the network?

scenes.text: A modem connects home to the ISP.
A switch connects lab computers.
A router finds the path to other networks.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Modem** (modulator–demodulator): converts digital signals to analog and back for transmission over telephone/cable lines
- **Ethernet card / NIC:** connects a computer to a network; has a unique **MAC address**
- **RJ45:** 8-pin connector used with twisted-pair Ethernet cables
- **Repeater:** regenerates weakened signals to extend distance (Ethernet twisted-pair segments are limited to about 100 m)
- **Hub:** connects devices; **broadcasts** incoming data to all ports
- **Switch:** connects devices; sends data only to the **intended** port (using MAC addresses) — fewer collisions
- **Router:** connects **different networks**, forwards packets using IP addresses, finds the best path
- **Gateway:** entry/exit point that connects dissimilar networks (often a router with protocol conversion)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Lab computers are slow because every frame goes to every computer → replace the **hub** with a **switch**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Two buildings 250 m apart connected by Ethernet cable show weak signals → add a **repeater** (or switch) in between.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a switch broadcasts like a hub.
- Confusing modem (signal conversion) with router (path selection).

activity.prompt: Match the device to its job
pairs: Forwards data to the intended device only
Connects different networks and selects paths

quiz.q: Device that sends data only to the destination port:
quiz.why: A switch learns which device is on which port and forwards data only to the destination port. A hub copies data to every port.

quiz.q: MAC address is stored in the:
quiz.why: The MAC address is built into the Network Interface Card (NIC) by the manufacturer.

quiz.q: Device that connects two different networks:
quiz.why: A router joins different networks and forwards data between them, for example a home LAN to the Internet.
Modulation turns digital data into an analog signal for transmission over lines such as telephone cables. Demodulation does the reverse.
Signals weaken over long cables. A repeater receives the weak signal and regenerates it, so it can travel further.

scenes.text: In the lab, every PC connects to a central switch.
Old offices used one long cable for all.
Critical systems link every node to every other.

steps.title: Topologies
steps.body:
- **Bus:** all nodes on a single backbone cable; cheap, easy to extend; one cable break stops the network; terminators at both ends
- **Star:** all nodes connect to a central hub/switch; easy to install and troubleshoot; central device failure stops the network; most common in LANs
- **Ring:** each node connects to two neighbours, forming a loop; data travels in one direction
- **Mesh:** each node connects to every other; highly reliable (multiple paths); expensive — links = n(n − 1)/2
- **Tree (hierarchical):** star networks connected via a bus/backbone; easy expansion

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A mesh network of 6 computers needs 6 × 5 / 2 = **15** cables.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A school wants easy fault isolation and to add PCs anytime → **star** topology with a switch.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying failure of one node stops a star network — only the central device's failure does.

quiz.why: In a star topology every node is connected to a central device such as a switch or hub.

lessons.title: Identifying nodes: MAC and IP addresses

scenes.text: Your NIC has a permanent MAC address from the factory.
Your network gives you an IP address, like a postal address.
Data finds you using both.

steps.title: MAC address
steps.body: **Media Access Control** address — a **48-bit** (6-byte) physical address burned into the NIC, written as 12 hexadecimal digits in pairs, e.g. **FC:F8:AE:CE:7B:16**. The first 6 digits identify the manufacturer (OUI); the last 6 identify the card. Usually permanent.

steps.title: IP address
steps.body:
**Internet Protocol** address — a logical address assigned to a device on a network; it can change.
**IPv4:** 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers (octets) 0–255 separated by dots, e.g. 192.168.0.178.
**IPv6:** 128 bits, written in hexadecimal groups separated by colons — created because IPv4 addresses were running out.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Which changes when a laptop moves from home Wi-Fi to school Wi-Fi? → the **IP address** (MAC stays the same).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying MAC is 32-bit (IPv4 is 32-bit; MAC is 48-bit).
- Allowing values above 255 in an IPv4 octet.

activity.prompt: Read lines until "END". For each line print "Valid" if it is a valid IPv4 address (exactly 4 parts, each an integer 0–255 with digits only), else "Invalid".
activity.solution:
while True:
    line = input()
    if line == "END":
        break
    parts = line.split(".")
    ok = len(parts) == 4 and all(p.isdigit() and 0 <= int(p) <= 255 for p in parts)
    print("Valid" if ok else "Invalid")
activity.hint: Split on ".", require 4 parts, each isdigit() and within 0–255.

quiz.why: A MAC address is 48 bits long, usually written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits.
IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255. IPv6 uses 128 bits.

quiz.q: Which is a valid IPv4 address?
quiz.why: A valid IPv4 address has four numbers, each from 0 to 255. 172.16.254.1 fits; 300 is too big, and the others have the wrong count of numbers.

quiz.q: Address that usually changes when you change networks:
quiz.why: The IP address depends on the network you join and normally changes when you move to another network. The MAC address is fixed in the hardware.
IPv4 has only about 4.3 billion addresses, which were running out as devices multiplied. IPv6 has a much larger 128-bit address space.

scenes.text: You type www.example.com in a browser.
DNS looks up its IP address.
The browser fetches the page with HTTP/HTTPS.

steps.title: WWW building blocks
steps.body:
- **HTML:** language to create web pages
- **URI/URL:** unique address of a resource, e.g. https://www.example.com/docs/index.html — protocol (https), domain name (www.example.com), path (/docs/index.html)
- **HTTP/HTTPS:** protocol for transferring web pages (HTTPS = encrypted)

steps.title: Domain names and DNS
steps.body: **Domain name:** human-friendly name for an IP address. Top-level domains: .com, .org, .edu, .gov, country codes .in, .uk. **DNS (Domain Name System)** translates domain names into IP addresses using a hierarchy of DNS servers (root servers, TLD servers, authoritative servers). Your device first checks its cache, then asks a resolver (often your ISP's).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: In https://www.ncert.nic.in/textbook.php → protocol **https**, domain **www.ncert.nic.in**, top-level domain **.in**, path **/textbook.php**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Typing an IP address directly into the browser can bypass DNS; typing a name needs DNS resolution first.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling DNS a browser.
- Thinking the URL's domain and the IP address are the same thing — DNS maps one to the other.

activity.prompt: Read a URL of the form protocol://domain/path (path may be missing). Print the protocol, the domain, the top-level domain (text after the last dot of the domain) and the path ("/" if missing), one per line.
activity.starter:
url = input()
# split into parts
activity.solution:
url = input()
protocol, rest = url.split("://", 1)
if "/" in rest:
    domain, path = rest.split("/", 1)
    path = "/" + path
else:
    domain, path = rest, "/"
print(protocol)
print(domain)
print(domain.split(".")[-1])
print(path)
activity.hint: Split once on "://", then once on the first "/".

quiz.why: The Domain Name System (DNS) translates domain names such as www.school.edu into IP addresses.
In a URL, the part before :// is the protocol, here https. www is the subdomain, and edu is the top-level domain.

quiz.q: Language used to create web pages:
quiz.why: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the language used to build web pages. SQL and Python do other jobs, and SMTP is a mail protocol.
.in is the top-level domain for India, a country-code domain. .com or .org are generic domains.

options: A service of linked web pages on the Internet
quiz.why: The World Wide Web is a service of linked web pages that runs on the Internet. The Internet is the underlying network.

questions.q: ARPANET started in:
questions.why: ARPANET, the forerunner of the Internet, began in 1969.

questions.q: Network spanning countries:
questions.why: A Wide Area Network (WAN) covers large areas such as countries or continents. LAN, MAN and PAN are smaller.

questions.q: Device converting digital to analog signals:
questions.why: A modem modulates digital data to analog for sending over lines and demodulates the incoming analog signal back to digital.

questions.q: An IPv4 address has ___ bits.
questions.why: An IPv4 address is 32 bits long, usually written as four decimal numbers.

questions.q: Hub vs switch: hub ___ data.
questions.why: A hub has no intelligence and broadcasts incoming data to all ports. A switch sends it only to the destination port.

questions.q: Assertion: Star topology is easy to troubleshoot. Reason: Each node has its own cable to the central device, so faults are isolated.
questions.why: Both are true. In a star, each node has its own cable to the central device, so a fault can be isolated to one cable or node, making troubleshooting easy.

questions.q: Cables for a full mesh of 8 nodes:
questions.why: A full mesh of n nodes needs n(n − 1)/2 cables. For 8 nodes that is 8 × 7/2 = 28.

questions.q: Which is a valid MAC address format?
questions.why: A MAC address has 48 bits, written as six pairs of hex digits separated by colons or hyphens, like 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E.

questions.q: A device that regenerates signals over long cable runs:
questions.why: A repeater receives a weakened signal and regenerates it, so it can travel on over longer cable runs.

questions.q: Case: A company with offices in 3 cities wants to connect them and to the Internet. Device to connect each office LAN to the outside network:
questions.why: A router (or gateway) joins each office LAN to other networks and the Internet, forwarding packets between them. A hub or repeater cannot route between networks.

questions.q: Case: In a school lab, all PCs stop working when one central device fails. Topology:
questions.why: When every PC fails together because one central device fails, all nodes are connected to that device, which is a star topology. A mesh or ring would have other paths.

questions.q: In https://mail.example.co.in/inbox, the top-level domain is:
questions.why: In the domain name mail.example.co.in the last part, .in, is the top-level domain. co is the second-level domain.

questions.q: Case: Two buildings 150 m apart must be linked by Ethernet twisted-pair cable. Suggest:
options: Use a repeater/switch in between (or fibre)
questions.why: Twisted-pair Ethernet is limited to about 100 m per segment, so 150 m needs a repeater or switch in between, or fibre. A hub alone would not extend the range.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: A MAC address is a physical 48-bit hardware address. An IP address is a logical network address, 32 bits in IPv4. The other pairs are wrong.

questions.q: Who proposed the WWW?
questions.why: Tim Berners-Lee proposed and created the World Wide Web.

questions.q: Connector used with Ethernet twisted-pair cables:
questions.why: Ethernet twisted-pair cables end in RJ45 connectors. RJ11 is for telephone lines.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Data Communication
courses.summary: Components of data communication, measuring capacity (bandwidth and data transfer rate), simplex/half-duplex/full-duplex communication, circuit and packet switching, guided and unguided transmission media, mobile telecommunication generations and network protocols — with Python activities on data rates and packetisation.
outcomes: Learners can name the components of data communication
Learners can compute transfer time from size and data rate
Learners can classify communication modes and switching techniques
Learners can compare transmission media
Learners can match protocols to their uses and describe mobile generations

scenes.text: Riya sends a 4 MB photo to her friend.
Her connection speed decides how long it takes.
Bits ÷ bits-per-second = seconds.

steps.title: Components
steps.body: **Sender** · **Receiver** · **Message** (data) · **Communication media** (wired/wireless path) · **Protocols** (rules for communication).

steps.title: Measuring capacity
steps.body:
**Bandwidth:** range of frequencies a channel can carry, measured in hertz (Hz, kHz, MHz, GHz); higher bandwidth → more data.
**Data transfer rate:** number of bits sent per second — bps, Kbps, Mbps, Gbps, Tbps.
1 byte = 8 bits. Time = data size in bits ÷ data rate in bps.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A 4 MB file over a 16 Mbps link (taking 1 MB = 8 megabits): 4 × 8 = 32 megabits ÷ 16 Mbps = **2 seconds**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A 1,000-byte message at 2,000 bps → 8,000 bits ÷ 2,000 = **4 seconds**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to convert bytes (B) to bits (b) — multiply by 8.
- Mixing MB (megabytes) with Mb (megabits).

activity.prompt: Read file size in megabytes (MB) and link speed in megabits per second (Mbps), one per line. Taking 1 byte = 8 bits, print the transfer time in seconds rounded to 2 decimals.
activity.starter:
size_mb = float(input())
speed_mbps = float(input())
# time = bits / rate
activity.solution:
size_mb = float(input())
speed_mbps = float(input())
print(round(size_mb * 8 / speed_mbps, 2))
activity.hint: Megabytes × 8 = megabits; divide by Mbps.

quiz.why: Protocols are the agreed rules that govern how devices communicate and exchange data.
Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a channel can carry, so it is measured in hertz (Hz).

quiz.q: Data transfer rate is measured in:
quiz.why: The data transfer rate is how many bits are sent per second, measured in bits per second (bps).
A byte is made of 8 bits.

quiz.q: Time to send 16,000 bits at 4,000 bps:
quiz.why: Time = data ÷ rate = 16,000 bits ÷ 4,000 bps = 4 seconds.

scenes.text: Radio broadcast: only one direction.
Walkie-talkie: both ways, but one at a time ("over").
Phone call: both talk at once.

steps.title: Modes of communication
steps.body:
- **Simplex:** one direction only — radio/TV broadcast, keyboard to computer
- **Half-duplex:** both directions, but **one at a time** — walkie-talkie
- **Full-duplex:** both directions **simultaneously** — telephone/mobile call

steps.title: Switching techniques
steps.body:
**Circuit switching:** a dedicated path is set up before communication and kept for the whole session (traditional telephone calls). Reliable order, but wastes capacity when idle.
**Packet switching:** data is broken into **packets** (with headers: source, destination, sequence number) that travel independently by possibly different routes and are reassembled at the destination (Internet). Efficient use of links.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A message of 1,050 bytes sent in packets of at most 500 bytes → **3 packets** (500, 500, 50).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Packets with sequence numbers 3, 1, 2 arrive out of order → the receiver **reorders** them by sequence number to rebuild the message.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling walkie-talkie full-duplex.
- Thinking packets must follow the same route.

activity.prompt: Packet switching simulation: first line a message; second line packet size k (characters). Split the message into packets of k characters, then print the packets in REVERSE order as "seq:data" (seq starting at 1) to show they may arrive out of order; finally print the reassembled message obtained by sorting by seq.
activity.starter:
msg = input()
k = int(input())
# make packets, show arrival in reverse, reassemble
activity.solution:
msg = input()
k = int(input())
packets = [(i // k + 1, msg[i:i + k]) for i in range(0, len(msg), k)]
arrived = packets[::-1]
for seq, data in arrived:
    print(f"{seq}:{data}")
print("".join(data for seq, data in sorted(arrived)))
activity.hint: Build (seq, chunk) tuples with slicing; sorting tuples orders them by seq.

quiz.why: In half-duplex both sides can send and receive, but not at the same time. A walkie-talkie works this way, with one speaking while the other listens.
Television broadcast goes only one way, from station to viewers, which is simplex.
The Internet breaks data into packets that share links and travel independently, which is packet switching.

quiz.q: Dedicated path for the whole call:
quiz.why: In circuit switching a dedicated path is reserved between the two ends for the whole call, like old telephone calls.
Packets may arrive in any order, so each carries a sequence number, and the receiver uses them to put the message back in order.

scenes.text: LAN cables are twisted copper pairs.
Undersea cables carry light in glass fibres.
Phones use radio waves through the air.

steps.title: Guided (wired) media
steps.body:
- **Twisted pair:** two insulated copper wires twisted together; UTP (unshielded) and STP (shielded); cheap, used in LANs/telephones; susceptible to interference
- **Coaxial cable:** copper core, insulation, braided shield; better shielding and bandwidth than twisted pair; cable TV
- **Optical fibre:** glass/plastic core carrying **light** by total internal reflection; very high bandwidth, long distances, immune to electromagnetic interference; costly and fragile

steps.title: Unguided (wireless) media
steps.body:
- **Radio waves** (about 3 kHz–1 GHz): omnidirectional, penetrate walls — FM, AM, mobile
- **Microwaves** (about 1–300 GHz): line of sight, directional; terrestrial towers and satellites
- **Infrared** (about 300 GHz–400 THz): very short range, cannot pass through walls — TV remotes
Also **Bluetooth** (short-range radio, PANs) and **WLAN/Wi-Fi**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Connecting two buildings 2 km apart with high bandwidth and no interference from nearby machines → **optical fibre**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A TV remote does not work from another room → **infrared** cannot pass through walls.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying optical fibre carries electrical signals (it carries light).
- Saying microwaves pass around obstacles like radio — they need line of sight.

activity.prompt: Guided or unguided medium?

quiz.why: Optical fibre carries light, not electricity, so electromagnetic interference does not affect it.
TV remote controls send signals as infrared light over short, direct distances.
Microwave links need a clear straight path (line of sight) between the transmitting and receiving antennas.
Cable TV usually uses coaxial cable, which carries many channels with good shielding.
Optical fibre sends data as pulses of light through thin glass or plastic strands.

scenes.text: 1G phones carried voice only, in analog form.
2G added SMS; 3G brought mobile internet.
4G streams video; 5G targets ultra-fast, low-latency links.

steps.title: Mobile generations
steps.body:
- **1G:** analog voice (1980s)
- **2G:** digital voice, SMS/MMS (GSM, CDMA)
- **3G:** mobile Internet, video calls
- **4G:** high-speed all-IP data (LTE), HD streaming
- **5G:** very high speed, very low latency, massive device connections (IoT)

steps.title: Protocols
steps.body:
- **HTTP / HTTPS:** web pages (HTTPS encrypted with TLS/SSL)
- **FTP:** file transfer
- **SMTP:** sending email · **POP3** (and IMAP): receiving email
- **TCP/IP:** core Internet protocol suite (TCP: reliable delivery; IP: addressing and routing)
- **PPP:** Point-to-Point Protocol (direct link, e.g. dial-up)
- **TELNET:** remote login (unencrypted)
- **VoIP:** voice calls over the Internet

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Uploading a website's files to a server → **FTP**. Sending an email from your app → **SMTP**; downloading it to your mail client → **POP3**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Making a WhatsApp/Internet voice call → **VoIP**. Logging into a remote server's command line (old method) → **TELNET**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying POP3 sends email (it receives).
- Calling HTTPS a different web — it is HTTP over an encrypted connection.

activity.prompt: Read lines until "END". Each line is a task; print the protocol: "send email"→SMTP, "receive email"→POP3, "web page"→HTTP, "secure web page"→HTTPS, "file transfer"→FTP, "internet call"→VoIP, "remote login"→TELNET; anything else → "Unknown".

tests.stdin:
send email
file transfer
secure web page
video game
END

activity.hint: A dictionary lookup with get(key, "Unknown").

quiz.why: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is used to send email. POP3 is used to receive it.

quiz.q: Protocol for receiving email to a client:
quiz.why: POP3 (Post Office Protocol) downloads email from the mail server to a client. SMTP is for sending.
Text messaging (SMS) arrived with 2G digital mobile networks. 1G was analog voice only.
Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) carries voice calls as packets over the Internet.
HTTPS is HTTP with SSL/TLS encryption, so it protects data on the web. HTTP, FTP and TELNET send data in plain text.

questions.q: Rules for communication are called:
questions.why: A protocol is the set of rules governing how data is communicated between devices.

questions.q: Telephone conversation is:
questions.why: On a telephone both people can talk and listen at the same time, which is full-duplex.

questions.q: Light-based guided medium:
questions.why: Optical fibre transmits data using light, so it is a light-based guided medium.

questions.q: Bandwidth is measured in:
questions.why: Bandwidth is a range of frequencies, so it is measured in hertz (Hz). bps measures the data rate.

questions.q: Protocol used to transfer files:
questions.why: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is used for transferring files between computers.

questions.q: Assertion: Packet switching uses links more efficiently than circuit switching. Reason: Links are shared among many packets instead of being reserved for one session.
questions.why: Both are true. In packet switching, links are shared by many packets, not reserved for one session, so unused capacity is not wasted.

questions.q: Time to send a 2 MB file at 8 Mbps (1 byte = 8 bits):
questions.why: 2 MB = 2 × 8 = 16 Mb. Time = 16 Mb ÷ 8 Mbps = 2 s.

questions.q: Which medium needs line of sight?
questions.why: Microwaves travel in straight lines, so the sender and receiver must see each other (line of sight). Radio waves can bend and reflect.

questions.q: A 2,600-byte message in packets of 1,000 bytes needs:
questions.why: 2,600 ÷ 1,000 = 2.6, so 2 full packets and one partly filled packet are needed: 3 packets.

questions.q: Case: Connect two campus blocks 1.5 km apart with high speed and immunity to interference from heavy machinery:
questions.why: Optical fibre gives high speed over 1.5 km and is not affected by electrical interference from machinery. UTP is limited to about 100 m and is affected by noise.

questions.q: Case: Uploading website files to a hosting server from a desktop client uses:
questions.why: FTP is used to upload or download files between a client and a server, such as web files to a host. SMTP and POP3 are for email.

questions.q: Case: An app needs very low latency for remote-controlled machines and many IoT sensors. Generation best suited:
questions.why: 5G offers very low latency and can connect huge numbers of devices, which suits remote-controlled machines and many IoT sensors.

questions.q: A 1,000-byte file over a 500 bps link takes:
Which pair is correct?
options: SMTP — sending mail; POP3 — receiving mail
questions.why: SMTP sends email and POP3 receives it. FTP is for file transfer, not web pages, and TELNET is for remote login, not encryption.

questions.q: Keyboard to computer communication is:
questions.why: A keyboard only sends data to the computer, never the other way, so it is one-way (simplex).

questions.q: Shielded twisted pair is abbreviated:
questions.why: Shielded twisted pair is STP. UTP is unshielded twisted pair.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Security Aspects
courses.summary: Malware — virus, worm, ransomware, Trojan, spyware, adware, keylogger — and how it spreads; antivirus and safe practices; spam; HTTP vs HTTPS; firewalls; cookies; hackers and crackers; network threats such as DoS/DDoS, snooping and eavesdropping — with Python activities on password strength and encryption basics.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish types of malware and how they spread
Learners can explain antivirus methods and safe practices
Learners can explain HTTPS, firewalls and cookies
Learners can describe hacking, DoS/DDoS, snooping and eavesdropping
Learners can write simple programs that check password strength and encrypt text

scenes.text: Aman downloads a "free" game from an unknown site.
Next morning his files are locked with a ransom note.
He learns about malware the hard way.

steps.title: Types of malware
steps.body:
- **Virus:** attaches itself to a file/program; spreads when the infected file is run or shared (needs a host and usually human action)
- **Worm:** standalone, **self-replicates** across networks without human action; consumes bandwidth
- **Ransomware:** encrypts or locks data and demands payment (e.g. the 2017 WannaCry attack)
- **Trojan:** appears legitimate but performs hidden harmful actions; does not self-replicate
- **Spyware:** secretly collects information (browsing, credentials)
- **Adware:** shows unwanted advertisements; may track behaviour
- **Keylogger:** records keystrokes (software or hardware) to steal passwords — on-screen keyboards reduce the risk

steps.title: How malware spreads
steps.body: Downloads from untrusted sites · email attachments and spam links · removable storage (pen drives) · network propagation (worms) · pirated software.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A program that spreads by itself to every computer on the office network overnight → **worm**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A "free PDF converter" that secretly opens a back door to the attacker → **Trojan**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every malware a "virus".
- Thinking a Trojan replicates like a worm.

steps.title: Stay safe
steps.body: Never pay a ransom without advice; keep backups; report cyber crime at the national portal cybercrime.gov.in or helpline 1930 (India).

activity.prompt: Match the malware to its behaviour
pairs: Attaches to files; spreads when they run
Looks legitimate but hides harmful code

quiz.q: Malware that self-replicates over networks without a host file:
quiz.why: A worm copies itself across networks on its own and does not need a host file or a user action. A virus must attach to a host file.
A Trojan pretends to be useful software but carries hidden harmful code.
WannaCry in 2017 was ransomware: it locked users' files and demanded payment.

quiz.q: A defence against keyloggers for passwords:
quiz.why: An on-screen keyboard avoids typing on the physical keyboard, so a keylogger that records keystrokes cannot capture the password.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a common way malware spreads?
quiz.why: Malware spreads through digital means such as pirated software, email attachments and pen drives, not by reading a printed newspaper.

scenes.text: Aman installs an antivirus and updates it.
He learns to ignore "You won a lottery!" emails.
His laptop stays clean.

steps.title: Antivirus
steps.body: Software that detects and removes malware. Methods: **signature-based** detection (matching known malware patterns), **sandbox** detection (running suspicious programs in an isolated environment), **heuristic/behaviour-based** detection (spotting suspicious behaviour), **data-mining/machine-learning** techniques. Must be **updated** regularly.

steps.title: Spam
steps.body: Unsolicited bulk messages (usually email) — advertising, scams, phishing links. Use spam filters; never click unknown links; never share OTPs or passwords.

steps.title: Safe practices
steps.body: Use licensed software and keep it updated; use strong, unique passwords and two-factor authentication; scan pen drives; back up data; avoid public Wi-Fi for banking; check URLs before entering credentials.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: An antivirus catches a file because its pattern matches a known malware sample → **signature-based** detection.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: An email says "Your bank account is blocked — click here and enter your PIN" → **phishing spam**; delete it and contact the bank officially.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Believing antivirus alone makes you fully safe — safe habits matter.

activity.prompt: Password checker: read passwords until "END". A password is "Strong" if it has length ≥ 8 and contains at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit and one special character (not a letter or digit); otherwise print "Weak". Print the verdict for each.
activity.solution:
while True:
    p = input()
    if p == "END":
        break
    ok = (len(p) >= 8 and any(c.isupper() for c in p) and any(c.islower() for c in p)
          and any(c.isdigit() for c in p) and any(not c.isalnum() for c in p))
    print("Strong" if ok else "Weak")
activity.hint: Use any() with str methods isupper, islower, isdigit and isalnum.

quiz.why: Signature-based detection compares files with stored patterns (signatures) of known malware.
Unwanted bulk email sent to many people is spam.
New malware appears every day, so antivirus software needs regular updates to recognise it.
A strong password mixes upper and lower case letters, digits and symbols, and is not based on your name or birthday, so it is hard to guess.

quiz.q: Running a suspicious program in an isolated environment:
quiz.why: Running a suspect program in an isolated environment to watch its behaviour is sandbox detection.

scenes.text: The browser shows a padlock on the bank site.
The office network has a firewall.
A shopping site remembers your cart with cookies.

steps.title: HTTP vs HTTPS
steps.body: **HTTP** sends data in plain text — anyone intercepting can read it. **HTTPS** encrypts data using **SSL/TLS**, verifies the website with a digital certificate, and shows a padlock. Use HTTPS for logins and payments.

steps.title: Firewall
steps.body: A hardware or software system that monitors and filters incoming and outgoing network traffic according to security rules. **Network firewall** protects a whole network (at the router/gateway); **host-based firewall** runs on a single computer.

steps.title: Cookies
steps.body: Small text files stored by websites in the browser to remember preferences, sessions and carts. **First-party cookies** come from the site you visit; **third-party cookies** come from other domains (often advertisers) and raise privacy concerns. They can be cleared/blocked in browser settings.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Simple shift cipher (Caesar) shows the idea of encryption: shift each letter by 3 → "HELLO" becomes "KHOOR". Real HTTPS uses far stronger mathematics.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A school blocks gaming sites and unknown incoming connections at its gateway → **network firewall**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking cookies are viruses — they are data files, though they can be misused for tracking.
- Thinking HTTPS means the site is honest — it means the connection is encrypted.

activity.prompt: Caesar cipher: read a shift k and a message (two lines). Shift each letter by k positions (wrap around the alphabet, keep case); leave other characters unchanged. Print the encrypted text, then decrypt it back and print the original.
activity.starter:
k = int(input())
msg = input()
# write encrypt(text, k) and use encrypt(text, -k) to decrypt
activity.hint: Use ord/chr with % 26 to wrap around; decrypt by shifting with −k.

quiz.why: HTTPS encrypts data between browser and server using SSL/TLS, so it cannot be easily read on the way.
A firewall checks network traffic against a set of rules and blocks or allows it, protecting a network from unauthorised access.

options: Small text files stored by websites
quiz.why: Cookies are small text files that websites store on your device to remember information about you.

options: Domains other than the site visited
quiz.why: Third-party cookies are set by domains other than the site you are visiting, often by advertisers.
HTTP sends data as plain text without encryption. HTTPS adds TLS encryption.

scenes.text: At a café, a network called "Free_WiFi" appears.
An attacker listens to everything sent through it.
That is eavesdropping.

steps.title: Hackers and crackers
steps.body: **Hackers** have deep computer knowledge. **White-hat (ethical) hackers** test systems with permission to find and fix weaknesses. **Black-hat hackers / crackers** break into systems illegally for theft, damage or profit. **Grey-hat** hackers act without permission but without malicious intent (still illegal). Unauthorised access is a crime under India's IT Act, 2000.

steps.title: Network threats
steps.body:
- **Denial of Service (DoS):** flooding a server with requests so genuine users cannot access it
- **Distributed DoS (DDoS):** the flood comes from many compromised computers (**botnet / zombies**)
- **Snooping:** unauthorised access to someone else's data (may be later, e.g. reading stored packets/logs)
- **Eavesdropping:** unauthorised **real-time** interception of private communication (calls, messages)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A bank website becomes unreachable because thousands of infected devices worldwide send it junk requests → **DDoS**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: An attacker records network packets in a hostel Wi-Fi and later reads the messages → **snooping**; listening to a VoIP call live → **eavesdropping**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling all hackers criminals — ethical hackers work legally with permission.
- Mixing DoS (single source) and DDoS (many sources).

activity.prompt: DoS detection: read n, then n lines "ip" of incoming requests. Print each IP that sent MORE than 3 requests, in order of first appearance, one per line; if none, print "No attack".
activity.solution:
n = int(input())
count = {}
for _ in range(n):
    ip = input().strip()
    count[ip] = count.get(ip, 0) + 1
flagged = [ip for ip, c in count.items() if c > 3]
print("\n".join(flagged) if flagged else "No attack")
activity.hint: Count with a dictionary, then select IPs whose count exceeds 3.

quiz.why: Ethical hackers test systems with permission to find weaknesses, and are called white-hat hackers. Black-hat hackers are malicious.
A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack floods a target with traffic from many compromised machines. A DoS attack uses one source.

quiz.q: Real-time interception of a private call:
quiz.why: Eavesdropping means secretly listening to or intercepting a private conversation or data as it happens.

quiz.q: A network of infected computers controlled by an attacker:
quiz.why: A botnet is a group of infected computers (bots or zombies) that an attacker controls remotely.

quiz.q: India's law covering unauthorised computer access:
quiz.why: The Information Technology Act, 2000 is India's law that deals with cybercrime, including unauthorised access to computers.

questions.q: Malware that locks files and demands money:
questions.why: Ransomware locks or encrypts a victim's files and demands money to restore access.

questions.q: HTTPS uses:
questions.why: HTTPS adds SSL/TLS encryption to HTTP, so data in transit is protected.

questions.q: A firewall filters:
questions.why: A firewall monitors and filters incoming and outgoing network traffic according to rules.

questions.q: A virus needs ___ to spread.
questions.why: A virus cannot spread alone: it attaches to a host file or program and spreads when that is run or shared.

questions.q: Unsolicited bulk email is called:
questions.why: Spam is unwanted bulk email, often advertising or scams.

questions.q: Assertion: A worm can spread faster than a virus. Reason: A worm self-replicates over networks without needing a host file or user action.
questions.why: Both are true. A worm replicates itself across networks with no host file and no user action needed, so it can spread much faster than a virus.

questions.q: Software that shows unwanted ads:
questions.why: Adware shows unwanted advertisements, often as pop-ups, and may track browsing as well.

questions.q: An attacker floods a server from a single machine. This is:
questions.why: Flooding a server from one machine is a Denial of Service (DoS) attack. DDoS uses many machines.

questions.q: Antivirus that matches stored patterns of known malware uses:
questions.why: Signature-based detection matches files against stored patterns of known malware. Sandboxing instead watches behaviour in isolation.

questions.q: Case: An employee's login details were stolen after he typed them on a café PC with a hidden USB device between keyboard and computer. Threat:
questions.why: A hidden device between keyboard and computer records every key typed, so it is a hardware keylogger that captured the login details.

questions.q: Case: A website remembers your language choice after you return next week. Mechanism:
questions.why: A cookie stored on your device lets a site remember settings, such as language, on your next visit.

questions.q: Caesar cipher with shift 2 turns "CAT" into:
questions.why: Shift each letter two places forward: C→E, A→C, T→V, giving ECV.

questions.q: Case: Thousands of hijacked smart cameras send requests to a news site, which goes offline. Identify the attack and the hijacked devices:
questions.why: Thousands of hijacked devices (a botnet of zombies) sending requests to overload a site is a DDoS attack.

questions.q: Which practice gives the best protection overall?
options: Updated software + antivirus + strong passwords + backups
questions.why: No single measure is enough. Updated software, antivirus, strong passwords and backups together protect from many different threats.

questions.q: Black-hat hackers are also called:
questions.why: Black-hat hackers break into systems for harm or gain, and are also called crackers.

questions.q: Reading someone's stored messages without permission is:
questions.why: Reading someone's stored data or messages without permission is snooping. Eavesdropping is about intercepting live communication.

steps.title: Sorting

Bubble/selection max comparisons
Sorted list

COUNT(*) counts NULL rows too
Columns / rows

Send vs receive email

A walkie-talkie lets both sides talk, but only one at a time, which is half-duplex.

quiz.why: A full mesh of n nodes needs n(n − 1)/2 cables: 7 × 6/2 = 21.

quiz.why: A Trojan looks like a useful program but secretly carries harmful code.

questions.q: Mock A4 · Postfix of A * (B − C) + D:
questions.why: Brackets first: B − C becomes B C −. Then A * (that) → A B C − *, and + D gives A B C − * D +.
int("7") + 1 gives 8 without error, so it prints 8. No ValueError occurs, so the except block is skipped and else prints E.

questions.q: Mock A6 · [9, 2, 7, 4] after pass 2 of selection sort:
questions.why: Pass 1 puts the minimum 2 first: [2, 9, 7, 4]. Pass 2 finds the minimum 4 in the rest and swaps with 9: [2, 4, 7, 9].

questions.q: Mock A7 · Binary search for 40 in [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70]: iterations
questions.why: first = 0, last = 6, so mid = 3, and L[3] = 40 is the key. It is found in the first iteration.

questions.q: Mock A8 · Assertion: fetchall() after fetchone() returns all rows. Reason: fetchall() always starts from the first row.
questions.why: Both are false. After fetchone(), fetchall() returns only the remaining rows, because it continues from the current position, not from the first row.

Mock A9 · Output:
import io
f = io.StringIO("ab\ncd\nef")
f.readline()
print(f.read(3))
questions.why: readline() reads "ab\n", leaving the pointer at "cd\nef". read(3) then returns the next three characters: c, d and the newline.

questions.q: Mock A10 · On STUDENT marks (88, 72, 95, 64, 81, NULL): SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(Marks) returns
questions.why: COUNT(*) counts all 6 rows and COUNT(Marks) counts the 5 non-NULL values, so the difference, the number of NULLs, is 1.

questions.why: A primary key identifies each row uniquely, so it cannot be NULL.

questions.q: Mock B2 · Protocol to receive email:
questions.why: POP3 is the protocol for receiving (downloading) email. SMTP sends it.

questions.why: All PCs connect to one central switch, so they all fail if it fails. That is a star topology.

questions.why: Degree adds the columns: 3 + 2 = 5. Cardinality multiplies the rows: 4 × 5 = 20.

questions.q: Mock B8 · Case: Link two buildings 1 km apart with high bandwidth in an area with heavy electrical machines:
questions.why: Optical fibre gives high bandwidth over 1 km and, because it carries light, is not affected by electrical interference from machines.

SELECT Class FROM STUDENT GROUP BY Class HAVING AVG(Marks) > 80;
questions.why: Group rows by class and filter the groups with HAVING AVG(Marks) > 80. WHERE cannot use aggregate functions.

questions.q: Mock B10 · Case: Thousands of infected IoT devices flood a website. Attack and defence idea:
options: DDoS; traffic filtering/firewall and DDoS protection services
questions.why: A flood of requests from many infected devices is a DDoS attack. Traffic filtering, firewalls and DDoS protection services help defend against it.

school-c12-economics-a.title: Class 12 Economics — Introductory Macroeconomics (Part A)
school-c12-economics-a.description: Class 12 Macroeconomics chapter by chapter: national income, money and banking, income determination, government budget and the open economy — with solved numericals.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Introduction
courses.summary: What macroeconomics studies, how it emerged after the Great Depression and Keynes, how it differs from microeconomics, the four sectors of an economy and features of a capitalist economy.
outcomes: Learners can explain the scope of macroeconomics
Learners can describe the emergence of macroeconomics
Learners can distinguish micro and macro economics
Learners can describe the four sectors and the features of a capitalist economy

scenes.text: Microeconomics asks: what price for one brand of tea?
Macroeconomics asks: why did prices of everything rise 6% this year?
It studies the economy as a whole.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Macroeconomics** studies the economy as a whole — aggregate output (GDP), employment, the general price level (inflation), money supply, interest rates, government budget and the balance of payments. It uses **aggregates** (sums) such as aggregate demand and aggregate supply.

steps.title: Typical macro questions
steps.body:
- Why does total output grow faster in some years?
- What causes unemployment of large numbers of people?
- Why does the general price level rise (inflation)?
- How do government spending, taxes and RBI's policies affect the economy?

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: "Rise in the price of onions" → micro (single good). "Rise in the general price level measured by CPI" → **macro**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: "Unemployment of a factory's workers after a machine is installed" → micro. "Unemployment rate in India" → **macro**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking macroeconomics is just microeconomics multiplied — aggregates can behave differently (e.g. paradox of thrift).
- Calling "industry demand" macro — it is still micro (one market).

activity.prompt: Micro or macro?

quiz.why: Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, looking at totals like national income, employment and the price level.
GDP is a total for the whole economy, so it is a macro variable. A household's income, a pen's price and a firm's output are micro.

quiz.q: General price level is studied in:
quiz.why: The general price level (inflation) is an economy-wide variable, so it is studied in macroeconomics.
Aggregate demand is the total demand for all goods and services in the whole economy.

quiz.q: Market demand for wheat is a ___ concept.
quiz.why: Demand in the market for one good, wheat, is part of microeconomics, which studies individual markets.

scenes.text: In 1929 the Great Depression hit the USA and Europe.
Output fell, millions lost jobs.
In 1936 Keynes explained why — macroeconomics was born.

steps.title: The Great Depression
steps.body: Began in **1929**. In the USA, output fell sharply and unemployment rose from about 3% to about 25% between 1929 and 1933. Classical economics (which assumed markets clear automatically at full employment) could not explain persistent unemployment.

steps.title: Keynes
steps.body: **John Maynard Keynes** published *The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money* in **1936**. He argued that aggregate demand determines output and employment in the short run, and that the economy can stay below full employment — supporting a role for government spending.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Classical view: if workers are unemployed, wages will fall until all are employed. Keynesian view: if demand is too low, firms will not hire even at lower wages → **involuntary unemployment** can persist.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: During a slump, the government builds roads → more incomes → more spending → more jobs. This is a Keynesian policy response (raising aggregate demand).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dating the General Theory to 1929 — it was 1936.
- Saying classical economists studied unemployment as a central problem — they assumed full employment.

activity.prompt: Put these events in order

events.text: Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations (classical economics)

quiz.why: The Great Depression began with the stock market crash in 1929.

quiz.q: The General Theory was written by:
quiz.why: John Maynard Keynes wrote The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money.

quiz.q: The General Theory was published in:
quiz.why: Keynes's General Theory was published in 1936, after the Great Depression began.
Classical economists believed markets adjust automatically and keep the economy at full employment.
Keynes said output and employment depend on aggregate demand, so low demand can cause unemployment.

lessons.title: Micro vs macro; sectors of the economy

scenes.text: Households supply labour and buy goods.
Firms produce and hire.
Government taxes and spends; the rest of the world trades with us.

steps.title: Micro vs macro
steps.body: Micro: individual units, price theory, partial equilibrium, tools: individual demand/supply. Macro: aggregates, income theory, general equilibrium, tools: aggregate demand/supply. They are interdependent.

steps.title: Four sectors
steps.body:
- **Households:** consume goods and supply factors of production (land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship)
- **Firms (producers):** hire factors, produce goods and services
- **Government:** taxes, spends, regulates, provides public goods
- **External sector (rest of the world):** exports, imports, capital flows

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A household earns wages from a firm (factor payment) and spends it on the firm's products (consumption expenditure) → household and firm sectors interact.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: India buys crude oil from abroad → **import** (external sector). An Indian IT firm sells software to a US client → **export**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Treating government only as a spender — it also earns (taxes) and produces (public enterprises).

activity.prompt: Match the activity to the sector

quiz.q: Factors of production are supplied by:
quiz.why: Households own the factors of production (land, labour, capital, enterprise) and supply them to firms.
Microeconomics is also called price theory, as it explains how prices are determined in individual markets.
Macroeconomics is also called income and employment theory, since it studies national income and employment levels.
Exports and imports are trade with the rest of the world, which is the external sector.
Micro and macro depend on each other, since the economy's totals result from many individual decisions, and aggregates affect individuals.

lessons.title: Capitalist economy and the circular flow

scenes.text: In a capitalist economy, firms are privately owned.
Workers sell labour for wages.
Money and goods flow in circles.

steps.title: Features of a capitalist economy
steps.body:
- Private ownership of means of production
- Production for sale in the market (profit motive)
- Sale and purchase of labour services at a wage rate
- Capitalists/entrepreneurs organise production and earn profit
Modern economies are mostly **mixed** — private and public sectors coexist.

steps.title: Circular flow (two-sector)
steps.body:
**Real flow:** households give factor services to firms; firms give goods and services to households.
**Money flow:** firms pay factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) to households; households spend on goods → consumption expenditure returns to firms.
In a simple model with no saving, **factor income = consumption expenditure = value of output**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Firms pay households ₹1,000 crore as wages, rent, interest and profit. If households spend it all on goods, firms receive ₹1,000 crore — the circle is complete.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: If households save ₹100 crore, firms receive only ₹900 crore from consumption — unless that saving is borrowed and spent as investment (via banks). This is a **leakage** and an **injection**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing real flow (goods, services) with money flow (payments).
- Forgetting that saving is a leakage and investment an injection.

activity.prompt: Real flow or money flow?

quiz.why: A capitalist economy has private ownership of the means of production and firms driven by the profit motive.

quiz.q: In the circular flow, wages are a:
quiz.why: Wages are a payment of money from firms to households, so they are a money flow. The matching real flow is labour services.

quiz.q: Saving in the circular flow is a:
quiz.why: Saving takes income out of the spending stream, so it is a leakage.
Investment adds spending to the circular flow, so it is an injection.

quiz.q: India is best described as a:
quiz.why: India has both a large private sector and a public sector, so it is a mixed economy.

questions.q: Macroeconomics deals with:
questions.why: Macroeconomics deals with aggregates, which are economy-wide totals such as national income and general price level.

questions.q: The General Theory (1936) was by:
questions.why: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936) was written by J. M. Keynes.

questions.q: Which is micro?
questions.why: The price of rice is a single market price, which is a micro concept. GDP, inflation and unemployment are economy-wide.

questions.q: Households supply:
questions.why: Households own and supply the factors of production, in return for factor incomes such as wages and rent.

questions.q: Great Depression began in:
questions.why: The Great Depression began in 1929, with the US stock market crash.

questions.q: Assertion: Classical economics could not explain the Great Depression. Reason: It assumed markets automatically ensure full employment.
questions.why: Both are true. Classical theory assumed markets automatically reach full employment, so it could not explain the long, severe unemployment of the 1930s.

questions.q: In a two-sector model with no saving, factor income equals:
questions.why: With no saving, households spend all their factor income on goods, so factor income equals consumption expenditure.

questions.q: Wages paid by firms to households:
questions.why: Wages are money paid by firms to households, so they are a money flow.

questions.q: Case: A government increases spending during a slump to create jobs. Which thinker's ideas support this?
questions.why: Keynes argued that government spending can raise aggregate demand and employment during a slump. Smith favoured laissez-faire.

questions.q: Case: Households save ₹200 crore, firms borrow ₹200 crore from banks to invest. Effect on circular flow:
questions.why: Households' saving of ₹200 crore is a leakage, and the firms borrowing ₹200 crore to invest is an injection of the same size, so the circular flow is maintained.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
options: Micro — income theory; Macro — price theory
Micro — price theory; Macro — income theory
questions.why: Microeconomics is price theory and macroeconomics is income (and employment) theory.

questions.q: Case: US unemployment rose from about 3% to about 25% within a few years. This refers to:
questions.why: US unemployment rose to about 25% during 1929–33, which is the Great Depression.

questions.q: Case: Firms in an economy are privately owned, hire workers at wages and sell output for profit. The economy is:
