questions.why: Private ownership of firms, wage labour and production for profit are the features of a capitalist economy.

questions.q: Assertion: Aggregates may behave differently from individual units. Reason: What is true for one individual (e.g. saving more) may not hold for the whole economy.
questions.why: Both are true. A fallacy of composition applies: if one person saves more, it may be good for them, yet if everyone does, total spending and income can fall.

questions.q: External sector includes:
questions.why: The external sector covers dealings with the rest of the world, which means exports and imports.

questions.q: Involuntary unemployment means:
options: People who do not want to work
People willing to work at the prevailing wage cannot find jobs
questions.why: Involuntary unemployment means people who are willing to work at the existing wage cannot find jobs, as opposed to those who choose not to work.

courses.title: Ch 2 · National Income Accounting
courses.summary: Basic concepts (final/intermediate goods, stocks/flows, investment, depreciation), circular flow, the product (value added), expenditure and income methods, macroeconomic aggregates and their conversions, nominal and real GDP with the GDP deflator, and GDP vs welfare.
outcomes: Learners can classify goods as final or intermediate and variables as stocks or flows
Learners can calculate national income by value added, expenditure and income methods
Learners can convert between GDP, NDP, GNP, NNP at market price and factor cost
Learners can compute real GDP and the GDP deflator
Learners can explain why GDP is not a perfect index of welfare

scenes.text: A farmer sells wheat to a miller.
The miller sells flour to a baker who sells bread to you.
Should we add wheat + flour + bread to find output?

steps.title: Key definitions
steps.body:
- **Final goods:** bought for final use (consumption or investment), not for resale or further processing in the same year
- **Intermediate goods:** used up as inputs in production within the year
- **Consumption goods** (durable, semi-durable, non-durable, services) vs **capital goods** (used to produce other goods over years, e.g. machines)
- **Stock:** measured at a point of time (wealth, capital, money supply)
- **Flow:** measured over a period (income, investment, depreciation)
- **Gross investment** = addition to capital stock including replacement; **Net investment** = gross investment − depreciation
- **Depreciation** (consumption of fixed capital): fall in value of fixed capital due to normal wear and tear and expected obsolescence

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Flour bought by a household → **final**. Flour bought by a bakery → **intermediate**. A tractor bought by a farmer → **final (capital good)** because it is not used up in the year.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Gross investment ₹500 crore; depreciation ₹80 crore → net investment = **₹420 crore** (net addition to capital stock).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Classifying by the type of good rather than its use.
- Calling "capital" a flow — it is a stock; investment is a flow.
- Counting intermediate goods → double counting.

activity.prompt: Stock or flow?

quiz.q: A machine bought by a factory is a:
quiz.why: A machine bought by a factory is used over many years to produce goods, so it is a capital good, a final good bought for investment, not an intermediate good.
Net investment = gross investment − depreciation, which is the net addition to the capital stock.
A stock is measured at a point in time. Wealth is a stock, while income, exports and depreciation are flows over a period.

quiz.q: Milk bought by a sweet shop is:
quiz.why: The sweet shop uses milk to make sweets that it will sell, so the milk is an intermediate good, not a final good.
Depreciation is the fall in value of fixed capital through wear and tear, and is also called consumption of fixed capital.

scenes.text: Farmer: wheat ₹100 (no purchased inputs).
Miller: flour ₹150; Baker: bread ₹200.
Value added: 100 + 50 + 50 = ₹200 — equals the bread.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
**Value added** = Value of output − Intermediate consumption. Value of output = Sales + Change in stock.
GVA at MP of all producing units in the domestic territory = **GDP at MP**.
NVA = GVA − depreciation; NVA at FC = NVA at MP − net indirect taxes (indirect taxes − subsidies).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Wheat ₹100 → flour ₹150 → bread ₹200. Value added: farmer 100, miller 50, baker 50 → total **₹200** = value of final good. Adding all sales (450) would double count.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Firm A: sales ₹500, closing stock ₹50, opening stock ₹30, purchases of inputs ₹200.
Value of output = 500 + (50 − 30) = 520; GVA at MP = 520 − 200 = **₹320**. If depreciation ₹20 and net indirect taxes ₹30 → NVA at FC = **₹270**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring change in stock.
- Subtracting capital goods purchases as intermediate consumption (they are not).
- Including the sale of second-hand goods as output (only brokerage/commission counts).

activity.prompt: Sales ₹800, change in stock −₹20, intermediate consumption ₹300, depreciation ₹40, indirect taxes ₹50. NVA at factor cost (₹)?

quiz.why: Value added = value of output − intermediate consumption. It is the value a producer adds to inputs.
If intermediate goods are counted along with final goods, the same value is counted more than once, which is double counting.
Value of output = sales + change in stock of inventories, because unsold output is also output.

quiz.q: Sum of GVA at MP of all producers in domestic territory =
quiz.why: The sum of gross value added at market price of all producers in the domestic territory equals GDP at market price.

quiz.q: Sale of a used car: what enters GDP?
quiz.why: Used goods were counted in GDP when first produced. Only the dealer's commission is a new service in this year's GDP.

scenes.text: Households consume.
Firms invest; government buys.
Foreigners buy our exports; we buy imports.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
GDP at MP = **C + I + G + (X − M)**
- C: private final consumption expenditure
- I: gross domestic capital formation (gross fixed capital formation + change in stock)
- G: government final consumption expenditure
- X − M: net exports
Only **final** expenditure counts; transfer payments (pensions, scholarships) are excluded because they are not for current goods/services.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Given: PFCE 4,000; GFCE 900; gross fixed capital formation 1,100; change in stock 100; net exports −200; depreciation 300; NIT 400; NFIA −50.
GDP MP = 4,000 + 900 + 1,200 − 200 = **5,900**. NNP FC = 5,900 − 300 − 400 − 50 = **5,150**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding imports instead of subtracting.
- Including government transfer payments (old-age pension) in G.
- Including purchase of financial assets (shares) as investment.

activity.prompt: C = 2,500; I = 700; G = 500; exports 300; imports 400. GDP at market price?

quiz.why: By the expenditure method GDP = C + I + G + (X − M): consumption, investment, government spending and net exports.
A pension is paid without any current production in return, so it is a transfer payment and is not counted in national income or GDP.
Gross domestic capital formation = gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) + change in stock.
Net exports X − M is negative when imports exceed exports.
Buying shares only transfers ownership of financial assets and produces no new goods or services, so it is not part of GDP.

scenes.text: Workers get wages.
Landowners get rent; lenders get interest.
Entrepreneurs get profit.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
**NDP at FC (domestic income)** = Compensation of employees + Operating surplus (rent + interest + profit) + Mixed income of self-employed.
- Compensation of employees = wages and salaries (cash + kind) + employer's contribution to social security
- Profit = corporate tax + dividends + retained earnings
Then NNP at FC (National Income) = NDP at FC + NFIA.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Compensation 500; rent 100; interest 80; profit 220; mixed income 100 → NDP FC = **1,000**. If NFIA = −20 → National income = **980**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Profit is given as: dividends 60, corporate tax 30, undistributed profit 20 → profit = **110**. Employer's contribution to PF must be added to compensation of employees; **employees'** own contribution is already inside wages — do not add again.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding employees' contribution to social security separately (double counting).
- Including transfer incomes (scholarship, pension, lottery wins) — not factor incomes.
- Forgetting mixed income.

activity.prompt: Wages 700; employer's contribution to social security 50; rent 80; interest 70; profit 200; mixed income 150; NFIA 30. National income (NNP at FC)?

quiz.why: Operating surplus is the income of property owners: rent + interest + profit.
Corporate tax is paid out of profits, so it is part of the profit component of operating surplus.
Scholarships are given without production in exchange, so they are a transfer and are excluded from factor income.
Mixed income is the income of the self-employed, which combines returns to their own labour, land and capital.
National income = NNP at factor cost = NDP at factor cost + net factor income from abroad (NFIA).

scenes.text: Subtract depreciation → net.
Subtract net indirect taxes → factor cost.
Add NFIA → national.

steps.title: Conversions
steps.body:
- **Gross − Depreciation = Net**
- **Market price − Net indirect taxes (NIT = indirect taxes − subsidies) = Factor cost**
- **Domestic + NFIA = National** (NFIA = factor income from abroad − factor income paid abroad)
So: NNP at FC = GDP at MP − depreciation − NIT + NFIA.

steps.title: Other aggregates
steps.body:
- **Personal income (PI)** = National income − undistributed profits − net interest payments made by households − corporate tax + transfer payments to households from government and firms
- **Personal disposable income (PDI)** = PI − personal tax payments − non-tax payments (fines, fees)
- **Per capita income** = National income ÷ population

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
GDP MP 5,000; depreciation 400; indirect taxes 350; subsidies 50; NFIA −100.
NIT = 300 → NNP FC = 5,000 − 400 − 300 − 100 = **4,200**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: NNP MP 6,000; NIT 500; NFIA 200 → NDP FC = 6,000 − 500 − 200 = **5,300** (remove NIT, then subtract NFIA to get domestic).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding NFIA to go from national to domestic (subtract it).
- Forgetting that subsidies reduce net indirect taxes.
- When NFIA is negative, adding a negative = subtracting.

activity.prompt: GNP at MP = 8,000; depreciation 600; indirect taxes 700; subsidies 100; NFIA = 150. Find NDP at FC.

quiz.why: Net values are gross values minus depreciation (consumption of fixed capital).
Factor cost = market price − net indirect taxes (indirect taxes minus subsidies).
National aggregates = domestic aggregates + net factor income from abroad (NFIA).

quiz.q: If subsidies exceed indirect taxes, FC is ___ MP.
quiz.why: If subsidies exceed indirect taxes, net indirect taxes are negative, so factor cost = MP − NIT is greater than market price.

quiz.q: NNP at FC is also called:
quiz.why: NNP at factor cost is also called national income, the total factor incomes of residents.

lessons.title: Real vs nominal GDP; GDP and welfare

scenes.text: Nominal GDP rose 10% this year.
But prices also rose 6%.
Real GDP rose only about 4%.

steps.title: Nominal and real GDP
steps.body:
**Nominal GDP:** output valued at current-year prices. **Real GDP:** output valued at constant (base-year) prices — measures actual change in output.
**GDP deflator** = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100. Other price indices: **CPI** (prices of a basket bought by consumers, includes imports) and **WPI** (wholesale prices). The deflator covers all goods and services produced domestically; CPI includes only consumer goods.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Nominal GDP ₹1,200 crore; deflator 120 → Real GDP = 1,200 × 100/120 = **₹1,000 crore**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Year 1: 10 units at ₹5; year 2: 12 units at ₹6 (base year 1). Nominal GDP Y2 = 72; Real GDP Y2 = 12 × 5 = 60; deflator = 72/60 × 100 = **120**.

steps.title: GDP and welfare
steps.body:
Higher GDP does not always mean higher welfare because of:
- **Distribution of GDP** (may be unequal)
- **Non-monetary exchanges** (household work, barter not counted)
- **Externalities** (pollution, a negative externality, not subtracted; positive ones not added)
Also composition of output matters (more weapons vs more food).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using nominal GDP to compare output across years.
- Inverting the deflator formula.

activity.prompt: Nominal GDP ₹2,750 crore; real GDP ₹2,500 crore. GDP deflator?

quiz.why: Real GDP values output at constant (base-year) prices, so it shows changes in quantity alone.
GDP deflator = (nominal GDP ÷ real GDP) × 100. It measures price change in the economy.
Pollution harms others without compensation, and GDP ignores this cost, so it is a negative externality.

quiz.q: Household services by a homemaker are:
quiz.why: Unpaid household work is not sold in a market, so it is not counted in GDP.
The Consumer Price Index tracks prices of the goods consumers buy, and includes imported goods too. WPI covers wholesale prices.

questions.q: Flour bought by a household is:
questions.why: Flour bought by a household is for final use, not for further production, so it is a final good.

questions.q: Which is a flow?
questions.why: Income is measured over a period of time, so it is a flow. Wealth, money supply and capital stock are stocks.

questions.q: NFIA is added to convert:
questions.why: Net factor income from abroad (NFIA) is added to a domestic aggregate to get the corresponding national aggregate.

questions.q: Transfer payments are:
questions.why: Transfer payments, like pensions, are made without any production in return, so they are excluded from national income.

questions.q: Gross investment ₹900, depreciation ₹150. Net investment:
questions.why: Net investment = gross investment − depreciation = 900 − 150 = ₹750.

questions.q: Assertion: Only final goods are included in GDP. Reason: Including intermediate goods leads to double counting.
questions.why: Both are true. Counting intermediate goods as well as final goods would count the same value several times, so only final goods are included.

questions.q: Sales 1,000; change in stock 50; intermediate consumption 400. GVA at MP:
questions.why: Value of output = sales + change in stock = 1,000 + 50 = 1,050. GVA = 1,050 − 400 = 650.

questions.q: Compensation 600, rent 100, interest 50, profit 150, mixed income 100. NDP FC:
questions.why: NDP at factor cost = compensation 600 + operating surplus (100 + 50 + 150 = 300) + mixed income 100 = 1,000.

questions.q: GDP MP 10,000; depreciation 800; NIT 900; NFIA −200. National income:
questions.why: National income = GDP at MP − depreciation − NIT + NFIA = 10,000 − 800 − 900 + (−200) = 8,100.

questions.q: Nominal GDP 3,600; deflator 120. Real GDP:
questions.why: Real GDP = (nominal GDP ÷ deflator) × 100 = (3,600 ÷ 120) × 100 = 3,000.

questions.q: Case: Profit components: dividend 40, corporate tax 25, retained 15. Profit:
questions.why: Profit = dividends + corporate tax + retained earnings = 40 + 25 + 15 = 80.

questions.q: NNP FC 5,000; NIT 300; depreciation 200; NFIA 100. GDP MP:
questions.why: GDP at MP = NNP at FC + NIT + depreciation − NFIA = 5,000 + 300 + 200 − 100 = 5,400.

questions.q: Case: GDP rose 8% but most gains went to the top 1% and air quality worsened. Why may welfare not rise?
questions.why: GDP growth can hide inequality when gains go to a few, and negative externalities like worse air quality are not subtracted. So welfare may not rise.

questions.q: Employer's contribution to social security is part of:
questions.why: An employer's contribution to social security is part of the cost of employing workers, so it is included in compensation of employees.

questions.q: Purchase of a new house by a household is:
questions.why: A new house is a lasting asset that adds to the capital stock, so a household buying one is counted as investment (capital formation).

questions.q: Brokerage on sale of second-hand goods is:
questions.why: Brokerage is a fee for a service rendered in the current year, so it is included in GDP, although the second-hand goods themselves are not.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Money and Banking
courses.summary: Functions of money, measures of money supply, how commercial banks create money (money multiplier), and the Reserve Bank of India's functions and instruments of monetary policy.
outcomes: Learners can explain the functions of money and problems of barter
Learners can define M1 and M3 and high-powered money
Learners can compute credit creation using the money multiplier
Learners can explain RBI's functions and its quantitative and qualitative tools

scenes.text: A weaver has cloth and wants rice.
The rice farmer wants shoes, not cloth.
Money solves the double coincidence problem.

steps.title: Problems of barter
steps.body:
- Lack of **double coincidence of wants**
- No common **measure of value**
- Difficulty in **storing value** (perishable goods)
- Indivisibility of goods
- Difficulty in making **deferred payments**

steps.title: Functions of money
steps.body:
**Primary:** medium of exchange; measure of value (unit of account).
**Secondary:** store of value; standard of deferred payments.
Money is anything generally accepted as a means of payment.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A shopkeeper prices a shirt at ₹500 and a pen at ₹50 — the shirt "equals" 10 pens. → money as **unit of account**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A worker saves ₹2,000 every month in a bank to use next year → **store of value**. A loan repaid in 12 instalments → **standard of deferred payment**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling "store of value" a primary function.
- Saying money has value only because of the material it is made of — modern money is **fiat money** (backed by government order).

activity.prompt: Match the example to the function of money
pairs: Keeping savings in a bank account
Repaying a home loan over 20 years

options: Lack of double coincidence of wants
quiz.why: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants: each party must have what the other wants, which is rare.

quiz.q: Medium of exchange is a ___ function.
quiz.why: Medium of exchange is the main (primary) function of money, as it removes the need for double coincidence of wants.

quiz.q: Store of value is a ___ function.
quiz.why: Store of value is a secondary function of money, as it follows from the primary function of exchange.

options: Money declared legal tender by government order
quiz.why: Fiat money has value because the government declares it legal tender by order, not because of any metal content.

quiz.q: Unit of account means money is used to:
quiz.why: As a unit of account, money gives a common measure for expressing the value of all goods and services.

scenes.text: Currency notes and coins with the public.
Plus money in savings and current accounts.
RBI measures it in layers: M1, M3.

steps.title: Measures (RBI)
steps.body:
- **M1** = CU (currency notes and coins with the public) + DD (net demand deposits with commercial banks) + other deposits with RBI
- **M2** = M1 + savings deposits with post office savings banks
- **M3** = M1 + net time deposits with commercial banks (**broad money**; most commonly used)
- **M4** = M3 + total deposits with post office savings organisations (excluding NSC)
M1 is the most liquid; liquidity falls from M1 to M4.

steps.title: High-powered money (reserve money)
steps.body: **H = CU + R** (currency held by public + reserves of commercial banks with RBI and cash in vaults). It is the monetary base created by RBI on which banks create further money.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: CU ₹20 lakh crore; DD ₹18 lakh crore; other deposits with RBI ₹1 lakh crore → **M1 = ₹39 lakh crore**. If net time deposits are ₹150 lakh crore → **M3 = ₹189 lakh crore**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Money held by the government and inter-bank deposits are **not** part of money supply — money supply counts money held by the **public**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding time deposits to M1 (they are in M3).
- Including government's cash balance in money supply.

activity.prompt: CU = 30, DD = 25, other deposits with RBI = 2, net time deposits = 120 (₹ lakh crore). M3 = ?

quiz.why: M1 (currency with the public plus demand deposits and other RBI deposits) is called narrow money.
M3 is broad money: M1 plus time deposits with banks.
High-powered money (reserve money) = currency held by the public (CU) + reserves (R).
M1 consists of the most easily spent forms of money, so it is the most liquid measure.

quiz.q: Money supply includes money held by:
quiz.why: Money supply is the stock of money held by the public. Holdings of the government, RBI and banks themselves are not counted.

scenes.text: You deposit ₹1,000 in a bank.
The bank keeps 20% and lends the rest; it returns as deposits elsewhere.
Total deposits can grow to ₹5,000.

steps.title: Credit creation
steps.body:
Banks keep a fraction of deposits as reserves (required by **CRR**) and lend the rest. Loans are spent and redeposited, creating new deposits. In the simplest model:
**Money multiplier = 1 / CRR** (or 1/LRR — legal reserve ratio)
**Total deposits created = Initial deposit × 1/CRR**.
Credit created (net new loans) = Total deposits − Initial deposit.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Initial deposit ₹1,000; CRR 20% → multiplier 5 → total deposits **₹5,000**; credit created **₹4,000**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Total deposits created ₹10,000 from initial deposit ₹2,000 → multiplier 5 → CRR = **20%**.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: Credit creation is lower if people hold more cash (currency drain), banks keep excess reserves, or there are few creditworthy borrowers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing total deposits with credit created.
- Using CRR as a whole number (use 0.2, not 20, in the formula).

activity.prompt: Initial deposit ₹5,000; legal reserve ratio 10%. Total deposits created (₹)?

quiz.why: The simple money multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve ratio (CRR): money creation per rupee of reserves.
Multiplier = 1/0.25 = 4, so total deposits = 4 × 400 = ₹1,600.
A higher CRR means banks must keep more in reserve and can lend less, so credit creation falls.
Credit created = total deposits − initial deposit, the extra money created by banks' lending.

quiz.q: A currency drain (people hold more cash) ___ credit creation.
quiz.why: If people keep more cash instead of depositing it, banks have less to lend, so credit creation is reduced.

lessons.title: Reserve Bank of India and monetary policy

scenes.text: The RBI was set up in 1935.
It issues currency (except one-rupee notes and coins, issued by the Government).
It controls credit with its policy tools.

steps.title: Functions of RBI
steps.body:
- **Currency authority:** sole issuer of currency notes (₹1 notes and coins issued by Government of India, distributed via RBI)
- **Banker to the government:** manages accounts, public debt, advises
- **Banker's bank and supervisor:** holds banks' reserves, regulates and supervises
- **Lender of last resort**
- **Controller of credit / money supply**
- **Custodian of foreign exchange reserves**

steps.title: Instruments of monetary policy
steps.body:
**Quantitative:**
- **Repo rate** (rate at which RBI lends short-term to banks against securities) and **reverse repo** (rate at which RBI absorbs funds)
- **Bank rate** (rate at which RBI lends to banks without collateral, long-term)
- **Open market operations (OMO):** buying/selling government securities
- **CRR:** % of deposits banks must keep with RBI
- **SLR:** % of deposits banks must keep in liquid assets (cash, gold, approved securities)
**Qualitative:** margin requirements, moral suasion, selective credit controls.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: To control inflation, RBI **raises repo rate**, **sells** government securities (OMO) and may **raise CRR** → loans become costlier and scarcer → spending falls.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: To fight a recession, RBI **cuts repo rate**, **buys** securities, lowers CRR → more credit → higher spending.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying RBI buys securities to control inflation (buying injects money).
- Confusing repo (RBI lends) with reverse repo (RBI borrows/absorbs).

activity.prompt: Which action does RBI take to control INFLATION vs fight a SLOWDOWN?

quiz.why: The Reserve Bank of India was established in 1935 and nationalised in 1949.

quiz.q: Selling government securities by RBI ___ money supply.
quiz.why: When the RBI sells securities, buyers pay with money, which moves from banks and public to the RBI, so money supply falls.

quiz.q: Rate at which RBI lends to banks short-term against securities:
quiz.why: The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks for the short term against government securities. The reverse repo rate is what the RBI pays when banks park funds with it.
Moral suasion is persuasion by the RBI, such as appeals and advice to banks, not a numerical rate or ratio. So it is a qualitative (selective) tool.

quiz.q: Lender of last resort is a function of:
quiz.why: As the lender of last resort, the RBI gives funds to commercial banks in financial difficulty when no one else will.

questions.q: Medium of exchange is a ___ function of money.
questions.why: Medium of exchange is the main (primary) function of money, as it removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.

questions.q: M1 includes:
options: CU + DD + other deposits with RBI
questions.why: M1 = currency with the public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with the RBI. Time deposits are in the broader measures.

questions.q: Repo rate is the rate at which:
questions.why: The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to banks against securities.

questions.q: Barter suffers from lack of:
questions.why: Barter needs each party to want what the other has, a double coincidence of wants, which makes exchange hard.

questions.q: High-powered money =
questions.why: High-powered (reserve) money is currency held by the public plus the reserves of banks, and it is the base for money creation.

questions.q: Assertion: Raising CRR reduces money supply. Reason: Banks have less to lend, lowering the money multiplier.
questions.why: Both are true. A higher CRR leaves banks less to lend, which lowers the money multiplier and reduces money supply.

questions.q: CRR 10%; initial deposit ₹2,000. Credit created:
questions.why: Multiplier = 1/0.10 = 10, so total deposits = ₹20,000. Credit created = 20,000 − 2,000 = ₹18,000.

questions.q: Total deposits ₹8,000 from initial deposit ₹1,000. CRR:
To curb inflation RBI should:
options: Sell securities and raise repo rate
questions.why: To curb inflation the RBI must reduce money supply: sell securities, which draws money in, and raise the repo rate, which makes borrowing dearer.

questions.q: Case: CU = 40, DD = 30, other deposits with RBI = 1, net time deposits = 100. M1 and M3:
questions.why: M1 = CU + DD + other deposits with RBI = 40 + 30 + 1 = 71. M3 = M1 + net time deposits = 71 + 100 = 171.

questions.q: Case: The economy is in recession. Which combination is appropriate?
options: Buy securities, cut repo rate, cut CRR
questions.why: In a recession the RBI should increase money supply and cheap credit: buy securities, cut the repo rate and cut the CRR.

questions.q: Case: RBI appeals to banks to avoid lending for speculative hoarding. Tool:
questions.why: An appeal or request to banks without a legal order is moral suasion.

questions.q: If CRR is cut from 20% to 10%, the money multiplier changes from:
questions.why: Multiplier = 1/CRR. At 20% it is 1/0.2 = 5, and at 10% it is 1/0.1 = 10.

questions.q: Case: Initial deposit ₹10,000; LRR 20%; but people keep some cash, so actual total deposits reach only ₹30,000. Why below ₹50,000?
questions.why: With LRR 20%, the multiplier is 5 and deposits could reach ₹50,000. People holding cash (currency drain) reduces the funds banks can lend, so total deposits are lower at ₹30,000.

questions.q: Money held by government is:
questions.why: Money supply counts only the money held by the public. Cash and deposits of the government are left out.

questions.q: Which is NOT an RBI function?
questions.why: The RBI issues currency, is banker to the government and lender of last resort. Income tax is collected by the government's tax department, not the RBI.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Determination of Income and Employment
courses.summary: Aggregate demand and its components, consumption and saving functions (APC, MPC, APS, MPS), investment, ex ante and ex post, equilibrium output in a two-sector model, the investment multiplier, and excess and deficient demand.
outcomes: Learners can explain aggregate demand and aggregate supply
Learners can calculate APC, MPC, APS and MPS
Learners can find equilibrium income from C = C̄ + cY and I
Learners can calculate the investment multiplier
Learners can explain excess and deficient demand and measures to correct them

scenes.text: In the short run, firms produce what people plan to buy.
Households spend most of their income.
Consumption depends on income.

steps.title: Aggregate demand (two-sector)
steps.body:
**AD = C + I** (planned consumption + planned investment). **AS** = total output (= national income Y) at each level.
All prices are assumed fixed (short run), so output adjusts to demand.

steps.title: Consumption function
steps.body:
**C = C̄ + cY** where C̄ = autonomous consumption (consumption at zero income), c = **MPC** = ΔC/ΔY (0 < c < 1).
**APC** = C/Y; **APS** = S/Y; **MPS** = ΔS/ΔY.
Identities: **APC + APS = 1**; **MPC + MPS = 1**. Saving function: **S = −C̄ + (1 − c)Y**.
At break-even income, C = Y and S = 0. APC can exceed 1 (at low incomes); MPC cannot.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Income rises from 2,000 to 2,500; consumption rises from 1,800 to 2,200. MPC = 400/500 = **0.8**; MPS = **0.2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying APC + MPC = 1 (wrong pair).
- Thinking MPC can exceed 1.
- Forgetting the negative intercept of the saving function.

activity.prompt: C = 50 + 0.75Y. Find the break-even level of income.

quiz.why: Of any extra income, part is consumed (MPC) and the rest is saved (MPS), so MPC + MPS = 1.
At break-even income, consumption equals income, so nothing is saved and saving is zero.
APC = C/Y is above 1 at low incomes where consumption exceeds income (dissaving, by borrowing or using savings).
Autonomous consumption is the consumption that takes place even at zero income, the constant term in the consumption function.

lessons.title: Investment, ex ante and ex post

scenes.text: At the start of the year firms plan to invest ₹100 crore.
Sales are lower than expected; unsold stock piles up.
Actual (ex post) investment ends up ₹120 crore.

steps.title: Investment
steps.body: **Investment** = addition to the stock of physical capital (machines, buildings) and change in inventory. In the simple model, planned investment is **autonomous** (Ī) — independent of income.

steps.title: Ex ante and ex post
steps.body:
- **Ex ante** = planned/intended values (planned C, planned I)
- **Ex post** = actual/realised values
Ex post saving always equals ex post investment (accounting identity) because unplanned inventory changes adjust. Equilibrium requires **ex ante** AD = AS (or ex ante S = ex ante I).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Planned I = 100; planned S at current income = 120 → output exceeds AD by 20 → unsold goods → **unplanned inventory accumulation** of 20 → firms cut output.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Planned I = 100; planned S = 80 → AD > output → inventories fall unplanned by 20 → firms raise output.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying equilibrium is when ex post S = I — that is always true; equilibrium needs ex ante equality.
- Forgetting unplanned inventory is part of ex post investment.

statements.s: Ex post saving always equals ex post investment.
Equilibrium occurs when planned saving equals planned investment.
If planned saving exceeds planned investment, inventories fall.
In the simple model, planned investment depends on income.

quiz.why: Ex ante means planned or expected, before the event. Ex post means actual, after the event.
If aggregate demand is less than aggregate supply, some output is not sold, so inventories pile up unintentionally (unplanned).
Autonomous investment does not change with the level of income. It depends on factors like expectations and technology.
The two-sector economy is in equilibrium when planned saving equals planned investment (S = I), which also means AD = AS.

quiz.q: If planned I > planned S, output will:
quiz.why: If planned investment exceeds planned saving, aggregate demand exceeds output, stocks fall and firms raise output.

scenes.text: Set Y = AD → Y = 750.

steps.title: Two approaches
steps.body:
**AD–AS approach:** Y = C̄ + cY + Ī → **Y* = (C̄ + Ī)/(1 − c)**.
**Saving–investment approach:** S = I → −C̄ + (1 − c)Y = Ī → same answer.
Graph: AD line (slope c, intercept C̄ + Ī) cuts the 45° line (AS, Y = AD) at equilibrium.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: S = −50 + 0.25Y; I = 100. Equilibrium: −50 + 0.25Y = 100 → **Y = 600**. Consumption at equilibrium = 600 − 100 = **500**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by c instead of (1 − c).
- Forgetting to add autonomous investment to the intercept.

activity.prompt: C = 80 + 0.6Y and I = 120. Equilibrium income?

quiz.q: In the 45° line diagram, the 45° line shows:
quiz.why: In the 45° line diagram every point on the line has Y equal to AD, so the 45° line shows aggregate supply (AS = Y).
At equilibrium Y = C + I = 40 + 0.9Y + 60, so 0.1Y = 100 and Y = 1,000.

quiz.q: Slope of the AD line equals:
quiz.why: The slope of the AD (= C + I) line equals the extra spending per extra income, which is the MPC.
Equilibrium requires planned saving equal to planned investment, S = I.
At equilibrium S = I: −20 + 0.2Y = 40, so 0.2Y = 60 and Y = 300.

scenes.text: Government-backed firms invest ₹100 crore more in roads.
Workers spend 80% of extra income; shopkeepers spend 80% of theirs…
Total income rises by ₹500 crore.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**k = ΔY/ΔI = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS**.
Higher MPC → bigger multiplier. Minimum value of k is 1 (when MPC = 0); it tends to infinity as MPC → 1.

steps.title: Paradox of thrift
steps.body: If everyone tries to save more (MPS rises), equilibrium income falls and total saving may not rise (it stays equal to autonomous investment, or falls if investment depends on income). What is good for one household may not be good for the whole economy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using k = 1/MPC.
- Forgetting that the multiplier works in reverse too (a fall in investment causes a multiple fall in income).

bands.text: Low MPC → multiplier close to 1 (about 1 to 1.25). Extra investment barely ripples.
MPC up to 0.5 → multiplier up to 2.
MPC up to 0.75 → multiplier up to 4.
High MPC → multiplier up to 10. Each rupee of investment creates many rupees of income.

quiz.why: k = 1/(1 − MPC). With MPC at its minimum of 0, k = 1, since there is no further round of spending.

quiz.q: Multiplier is larger when MPC is:
quiz.why: A higher MPC means more of each extra income is spent again, so each round adds more and the multiplier is larger.

scenes.text: AD above full-employment output → prices rise.
AD below it → unemployment.
Fiscal and monetary policy can close the gap.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
**Full employment:** all who are willing and able to work at the prevailing wage get work (only frictional/voluntary unemployment remains).
**Excess demand (inflationary gap):** AD > AS at full-employment level → inflation (output cannot rise further).
**Deficient demand (deflationary gap):** AD < AS at full-employment level → involuntary unemployment, falling output.

steps.title: Measures
steps.body:
**For excess demand:** raise taxes, cut government spending (fiscal); raise repo/bank rate, sell securities (OMO), raise CRR/SLR, raise margin requirements (monetary).
**For deficient demand:** the opposite — cut taxes, raise government spending, cut rates, buy securities, lower CRR/SLR.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Full-employment output ₹5,000 crore; AD at that output ₹5,400 crore → **inflationary gap of ₹400 crore**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Full-employment output ₹5,000 crore; AD ₹4,700 crore → **deflationary gap ₹300 crore**. With MPC 0.75 (k = 4), the economy's equilibrium income would fall short of full employment by 300 × 4 = ₹1,200 crore.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a deflationary gap "low prices" — it is mainly about unemployment.
- Recommending RBI buy securities to fight inflation.

activity.prompt: Which gap does each measure help correct?

quiz.q: Inflationary gap arises when AD at full employment is:
quiz.why: An inflationary gap exists when aggregate demand at full employment is greater than aggregate supply, which pushes up prices.
Deficient demand means aggregate demand is below the full employment level, so some workers willing to work cannot find jobs. This is involuntary unemployment.

quiz.q: To reduce excess demand government should:
quiz.why: To reduce excess demand, the government should cut its spending or raise taxes, which reduces aggregate demand.
Raising CRR reduces banks' lending and money supply, which lowers demand. So it corrects excess demand.
Full employment means no involuntary unemployment: everyone willing to work at the existing wage has a job. Some frictional and voluntary unemployment can still exist.

questions.q: MPC + MPS =
questions.why: MPC + MPS = 1, since extra income is either consumed or saved.

questions.q: AD in a two-sector model =
questions.why: In a two-sector model (households and firms) aggregate demand is consumption plus investment, AD = C + I.

questions.q: Ex post saving equals ex post investment:
questions.why: Ex post (actual) saving always equals ex post investment, since unplanned stock changes count as investment. Only ex ante values may differ.

questions.q: Multiplier formula:
questions.why: The investment multiplier is k = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS.

questions.q: Assertion: The value of multiplier is greater when MPC is higher. Reason: A larger part of each round of extra income is spent.
questions.why: Both are true. With a higher MPC, a larger part of each round of extra income is spent again, so total income rises by more and the multiplier is larger.

questions.q: C = 100 + 0.75Y; I = 150. Equilibrium Y:
Income rises 1,000 → 1,500; saving rises 100 → 200. MPC:
S = −40 + 0.2Y; I = 60. Equilibrium consumption:
Case: MPS 0.25. Investment rises by ₹300 crore. Change in income:
Case: Planned saving at current income is 150, planned investment 100. What happens?
questions.why: Planned saving (150) exceeds planned investment (100), so demand is below output. Unsold goods pile up as unplanned inventory, and firms cut output.

questions.q: Case: Economy at full employment; AD exceeds AS. Suitable monetary measure:
questions.why: Excess demand at full employment is inflationary. Raising the repo rate makes credit costlier and reduces demand.

questions.q: C = 50 + 0.8Y; I = 70. If I rises to 100, new equilibrium Y:
questions.why: The multiplier is 1/(1 − 0.8) = 5. Investment rises by 30, so ΔY = 30 × 5 = 150, and Y rises from 600 to 750.

questions.q: At Y = 0, C = 40; at Y = 200, C = 200. Consumption function and MPC:
questions.why: At Y = 0, C = 40 is the intercept. MPC = (200 − 40)/200 = 0.8, so C = 40 + 0.8Y.

questions.q: APC at income 400 when C = 300:
Paradox of thrift suggests:
options: Higher saving by all can reduce income
questions.why: The paradox of thrift says that if everyone tries to save more, total spending and income fall, so total saving may not rise.

questions.q: Deficient demand can be corrected by:
questions.why: Deficient demand needs more spending. Higher government spending raises aggregate demand, while higher CRR, selling securities and higher taxes would reduce it.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Government Budget and the Economy
courses.summary: Meaning and objectives of the government budget, revenue and capital budgets, classification of receipts and expenditure, direct and indirect taxes, types of budget, and measures of deficit — revenue, fiscal and primary deficits — with solved numericals.
outcomes: Learners can state the objectives of a government budget
Learners can classify receipts and expenditure as revenue or capital
Learners can distinguish direct and indirect taxes
Learners can calculate revenue, fiscal and primary deficits and interpret them

lessons.title: Meaning and objectives of the budget

scenes.text: Every year the Union Finance Minister presents the Budget in Parliament.
It shows expected receipts and expenditure for the coming financial year (April–March).
It is a tool to achieve economic goals.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: The **government budget** is an annual financial statement showing estimated receipts and expenditure of the government for a financial year (1 April–31 March). Article 112 of the Constitution requires the Union government to present an "Annual Financial Statement".

steps.title: Objectives
steps.body:
- **Allocation of resources** (public goods like defence, roads, which markets under-provide)
- **Reducing inequalities** of income and wealth (redistribution — progressive taxes, subsidies, welfare spending)
- **Economic stability** (controlling inflation and deflation, fluctuations)
- **Economic growth**
- **Managing public enterprises**
- **Reducing regional disparities**

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Higher income-tax rates on the rich and free meals in schools → objective: **reducing inequality**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Cutting government spending and raising taxes during high inflation → **economic stability**.

steps.title: Public goods
steps.body: Non-rival (one person's use does not reduce availability) and non-excludable (cannot easily exclude non-payers) — e.g. national defence, street lighting. Free-rider problem → markets under-supply them → government provides.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the budget is only about taxes.
- Confusing public goods with goods produced by public enterprises.

activity.prompt: Match the budget measure to its objective

quiz.why: India's financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March.
Public goods are non-rival (one person's use does not reduce another's) and non-excludable (no one can be kept from using them).
Progressive taxes take a higher share from higher incomes, which narrows the gap between rich and poor.
The annual financial statement (the Budget) is laid before Parliament under Article 112 of the Constitution.

quiz.q: Controlling inflation through the budget is the ___ objective.
quiz.why: Using the budget to control inflation and keep prices stable is the stabilisation function.

scenes.text: Salaries, interest and subsidies — revenue expenditure.
Building a dam — capital expenditure.
Borrowing — capital receipt.

steps.title: Revenue budget
steps.body:
**Revenue receipts** (neither create liability nor reduce assets): tax revenue (direct and indirect) and non-tax revenue (interest receipts, dividends and profits of PSUs, fees, fines, grants).
**Revenue expenditure** (neither creates assets nor reduces liabilities): salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies, grants to states.

steps.title: Capital budget
steps.body:
**Capital receipts** (create liability or reduce assets): borrowings (market loans, from RBI, from abroad), recovery of loans, disinvestment (sale of PSU shares), small savings.
**Capital expenditure** (creates assets or reduces liabilities): construction of roads, buildings, purchase of machinery, loans given to states, repayment of loans, investment in shares.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Classify: Disinvestment → capital receipt (reduces assets). Interest received on loans given → revenue receipt. Repayment of a loan by the government → capital expenditure (reduces liability). Payment of interest → revenue expenditure.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Grants to states for building schools — in central budget accounting, grants are treated as **revenue expenditure** (they do not create assets for the Centre), even if the state builds assets.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling recovery of loans a revenue receipt — it is a capital receipt (reduces assets).
- Calling interest payment capital expenditure.

activity.prompt: Classify for the central government

quiz.q: Borrowing by the government is a:
quiz.why: Borrowing creates a liability for the government, so it is a capital receipt.
Subsidies are government payments that do not create an asset, so they are revenue expenditure.
Recovery of loans reduces the government's assets, so it is a capital receipt.
Fines and penalties are not taxes and create no liability or asset reduction, so they are non-tax revenue.
Loans given to states create a financial asset for the central government, so they are capital expenditure.

scenes.text: Income tax is paid and borne by the same person.
GST is collected by the seller but borne by the buyer.
Direct vs indirect.

steps.title: Direct and indirect taxes
steps.body:
**Direct tax:** impact and incidence on the same person; cannot be shifted — personal income tax, corporation tax.
**Indirect tax:** impact on one, incidence shifted to another — **GST** (introduced 1 July 2017), customs duties, excise on certain items.
Direct taxes are usually progressive; indirect taxes tend to be regressive (same rate for rich and poor).

steps.title: Types of budget
steps.body:
- **Balanced:** estimated receipts = estimated expenditure
- **Surplus:** receipts > expenditure
- **Deficit:** expenditure > receipts (common in developing economies)
A deficit budget can stimulate demand during a slowdown; a surplus budget can curb inflation.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A 5% GST on toothpaste is paid by the shopkeeper to the government but included in the price paid by the customer → **indirect tax**; incidence on the customer.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Estimated receipts ₹40 lakh crore; estimated expenditure ₹45 lakh crore → **deficit budget** of ₹5 lakh crore.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling GST a direct tax.
- Saying all deficits are bad — the use of borrowed money (productive or not) matters.

activity.prompt: Direct or indirect tax?

items.text: Tax whose burden can be shifted

quiz.q: GST was introduced in India on:
quiz.why: The Goods and Services Tax came into force in India on 1 July 2017.
Corporation tax is paid directly by companies on their income and cannot be passed on, so it is a direct tax.

quiz.q: Incidence of an indirect tax can be:
quiz.why: Indirect taxes can be shifted: the seller can pass them to the buyer through higher prices.
When receipts are more than expenditure, the budget is a surplus budget.
Direct taxes such as income tax are usually progressive, with higher rates on higher incomes.

story.title: How much does the government borrow?

scenes.text: Revenue receipts ₹800; revenue expenditure ₹1,000.
Capital expenditure ₹300; non-debt capital receipts ₹50.
Fiscal deficit = ₹450 — the borrowing need.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Revenue deficit (RD)** = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts
- **Fiscal deficit (FD)** = Total expenditure − (Revenue receipts + Non-debt creating capital receipts) = **Borrowing and other liabilities**
  Non-debt capital receipts = recovery of loans + disinvestment (+ other receipts)
- **Primary deficit (PD)** = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments
  (PD shows borrowing needed for current needs excluding interest on past debt)

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: FD 6.4% of GDP; interest payments 3.4% of GDP → PD = **3.0% of GDP**. If RD is 4% of GDP, then about 62.5% of borrowing (4/6.4) finances consumption-type spending — a warning sign.

steps.title: Implications
steps.body: RD: government is dissaving; borrowing to meet consumption — reduces future capacity. FD: total borrowing; leads to rising debt and interest burden, may cause inflation (if financed by RBI) and crowd out private investment. PD = 0 means borrowing only to pay interest.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting borrowings as a capital receipt in FD — borrowings are what FD measures.
- Subtracting interest twice.
- Forgetting that recovery of loans and disinvestment reduce FD.

activity.prompt: Total expenditure 2,500; revenue receipts 1,700; recovery of loans 60; disinvestment 40; interest payments 350. Primary deficit?

quiz.why: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total receipts excluding borrowing, which is the amount the government must borrow.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments. It shows borrowing apart from interest on past debt.
Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts = 500 − 420 = 80.
Primary deficit = FD − interest payments = 300 − 300 = 0.
A revenue deficit means current spending exceeds current income, so the government is dissaving on its current account and must borrow even for its day-to-day needs.

questions.q: Union budget covers:
questions.why: The Union Budget covers one financial year, April to March.

questions.q: Borrowing is a:
questions.why: Borrowing creates a liability, so it is a capital receipt, not revenue.

questions.q: GST is a/an:
questions.why: GST is levied on the supply of goods and services and can be passed on to the buyer, so it is an indirect tax.

questions.q: Interest payment is:
questions.why: Interest payment is a current spending that does not create an asset, so it is revenue expenditure.

questions.q: Disinvestment:
questions.why: Selling government shares in public companies reduces assets and brings in money, so disinvestment is a capital receipt.

questions.q: Assertion: Fiscal deficit indicates total borrowing of the government. Reason: It is the gap between total expenditure and receipts excluding borrowings.
questions.why: Both are true. Fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus receipts other than borrowing, and that gap has to be financed by borrowing, so it indicates total borrowing.
Revenue deficit = RE − RR = 1,200 − 900 = 300.

questions.q: TE 1,500; RR 1,000; non-debt capital receipts 100. FD:
questions.why: FD = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts) = 1,500 − (1,000 + 100) = 400.

questions.q: FD 400; interest 180. PD:
questions.why: PD = FD − interest payments = 400 − 180 = 220.

questions.q: Case: Revenue receipts 600; revenue expenditure 750 (interest 120); capital expenditure 250; recovery of loans 30; disinvestment 20. FD and PD:
Case: Government cuts spending and raises taxes during high inflation. Objective:
questions.why: Cutting spending and raising taxes lowers demand to control inflation, which is the stabilisation objective of the budget.

questions.q: Case: Street lights are provided by the municipality because people cannot be excluded from using them. Concept:
questions.why: Street lights benefit everyone and no one can be excluded, so it is a public good, provided by the government.

questions.q: Case: RD is 3% of GDP and FD is 5% of GDP. Share of borrowing used to cover revenue deficit:
questions.why: The part of borrowing (FD) that finances the revenue deficit is RD/FD = 3/5 = 60%.

questions.q: Case: If primary deficit is zero but fiscal deficit is positive, it means:
options: Borrowing is only to pay interest on past debt
questions.why: PD = FD − interest. If PD is zero while FD is positive, the whole borrowing equals interest on earlier debt.

questions.q: Grants-in-aid to states (central budget) are:
questions.why: Grants-in-aid to states do not create assets for the Centre, so they are revenue expenditure.

questions.q: Which is a non-tax revenue?
questions.why: Dividends from public sector units are income from government-owned companies, not a tax, so they are non-tax revenue. Customs, GST and income tax are taxes.

questions.q: Deficit budget means:
questions.why: A deficit budget has expenditure greater than receipts.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Open Economy Macroeconomics
courses.summary: Openness in product, financial and labour markets; balance of payments — current and capital account, surplus and deficit, autonomous and accommodating transactions; foreign exchange rate — flexible, fixed and managed floating systems; depreciation, devaluation and appreciation.
outcomes: Learners can explain the three kinds of openness
Learners can classify transactions in the current and capital accounts of the BoP
Learners can compute trade balance and current account balance
Learners can explain how a flexible exchange rate is determined and compare exchange-rate systems

lessons.title: Open economy and balance of payments

scenes.text: India imports oil and exports software.
Indians abroad send money home.
All these are recorded in the balance of payments.

steps.title: Open economy
steps.body: An **open economy** interacts with other economies through: **output markets** (trade in goods and services), **financial markets** (buying and selling financial assets across borders), and **labour markets** (movement of workers).

steps.title: Balance of payments (BoP)
steps.body:
A systematic record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world in a year.
**Current account:** trade in goods (**visible** items — merchandise), trade in services (**invisible** items — IT, tourism, shipping, insurance), **income** (interest, profits, dividends, wages) and **transfers** (remittances, gifts, grants).
**Capital account:** foreign direct investment (FDI), foreign portfolio investment (FPI), external commercial borrowings, loans, banking capital, changes in foreign exchange reserves (official reserve transactions).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Classify: Import of crude oil → current account (visible). Indian student's fee paid to a US university → current account (services). A US firm buys 15% stake in an Indian company → capital account (FDI). Remittance from a worker in Dubai → current account (transfers).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Exports of goods ₹500; imports of goods ₹700 → **trade deficit ₹200**. Net invisibles (services + income + transfers) +₹150 → **current account deficit ₹50**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting remittances in the capital account — they are current transfers.
- Confusing balance of trade (only goods) with current account balance (goods + invisibles).

activity.prompt: Current account or capital account?

items.text: Foreign investor buys Indian shares on the stock exchange

quiz.why: Balance of trade covers only exports and imports of goods (visible items), and not services or transfers.
Remittances are transfers, and transfers are in the current account.
Foreign direct investment is a capital flow, so it is recorded in the capital account.

quiz.q: Exports of goods 300, imports of goods 450. Trade balance:
quiz.why: Trade balance = exports − imports of goods = 300 − 450 = −150.
Invisible items are services, income and transfers, which cannot be seen at borders. Goods are visible.

lessons.title: BoP surplus and deficit; autonomous and accommodating transactions

scenes.text: In accounting terms, the BoP always balances.
But economists talk about BoP surplus or deficit.
The difference lies in reserve changes.

steps.title: Autonomous vs accommodating
steps.body:
**Autonomous transactions:** undertaken for their own sake (profit, business needs) — independent of the BoP position ("above the line").
**Accommodating transactions:** undertaken to cover the gap in autonomous transactions — e.g. RBI drawing down or adding to foreign exchange reserves, borrowing from the IMF ("below the line").

steps.title: Surplus and deficit
steps.body:
If autonomous receipts > autonomous payments → **BoP surplus** (reserves rise). If autonomous receipts < payments → **BoP deficit** (reserves fall or official borrowing). The overall BoP (including accommodating items) always balances.
A current account deficit can be financed by a capital account surplus (net inflows).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Autonomous receipts ₹1,000 crore; autonomous payments ₹1,200 crore → BoP deficit ₹200 crore → RBI sells ₹200 crore of reserves (accommodating).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: CAD ₹50 crore; net capital inflows ₹80 crore → overall surplus ₹30 crore → **reserves rise by ₹30 crore**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying BoP is "always in balance" so there is never a deficit — the deficit refers to autonomous transactions.
- Counting reserve changes as autonomous.

activity.prompt: Current account deficit = ₹120 crore; net capital account inflow (excluding reserves) = ₹90 crore. By how much do foreign exchange reserves change? (Enter negative for a fall.)

quiz.why: Accommodating transactions, such as changes in reserves, are done to cover the gap between autonomous receipts and payments.

quiz.q: A fall in forex reserves signals:
quiz.why: Falling reserves mean the RBI is paying out foreign exchange to cover a gap, which signals a deficit in the autonomous transactions of the BoP.
Autonomous transactions are made for their own reasons (profit, trade), regardless of the BoP position.
By double-entry accounting every credit has a matching debit, so the BoP always balances in accounting terms. A surplus or deficit shows in the autonomous items.
A current account deficit can be financed by a capital account surplus (net inflows) or by drawing on foreign exchange reserves.

scenes.text: One US dollar costs ₹83 today.
More Indians want dollars to study abroad.
Demand for dollars rises — the rupee weakens.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: The **foreign exchange rate** is the price of one currency in terms of another (e.g. ₹83 = $1).

steps.title: Flexible exchange rate
steps.body:
Determined by **demand for** and **supply of** foreign exchange in the market.
**Demand for $ comes from:** imports, Indians travelling/studying abroad, Indians investing abroad, speculation (expecting $ to rise), repaying foreign loans.
**Supply of $ comes from:** exports, foreign tourists in India, FDI/FPI into India, remittances, speculation.
Demand curve slopes downward (cheaper $ → more demand); supply curve slopes upward.

steps.title: Depreciation, appreciation, devaluation, revaluation
steps.body:
- **Depreciation:** fall in value of domestic currency under a flexible rate (₹80 → ₹85 per $)
- **Appreciation:** rise in value (₹85 → ₹80 per $)
- **Devaluation / revaluation:** deliberate fall/rise by the government/central bank under a fixed rate
Depreciation makes exports cheaper for foreigners and imports costlier for residents.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Rate changes from ₹80/$ to ₹84/$ → rupee **depreciates** by 5% (in rupee terms the dollar is 5% dearer). An Indian shirt priced ₹840 now costs a US buyer $10 instead of $10.50 → exports tend to rise.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A rise in foreign investment into India increases supply of dollars → rupee **appreciates**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying "rate rose from ₹80 to ₹84, so rupee appreciated" — it depreciated (more ₹ per $).
- Using "devaluation" for market-driven changes.

activity.prompt: Does each event increase DEMAND for dollars or SUPPLY of dollars in India?

items.text: Indian students go to study in the USA
Foreign firm sets up a factory in India (FDI)
Indian company repays a dollar loan

quiz.q: Rate moves from ₹82/$ to ₹86/$. The rupee has:
quiz.why: More rupees are now needed to buy one dollar (₹86 against ₹82), so the rupee has depreciated.
Depreciation makes exports cheaper for foreigners and imports costlier at home, so exports tend to rise and imports to fall.

quiz.q: Under a flexible system the rate is determined by:
options: Demand and supply of foreign exchange
quiz.why: In a flexible (floating) system the exchange rate is set by the demand and supply of foreign exchange in the market.

quiz.q: Deliberate reduction in value under fixed rate:
quiz.why: Under a fixed exchange rate, a deliberate cut in the official value of the currency by the government is devaluation.
More FDI inflow raises the supply of foreign currency, so the rupee gains value, which is appreciation.

scenes.text: Under a fixed system, the government pegs the rate.
Under a flexible system, the market decides.
India follows a managed float.

steps.title: Fixed exchange rate
steps.body: Rate fixed by the government/central bank (historically linked to gold or a major currency). Merits: stability, no speculation, encourages trade and investment. Demerits: needs large reserves to defend; may lead to black markets; less independence of monetary policy.

steps.title: Flexible (floating) exchange rate
steps.body: Rate decided by market forces. Merits: no need for large reserves, automatic BoP adjustment, independent monetary policy. Demerits: instability, speculation, uncertainty for trade.

steps.title: Managed floating ("dirty floating")
steps.body: Market determines the rate, but the central bank intervenes (buying/selling foreign currency) to reduce excessive fluctuations. **India follows a managed floating system** (RBI intervenes to smooth volatility).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: The rupee is falling sharply; RBI **sells dollars** from its reserves → supply of $ rises → rupee's fall is moderated. This is managed floating.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: The rupee is rising too fast and hurting exporters; RBI **buys dollars** → demand for $ rises → appreciation slows (and reserves rise).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying India has a fixed exchange rate.
- RBI sells dollars to stop the rupee falling (not buys).

activity.prompt: Match the feature to the exchange-rate system
pairs: Rate set purely by market demand and supply
Needs large reserves to maintain the rate

quiz.why: India follows a managed floating system: the rate is market-determined, with RBI stepping in when needed.

quiz.q: To stop a sharp fall of the rupee, RBI:
quiz.why: Selling dollars from reserves raises the supply of dollars, so rupee falls less steeply.

quiz.q: A merit of a fixed rate:
quiz.why: A fixed exchange rate gives stability, which helps trade and investment planning.

quiz.q: A demerit of a flexible rate:
quiz.why: Flexible rates can change often and by a lot, creating uncertainty for traders and investors.
Managed floating is also called dirty floating, because the central bank intervenes, unlike pure (clean) floating.

questions.q: BoP is a record of:
options: All economic transactions with the rest of the world
questions.why: The balance of payments records all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world in a period.

questions.q: Trade in services is:
questions.why: Services such as banking, software and tourism cannot be seen at the border, so trade in services is invisible trade.

questions.q: India's exchange-rate system:
questions.why: India follows a managed floating exchange rate system.

questions.q: FDI is recorded in:
questions.why: Foreign direct investment is a capital flow, so it appears in the capital account.

questions.q: Rupee falls from ₹80/$ to ₹83/$:
questions.why: More rupees are needed per dollar, from ₹80 to ₹83, so the rupee has depreciated. The market caused it, so it is not devaluation.

questions.q: Assertion: Depreciation of the domestic currency may raise exports. Reason: Domestic goods become cheaper for foreigners.
questions.why: Both are true. A fall in the home currency makes domestic goods cheaper in foreign currency terms, so foreign demand and exports may rise.

questions.q: Exports of goods 400; imports of goods 550; net invisibles +100. Current account balance:
questions.why: Trade balance = 400 − 550 = −150. Adding net invisibles of +100 gives a current account balance of −50 (a deficit).

questions.q: Which raises the supply of dollars in India?
questions.why: Foreign tourists spending in India bring in dollars, so they increase the supply of dollars. The other options use up dollars.

questions.q: Case: RBI buys dollars in the market to stop rapid appreciation. Effect on reserves:
questions.why: Buying dollars means the RBI adds foreign currency to its stock, so reserves rise.

questions.q: Case: CAD ₹200 crore; net capital inflow ₹150 crore. Reserves:
questions.why: The deficit of 200 is financed by 150 of capital inflow and the remaining 50 from reserves, so reserves fall by ₹50 crore.

questions.q: Case: A government officially lowers the pegged value of its currency. Term:
questions.why: Under a pegged system, an official cut in the currency's value by the government is devaluation.

questions.q: Case: Indian goods priced ₹1,000; rate moves from ₹80/$ to ₹100/$. Price for a US buyer changes from:
questions.why: At ₹80/$ the price is 1,000/80 = $12.50. At ₹100/$ it is 1,000/100 = $10, so goods become cheaper to US buyers.

questions.q: Case: Autonomous receipts ₹900, autonomous payments ₹750. Position and accommodating action:
questions.why: Autonomous receipts exceed payments by 900 − 750 = ₹150, a surplus, which the RBI covers by buying foreign exchange, so reserves rise.

questions.q: Case: Speculators expect the dollar to rise and buy dollars now. Effect under flexible rate:
questions.why: Buying dollars raises the demand for dollars, which raises their price in rupees, so the rupee depreciates.

questions.q: Remittances from abroad are:
questions.why: Money sent home from abroad is a transfer without a service in return, so it is a current transfer in the current account.

questions.q: Balance of trade deficit means:
options: Imports of goods > exports of goods
questions.why: A deficit in the balance of trade means imports of goods exceed exports of goods.

school-c12-economics-b.title: Class 12 Economics — Indian Economic Development (Part B)
school-c12-economics-b.description: Class 12 Indian Economic Development chapter by chapter — from the colonial economy to LPG, human capital, rural development, employment, environment and comparisons with neighbours — plus Revision & Practice for all of Class 12 Economics.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
courses.summary: The state of India's economy under colonial rule: low growth, agricultural stagnation, de-industrialisation, foreign trade pattern and drain, demographic conditions, occupational structure and infrastructure.
outcomes: Learners can describe the low level of economic development under colonial rule
Learners can explain causes of agricultural stagnation
Learners can explain de-industrialisation and the state of modern industry
Learners can describe the foreign trade pattern, demographic condition, occupational structure and infrastructure in 1947

lessons.title: Low economic development under colonial rule

scenes.text: Indian muslins and silks were famous across the world.
Under about two centuries of British rule, the economy stagnated.
By 1947, India was one of the poorest countries.

steps.title: Pre-colonial economy
steps.body: India was known for handicrafts — cotton and silk textiles, metal work, precious-stone work — and had a largely agrarian but self-sufficient economy.

steps.title: Colonial rule and growth
steps.body: The colonial government never seriously estimated India's national income. Estimates were made by individuals such as **Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V.K.R.V. Rao and R.C. Desai** (Rao's estimates are considered significant). Growth of aggregate real output in the first half of the 20th century was **less than 2%** a year and per capita output growth only about **half a per cent** a year.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Why was growth so low? → British economic policies served Britain's interests: India became a supplier of raw materials and a market for British manufactures.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Question: "Name two economists who estimated India's per capita income during colonial rule." → Dadabhai Naoroji and V.K.R.V. Rao (also Digby, Shirras, Desai).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the British government regularly published national income — it did not.
- Confusing Dadabhai Naoroji's "drain" idea with national income accounting by the state.

statements.s: The colonial government made official, regular national income estimates.
Per capita output growth was only about 0.5% per year in the first half of the 20th century.
India was famous for handicrafts before British rule.
British policies aimed mainly at developing Indian industry.

quiz.q: Aggregate real output growth (first half of 20th century) was:
quiz.why: Under British rule real output grew by less than 2% a year during the first half of the 20th century, which is very slow.

quiz.q: Whose national income estimates are considered significant?
quiz.why: V.K.R.V. Rao made important early estimates of India's national income, and Dadabhai Naoroji before him.

quiz.q: Under colonial rule India was mainly a:
options: Supplier of raw materials and market for British goods
quiz.why: The colonial economy was organised to supply raw materials to British industry and buy British manufactured goods.
India was well known for handicraft products such as fine cotton and silk textiles.

quiz.q: Per capita output growth was about:
quiz.why: Per capita output grew by only about 0.5% a year, because the population was growing as well.

scenes.text: About 85% of people lived in villages; most depended on agriculture.
Zamindars collected rent; cultivators remained poor.
Productivity stayed low.

steps.title: Key features
steps.body:
- Around **85%** of the population lived in villages; about **70–75%** depended directly or indirectly on agriculture
- **Stagnation** and low productivity despite expansion of area
- **Zamindari system** (Permanent Settlement in the Bengal Presidency): zamindars collected rent with little interest in improving land; fixed revenue dates caused hardship
- **Commercialisation of agriculture:** shift to cash crops (indigo, cotton, jute) for British industries rather than food
- Low technology, little irrigation and fertiliser use
- **Partition** sent much of the jute-producing area to East Pakistan, hurting Indian jute mills

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Why did zamindars not invest in land? → They were concerned only with collecting rent; land revenue terms gave them no incentive to improve agriculture.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A farmer grows indigo for export under pressure instead of food → **commercialisation of agriculture**, which raised the risk of food shortages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking commercialisation benefited farmers — gains mostly went to traders and British industry.
- Forgetting the role of Partition in the jute shortage.

activity.prompt: Tick each cause of agricultural stagnation under colonial rule
items: Zamindari system and land revenue arrangements
Commercialisation of agriculture for British needs
Low level of technology
Lack of irrigation facilities
Negligible use of fertilisers
Partition (jute areas lost)

quiz.why: The Permanent Settlement of 1793 was introduced in the Bengal Presidency, fixing the land revenue permanently.
Commercialisation of agriculture means farmers grew cash crops such as indigo or cotton for sale or export, not food for their own use.

quiz.q: Share of population dependent on agriculture:
quiz.why: About 70–75% of India's population depended on agriculture at independence.
At Partition, most jute-producing areas went to East Pakistan, while the jute mills stayed in India, hurting the industry.
Zamindars were interested only in collecting rent, whatever the condition of the land, so they did not invest in improving it.

scenes.text: Handlooms lost to cheap British cloth.
A few cotton and jute mills appeared.
TISCO started in 1907 — but capital goods industry stayed tiny.

steps.title: De-industrialisation
steps.body: Decline of India's handicraft industries. Twin motive of British policy: (1) reduce India to an exporter of raw materials for British industries; (2) turn India into a market for British manufactures. Result: unemployment of artisans and a new demand pattern for imported goods.

steps.title: Modern industry
steps.body: Started in the second half of the 19th century: **cotton textile mills** (mostly Indian-owned, western India — Maharashtra, Gujarat) and **jute mills** (mostly foreign-owned, Bengal). **TISCO** was incorporated in **1907**; sugar, cement and paper came after World War II. Very little **capital goods industry**; low industrial growth; public sector limited to railways, power, communications, ports and some departmental undertakings.

steps.title: Foreign trade
steps.body: India exported primary products (raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo, jute) and imported finished consumer goods and capital goods (machinery) from Britain. Britain had a monopoly over more than half of India's trade. The **Suez Canal (1869)** cut transport costs. India had an **export surplus**, but it was used to pay for the colonial administration, wars and invisible items — a **drain of wealth**, not an inflow of gold or goods.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Why did export surplus not help India? → It was used to meet British expenses (administration, wars, imports of invisible services) — so no real gain for India.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Where were jute mills concentrated and who owned them? → Mainly in **Bengal**, mostly by **foreigners**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying India had a trade deficit — it had an export surplus (but drained).
- Locating cotton mills in Bengal — they were mainly in western India.

activity.prompt: Match the item to the colonial-era fact

quiz.why: De-industrialisation was the decline of India's traditional handicraft industries under colonial policy.
The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) was incorporated in 1907.
India mainly exported raw materials such as cotton, jute and indigo and imported finished British goods.
Britain controlled more than half of India's foreign trade, as the Suez Canal and tariff policies favoured British interests.

quiz.q: Capital goods industry under British rule was:
quiz.why: There was hardly any capital goods industry that could produce machines, so it was largely absent.

scenes.text: High birth and death rates; low literacy.
Most worked in agriculture.
Railways spread — mostly to serve colonial needs.

steps.title: Demographic condition
steps.body: First census: **1881**. Before **1921**, India was in the first stage of demographic transition (high birth and death rates); **1921** is called the **"year of the great divide"** (after it, population grew steadily). At independence: overall literacy **less than 16%** (female about **7%**), infant mortality about **218 per 1,000**, life expectancy about **32 years**; public health facilities were very poor.

steps.title: Occupational structure
steps.body: Agriculture: about **70–75%** of the workforce; manufacturing: about **10%**; services: about **15–20%**. Regional variation — parts of the Madras Presidency, Bombay and Bengal saw some rise in manufacturing and services while Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab saw a rise in agriculture's share.

steps.title: Infrastructure
steps.body: Railways (introduced in the 1850s; the first passenger train ran in 1853), roads, ports, inland waterways, posts and telegraph developed — mainly to move raw materials and troops and to sell British goods. Railways changed the structure of the economy: widened markets, enabled commercialisation of agriculture, but hurt self-sufficiency of villages.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Why is 1921 called the year of the great divide? → It marks the shift from the first to the second stage of demographic transition — after 1921 population grew steadily as death rates began to fall.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: State one positive and one negative effect of railways. → Positive: widened markets and travel; Negative: drained raw materials and supported commercialisation that hurt food security.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the first census was in 1921 — it was 1881.
- Overstating literacy at independence (it was below 16%).

activity.prompt: Arrange these colonial-era events in order

events.text: First passenger train runs in India
"Year of the great divide" in population growth

quiz.q: The first census was conducted in:
quiz.why: The first census of India was conducted in 1881.
After 1921 population growth became steady. Birth and death rates changed, so 1921 is called the year of the great divide.
The literacy rate at independence was below 16%, and female literacy was very low.

quiz.q: Share of workforce in agriculture at independence:
quiz.why: About 70–75% of the workforce depended on agriculture at independence.

quiz.q: Infrastructure under British rule was developed mainly to:
quiz.why: The British built railways, roads and ports mainly to move raw materials and strengthen colonial control, not to develop India.

questions.q: Who made national income estimates during colonial rule?
questions.why: Early estimates of national income were made by Dadabhai Naoroji and V.K.R.V. Rao, who were Indians.

questions.q: First census of India:
questions.why: The first census of India was held in 1881.

questions.q: TISCO was set up in:
questions.why: TISCO was set up in 1907 in Jamshedpur.

questions.q: Permanent Settlement is linked to:
questions.why: The Permanent Settlement fixed land revenue permanently with zamindars, so it is linked to the zamindari system.

questions.q: Suez Canal opened in:
questions.why: The Suez Canal opened in 1869, shortening the sea route between India and Britain.

questions.q: Assertion: India's export surplus did not benefit the economy. Reason: It was used to pay for British administration, wars and invisible items.
questions.why: Both are true. The export surplus did not bring in goods or investment for India. It paid for British administration, wars and other invisible items, so it did not help the economy.

questions.q: Jute mills under colonial rule were mainly in:
questions.why: Jute mills were mainly in Bengal, and mostly owned by foreigners.

questions.q: De-industrialisation was due to British aim of making India:
options: Raw-material exporter and market for British goods
questions.why: British policy aimed to make India a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods, which ruined India's handicrafts.

questions.q: Infant mortality rate at independence (approx.):
