questions.why: The infant mortality rate was very high, about 218 per thousand, at independence.

questions.q: Case: A village switches from growing food grains to indigo for export; later it faces food shortage. Concept:
questions.why: Replacing food grains with an export cash crop like indigo is commercialisation of agriculture, which cut local food supply.

questions.q: Case: Weavers lost their livelihood as cheap mill-made British cloth flooded markets. Concept:
questions.why: When cheap British mill cloth destroyed Indian handicrafts and weavers' livelihoods, it was de-industrialisation.

questions.q: Which statement on occupational structure at independence is correct?
questions.why: At independence agriculture employed about 70–75% of the workforce, manufacturing about 10% and services about 15–20%.

questions.q: Case: After 1921 population rose steadily because death rates fell while birth rates stayed high. This shows:
options: Transition to the second stage of demographic transition
questions.why: After 1921 death rates fell but birth rates stayed high, so population grew steadily. This marks the shift toward the second stage of demographic transition.

questions.q: Assertion: Railways helped commercialisation of Indian agriculture. Reason: They connected distant markets and ports.
questions.why: Both are true. Railways linked distant markets and ports, so farmers could sell cash crops widely, which promoted commercialisation.

questions.q: Life expectancy at independence (approx.):
questions.why: Life expectancy was only about 32 years at independence.

questions.q: Capital goods industry at independence was:
questions.why: At independence the capital goods industry was very small, so India depended on imported machines.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Indian Economy 1950–1990
courses.summary: Planning in India — the Planning Commission, Five Year Plans and their goals; agriculture — land reforms, the Green Revolution and the subsidy debate; industry and trade — the Industrial Policy Resolution 1956, small-scale industry, licensing and import substitution; and an appraisal.
outcomes: Learners can explain the goals of Five Year Plans
Learners can evaluate land reforms and the Green Revolution
Learners can explain the IPR 1956, licensing and the role of the public sector
Learners can explain import substitution and appraise 1950–1990 policies

story.title: A new nation chooses its path

scenes.text: In 1950 India set up the Planning Commission.
The First Five Year Plan began in 1951.
India chose a mixed economy.

steps.title: Planning in India
steps.body:
India chose a **mixed economy** — coexistence of public and private sectors, with the state playing a leading role. The **Planning Commission** was set up in **1950** with the Prime Minister as chairperson. Plans were for five years (**First Plan 1951–56**). In **2015** the Planning Commission was replaced by **NITI Aayog** (National Institution for Transforming India).
The **Second Plan (1956–61)** was based on the ideas of **P. C. Mahalanobis** — emphasis on heavy industry.

steps.title: Goals of Five Year Plans
steps.body:
- **Growth:** increase in GDP (capacity to produce)
- **Modernisation:** adoption of new technology and changes in social outlook (e.g. women's rights)
- **Self-reliance:** avoid dependence on foreign countries, especially for food
- **Equity:** benefits of growth should reach the poor

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
"A plan targets use of HYV seeds and new machines." → goal: **modernisation**.
"A plan restricts food imports and boosts domestic production." → **self-reliance**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Why is equity a goal? → Growth alone can concentrate gains among the rich; plans aimed to ensure basic needs (food, housing, education, health) for all.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying NITI Aayog was created in 1950.
- Confusing modernisation (technology + social change) with growth (output).

activity.prompt: Match the policy to the plan goal
pairs: Adopting new technology; equal rights for women
Producing our own food rather than importing

quiz.q: Planning Commission was set up in:
quiz.why: The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950.

quiz.q: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in:
quiz.why: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.

quiz.q: The Second Five Year Plan was based on ideas of:
quiz.why: The Second Five Year Plan (1956–61) followed the model of P. C. Mahalanobis, stressing heavy industry.
India adopted a mixed economy, with both public and private sectors.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a goal of the plans?
quiz.why: The plans aimed at growth, modernisation, self-reliance and equity. They did not aim at privatising all industry.

scenes.text: Tenants worked land owned by absentee zamindars.
After 1947, laws abolished intermediaries.
Some tillers became owners.

steps.title: Land reforms
steps.body:
- **Abolition of intermediaries** (zamindars) — about 200 lakh tenants came into direct contact with the government
- **Land ceiling** — fixing the maximum land an individual can own; surplus redistributed to the landless
- **Tenancy reforms** — regulating rent, security of tenure, ownership rights
Success was greatest in **Kerala** and **West Bengal** (governments committed to land-to-the-tiller). Elsewhere, loopholes (transfer of land to relatives, delays in courts) limited impact.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Why does ownership raise productivity? → An owner-cultivator gains from improvements, so he invests more in land (incentive effect).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Why did land ceiling fail in many states? → Big landowners used loopholes (registering land in relatives' names), challenged laws in courts and delayed implementation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying land reforms succeeded everywhere.
- Confusing land ceiling (limit on holding) with consolidation of holdings.

statements.s: Land reforms were most successful in Kerala and West Bengal.
Land ceiling means the minimum land a farmer must own.
Owner-cultivators have a greater incentive to invest in land.
Abolition of intermediaries ended all inequality in land ownership.
statements.why: Many big landlords retained large holdings.

quiz.why: A land ceiling fixes the maximum amount of agricultural land that one person or family may own.

quiz.q: Abolition of intermediaries refers to removing:
quiz.why: Abolition of intermediaries meant removing zamindars, jagirdars and others between the state and the cultivator.

quiz.q: Land reforms were most successful in:
quiz.why: Land reforms worked best in Kerala and West Bengal, where tenants gained rights and land was redistributed.

quiz.q: A reason for limited success of land ceiling:
quiz.why: Land ceiling had limited success because big owners found loopholes, such as dividing land among relatives, and court cases delayed it.

quiz.q: Land to the tiller aims to:
quiz.why: Land to the tiller aims to give ownership of the land to those who actually cultivate it.

scenes.text: In the mid-1960s HYV seeds of wheat and rice arrived.
With fertilisers and irrigation, yields jumped.
India became self-sufficient in food grains.

steps.title: Green Revolution
steps.body:
Large increase in production of food grains from use of **high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds** together with fertilisers, pesticides and regular water supply.
**Phase 1 (mid-1960s to mid-1970s):** limited to states with assured irrigation — **Punjab, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu**; mainly wheat (and rice).
**Phase 2 (mid-1970s to mid-1980s):** spread to more states and crops.
Benefits: self-sufficiency in food grains; **marketed surplus** (portion sold in the market) rose → lower food prices; government built buffer stocks.
Concerns: benefits initially favoured richer farmers; risk of pest attacks; regional inequality.

steps.title: Subsidy debate
steps.body: Subsidies on fertilisers, power and water encouraged adoption of new technology by small farmers. Critics argue they are a fiscal burden, benefit the fertiliser industry and richer farmers, and lead to overuse of resources. Supporters argue farming is risky and most farmers are poor — so targeted subsidies are justified.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Why did Punjab benefit first? → It had **assured irrigation** and better infrastructure, needed for HYV seeds.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A farmer produces 100 quintals, keeps 20 for family use, sells 80 → **marketed surplus = 80 quintals**.

steps.title: Agriculture by 1990
steps.body: Agriculture's share in GDP fell, but its share of the workforce remained high (around 65% in 1990) — industry and services did not absorb enough workers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Green Revolution covered all crops equally from the start — it was mainly wheat and rice.
- Confusing marketed surplus with total output.

activity.prompt: A farmer produces 250 quintals of wheat, keeps 40 quintals for family consumption and 10 for seed. Marketed surplus (quintals)?

quiz.why: HYV stands for high-yielding variety, the improved seeds of the Green Revolution.

quiz.q: Green Revolution first phase was limited to:
quiz.why: In the first phase the Green Revolution was limited to wheat and rice in Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.

options: Portion of output sold in the market
quiz.why: Marketed surplus is the part of a farm's output that is sold in the market, after the farmer's own use.

options: Fiscal burden and overuse of resources
quiz.why: Farm subsidies are criticised for placing a heavy burden on government finances and for encouraging overuse of fertiliser and water.

quiz.q: Main crops in the first phase:
quiz.why: The first phase of the Green Revolution mainly raised wheat (and rice) output.

scenes.text: Private capital was scarce in 1950.
The state set up steel plants, power and heavy industry.
Licences controlled who could produce what.

steps.title: Industrial Policy Resolution 1956
steps.body: Classified industries into three categories: (1) industries **exclusively owned by the state**; (2) industries where the **private sector supplements** the state (state starts new units); (3) remaining industries left to the **private sector**. Private industry was controlled through **industrial licensing** (licence needed to start a unit or expand). Licences were also used to promote industry in backward regions.

steps.title: Small-scale industry
steps.body: The **Karve Committee** (Village and Small-Scale Industries Committee, 1955) recommended using small industry for rural development. Small-scale units are labour-intensive (more employment). Many products were **reserved** for small-scale industry; they got concessions (lower excise duty, bank loans at lower interest).

steps.title: Trade policy: import substitution
steps.body: Inward-looking trade strategy — produce at home what was imported. Tools: **tariffs** (taxes on imports) and **quotas** (limits on quantity). Aim: protect domestic (infant) industries from foreign competition and save foreign exchange.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Why was the public sector given a leading role? → Private industrialists lacked capital and the market was too small; the state wanted to control the "commanding heights" of the economy.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A quota allows only 10,000 imported cars a year → **quantitative restriction** (import substitution tool) to protect domestic car makers.

steps.title: Effects of industrial policies
steps.body: Industry's share of GDP rose substantially; industry became diversified. But many public sector units made losses; licensing ("permit licence raj") led to delays and corruption; protection reduced incentives to improve quality; inefficiency persisted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying IPR 1956 nationalised all industry.
- Confusing tariff (tax) with quota (quantity limit).

activity.prompt: Tariff or quota?

items.text: Only 5,000 tonnes of steel may be imported

quiz.why: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 divided industries into three categories: state-owned, mixed, and private.
The Karve Committee (1955) looked at how to promote village and small-scale industries.

options: Producing at home what was imported
quiz.why: Import substitution means producing at home goods that were earlier imported, to reduce dependence on imports.

options: A limit on quantity of imports
quiz.why: A quota sets an upper limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported.

options: Regulate private industry and promote regional balance
quiz.why: Industrial licensing aimed to regulate private industry and spread industry to backward regions, promoting regional balance.

scenes.text: Food self-sufficiency, diversified industry.
Loss-making PSUs, red tape, little competition.
Leading to the 1991 reforms.

steps.title: Achievements
steps.body:
- Self-sufficiency in food grains (Green Revolution)
- Diversified industrial base; growth of heavy industry
- Large public sector in infrastructure and basic industries
- Expansion of education and research institutions

steps.title: Shortcomings
steps.body:
- Many PSUs incurred losses; drain on government resources
- "Permit licence raj" — excessive controls, delays, corruption
- Protection from foreign competition reduced efficiency and quality
- Agriculture still employed most workers; poverty and inequality remained high
- These problems contributed to the push for reforms in **1991**

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: "Even after 40 years, about 65% of the workforce was in agriculture." → industry and services failed to absorb labour.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A consumer had to wait years for a car or telephone connection → result of licensing and lack of competition.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the 1950–90 period had no achievements.
- Ignoring that protection was meant to help infant industries initially.

activity.prompt: Achievement or shortcoming of 1950–90 policies?

quiz.why: A major achievement of the 1950–90 period was self-sufficiency in food grains, thanks to the Green Revolution.
The permit licence raj refers to the heavy, detailed government controls and licences over private business.

quiz.q: Share of workforce in agriculture in 1990 was about:
quiz.why: In 1990 about 65% of the workforce still depended on agriculture, little changed from independence.
Protection from foreign competition reduced pressure to improve, so efficiency and quality suffered.
The shortcomings of the 1950–90 policy, such as low growth and inefficiency, led to the 1991 economic reforms.

questions.q: Planning Commission chairperson:
questions.why: The Prime Minister was the chairperson of the Planning Commission.

questions.q: First Five Year Plan period:
questions.why: The First Five Year Plan ran from 1951 to 1956.

questions.q: NITI Aayog came in:
questions.why: NITI Aayog was set up in 2015, replacing the Planning Commission.

questions.q: Land ceiling means:
questions.why: A land ceiling sets the maximum land holding an individual or family may have.

questions.q: Green Revolution relied on:
questions.why: The Green Revolution depended on HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers and assured irrigation.

questions.q: Assertion: Small-scale industries were promoted. Reason: They are more labour-intensive and generate employment.
questions.why: Both are true. Small-scale industries need more workers per unit of capital, so they create more jobs, which is why they were promoted.

questions.q: Import substitution tools:
questions.why: Import substitution used tariffs (taxes on imports) and quotas (limits on quantity) to protect home industries.

questions.q: Case: A state introduces a law fixing maximum family land at 15 acres and redistributes the rest. Policy:
questions.why: Fixing a maximum landholding and redistributing the excess is a land ceiling.

questions.q: Case: Farmer produces 120 quintals; consumes 30; sells 90. Marketed surplus:
questions.why: Marketed surplus is output sold: 120 − 30 kept for own use = 90 quintals.

questions.q: Case: A plan promotes use of computers and equal rights for women. Goal:
questions.why: Using computers and giving women equal rights are part of modernising technology and social outlook, so the goal is modernisation.

questions.q: Case: Under IPR 1956, the state alone could set up units in atomic energy and arms. Category:
questions.why: In IPR 1956 industries like atomic energy and arms were reserved for the state, so they were exclusively state-owned.

questions.q: Case: Critics say fertiliser subsidies mostly benefit richer farmers and the fertiliser industry. Counter-argument:
options: Farming is risky and most farmers are poor; targeted subsidies help adoption
questions.why: Defenders argue that farming is risky and most farmers are poor, so subsidies, if targeted, help them adopt new technology.

questions.q: Why did Green Revolution first succeed in Punjab?
questions.why: Punjab had assured irrigation, good infrastructure and prosperous farmers, so HYV seeds worked there first.

questions.q: Case: Despite rising industrial output, a large share of workers remained in farming in 1990. Interpretation:
options: Industry and services failed to absorb enough labour
questions.why: If many workers remain in farming despite industrial growth, then industry and services have not created enough jobs to absorb them.

questions.q: Assertion: Protection from imports helped infant industries but later reduced efficiency. Reason: Lack of competition reduces the pressure to improve quality and cut costs.
questions.why: Both are true. Protection helped young industries start, but without competition firms had little pressure to improve quality or cut costs, so efficiency fell.

questions.q: The Second Plan emphasised:
questions.why: The Second Plan (1956–61) emphasised the growth of heavy industry such as steel and machinery.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal
courses.summary: The 1991 crisis, the New Economic Policy — stabilisation and structural reforms; liberalisation of industry, finance, taxes, foreign exchange and trade; privatisation and disinvestment; globalisation, outsourcing and the WTO; and an appraisal of the reforms.
outcomes: Learners can explain the causes of the 1991 economic crisis
Learners can describe liberalisation measures in each sector
Learners can explain privatisation and disinvestment
Learners can explain globalisation, outsourcing and the WTO
Learners can appraise the reforms with arguments for and against

lessons.title: The 1991 crisis and the New Economic Policy

scenes.text: By 1991 India's foreign exchange reserves could pay for only about two weeks of imports.
India approached the World Bank and the IMF.
In July 1991 the New Economic Policy began.

steps.title: Causes of the crisis
steps.body:
- Persistent **fiscal deficits** — government spending far exceeded revenue; development spending on social sector did not generate quick returns
- **Balance of payments crisis** — imports grew faster than exports; foreign exchange reserves fell to a level that could finance only about **two weeks of imports**
- High **inflation**; essential goods became costly
- Inability to repay foreign loans

steps.title: New Economic Policy (NEP), 1991
steps.body:
India borrowed about **$7 billion** from the World Bank (IBRD) and the IMF, agreeing to reforms.
**Stabilisation measures** (short-term): correct BoP and control inflation — maintain adequate reserves, keep prices under control.
**Structural reform measures** (long-term): improve efficiency and international competitiveness by removing rigidities — liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: "Reducing the fiscal deficit and building up foreign exchange reserves in 1991–92" → **stabilisation**. "Removing industrial licensing" → **structural reform**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Why did India go to the IMF? → It needed foreign exchange urgently to pay for imports and repay loans; reserves were almost exhausted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing stabilisation (short-term fire-fighting) with structural reform (long-term change).
- Dating the NEP to 1990 — it was 1991.

activity.prompt: Stabilisation or structural reform?

quiz.why: The New Economic Policy was announced in 1991.

quiz.q: In 1991 reserves could pay for imports of about:
quiz.why: In 1991 foreign exchange reserves had fallen so low that they could finance imports for only about two weeks.
Stabilisation measures are short-term steps to fix problems such as the balance of payments and inflation.
India took loans from the World Bank and the IMF in 1991, and agreed to reforms in return.

quiz.q: A root cause of the crisis:
quiz.why: Large fiscal deficits over years meant heavy government borrowing and high inflation, which was a root cause of the 1991 crisis.

scenes.text: Licences abolished for almost all industries.
Private and foreign banks allowed to grow.
Tax rates cut; tariffs lowered.

steps.title: Industrial sector
steps.body: Industrial licensing abolished for almost all products except a few (alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, industrial explosives, electronics, aerospace, drugs and pharmaceuticals). Industries reserved for the public sector reduced to a few (defence equipment, atomic energy generation, railway transport). Many goods de-reserved from small-scale industry; market allowed to set prices in many industries.

steps.title: Financial sector
steps.body: RBI's role shifted from **regulator to facilitator**; private sector banks (Indian and foreign) allowed; foreign investment limit in banks raised (to about 74%); foreign institutional investors (FIIs) allowed to invest in Indian financial markets.

steps.title: Tax, foreign exchange and trade
steps.body:
**Tax reforms:** reduction in personal income tax and corporation tax rates; simplification; GST introduced in **July 2017** (one nation, one tax).
**Foreign exchange:** rupee **devalued** in 1991; later the rate became largely market-determined.
**Trade and investment:** quantitative restrictions on imports dismantled (by 2001), tariff rates reduced, export duties removed, licensing for imports eased.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A company wants to start a new steel plant. Before 1991 it needed a licence; after 1991 → **no licence required** (de-licensing).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: RBI now allows banks to fix many interest rates themselves → RBI as **facilitator**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all industries were de-licensed — a few remain.
- Saying GST was introduced in 1991.

activity.prompt: Match the reform to its sector
pairs: Removal of quantitative restrictions on imports

quiz.q: After 1991, RBI became more of a:
quiz.why: After 1991 the RBI moved from controlling banks directly to being a facilitator, letting banks take their own decisions.
GST was introduced in July 2017 as a major tax reform.
In July 1991 the rupee was devalued against foreign currencies to improve exports and the balance of payments.

quiz.q: Which still needs a licence after 1991?
quiz.why: Some industries, such as industrial explosives, remained subject to licensing for safety and strategic reasons.

quiz.q: Removal of quantity limits on imports relates to:
quiz.why: Removing quantitative limits (quotas) on imports is a trade policy reform.

scenes.text: A government company sells part of its shares to the public.
The government raises money; the firm gets market discipline.
Top PSUs get Navratna/Maharatna status for autonomy.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Privatisation** = shedding ownership or management of a government-owned enterprise. It can happen by (1) withdrawal of government from ownership/management, or (2) outright sale of PSUs. **Disinvestment** = sale of part of government's equity in PSUs to the public. Purpose: improve financial discipline and efficiency, raise funds, encourage private capital and technology.

steps.title: Navratna and Maharatna
steps.body: To improve efficiency, profit-making PSUs were given greater managerial and financial autonomy: **Maharatna**, **Navratna** and **Miniratna** status (Navratna policy introduced in 1997). Many became globally competitive.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: The government sells 10% of its shares in a public sector oil company through the stock exchange → **disinvestment**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A profitable PSU is allowed to decide investments without seeking government approval up to a large limit → effect of **Navratna/Maharatna** status (autonomy).

steps.title: Criticism
steps.body: Critics say PSU assets were sometimes undervalued during disinvestment, and funds were used to cover revenue shortfalls rather than for development or improving PSUs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating privatisation with liberalisation.
- Saying every disinvestment means full sale — often only part of the shares are sold.

statements.s: Disinvestment means selling part of government equity in PSUs.
Navratna status reduced autonomy of PSUs.
One criticism is undervaluation of PSU assets.
Privatisation always means the government sells 100% of shares.

quiz.why: Disinvestment means selling government shares in public sector companies, which is a form of privatisation.
The Navratna policy was introduced in 1997 to give better public sector units more freedom.
Privatisation aims to bring in efficiency and market discipline through private ownership and competition.
Critics say disinvestment sold public assets at less than their true worth, so the government lost money.
Maharatna status gives the largest PSUs more financial and managerial autonomy.

scenes.text: A bank customer in London calls a helpline answered in Bengaluru.
India became a hub for outsourcing.
The WTO set the rules for world trade.

steps.title: Globalisation
steps.body: Integration of the economy with the world economy — through trade, investment, technology and movement of people. Policies: reduction of trade barriers, openness to FDI and portfolio investment.

steps.title: Outsourcing
steps.body: A company hires regular services from external sources, often from other countries. India gained from **IT-enabled services**: call centres (voice-based BPO), record keeping, accountancy, banking services, music recording, film editing, book transcription, clinical advice, teaching. Reasons: cheap skilled labour, English-speaking workforce, IT revolution.

steps.title: World Trade Organization (WTO)
steps.body: Founded in **1995** as the successor to **GATT** (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, 1948). India is a founding member. Aims: establish a rule-based trade regime; remove tariff and non-tariff barriers; enlarge markets; protect the environment; facilitate trade in goods and services (including intellectual property).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A US hospital sends medical transcription work to a firm in Chennai → **outsourcing**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: India reduces customs duties on imports as per WTO commitments → **globalisation** through trade liberalisation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying WTO was founded in 1948 (that was GATT).
- Thinking outsourcing is only call centres.

activity.prompt: Put these in chronological order

events.text: WTO established as successor to GATT

quiz.why: The WTO was founded in 1995.
The WTO took over from GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade) as the body for world trade rules.
Outsourcing means hiring services, or parts of work, from outside sources, often in another country.

quiz.q: India gained from outsourcing due to:
quiz.why: India gained from outsourcing because of its large pool of skilled, English-speaking workers at low cost.
Globalisation means integration of the domestic economy with the world economy through trade, investment and technology.

scenes.text: GDP growth rose, forex reserves soared.
But farm distress and jobless growth were concerns.
Economists still debate.

steps.title: Positive outcomes
steps.body:
- Higher GDP growth (especially services)
- Rise in FDI and foreign institutional investment; large foreign exchange reserves
- India became a major exporter of IT services, auto parts, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals
- More consumer choice; better quality goods

steps.title: Criticisms
steps.body:
- **Neglect of agriculture:** public investment in agriculture (irrigation, power, roads, research) declined; removal of fertiliser subsidy raised costs; shift to export crops reduced food production; reduced tariffs exposed farmers to global price swings
- **Industrial sector:** cheaper imports hurt some domestic industries; inadequate infrastructure; developed countries kept their own barriers
- **Disinvestment:** undervaluation; proceeds used for revenue shortfalls
- **Fiscal policies:** tax cuts did not always raise revenue; reduced scope for social spending
- **Uneven benefits:** growth concentrated in some sectors and regions; job creation lagged (jobless growth)

steps.title: Demonetisation (2016)
steps.body: On **8 November 2016**, ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes were withdrawn as legal tender. Stated aims: curb black money, counterfeit currency and terror financing, and promote digital payments. Effects are debated: digital payments grew, but the informal sector faced short-term disruption.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: "Farmers growing cotton faced losses when world prices crashed after tariffs were cut." → criticism: **exposure of agriculture to global markets**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: "Services such as IT grew fast and attracted foreign investment." → positive outcome of liberalisation and globalisation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Presenting only positives or only negatives — exams expect a balanced appraisal.

activity.prompt: Positive outcome or criticism of the reforms?

items.text: Decline in public investment in agriculture
Growth concentrated in a few sectors

quiz.q: Which sector grew fastest after reforms?
quiz.why: The services sector grew fastest after the 1991 reforms and now has the largest share of GDP.

quiz.q: A criticism of reforms for agriculture:
quiz.why: Critics say agriculture suffered because public investment in it fell after the reforms.

quiz.q: Demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes was announced on:
quiz.why: Demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes was announced on 8 November 2016.

options: Output grows without matching growth in employment
quiz.why: Jobless growth means output rises without a matching rise in employment.
After the reforms foreign exchange reserves rose substantially, from a very low level in 1991.

questions.q: The New Economic Policy was announced in:
questions.why: The New Economic Policy was announced in 1991.

questions.q: WTO was established in:
questions.why: The WTO was established in 1995.

questions.q: Disinvestment is linked to:
questions.why: Disinvestment is the sale of government shares in public sector units, so it is part of privatisation.

questions.q: Stabilisation measures aim at:
questions.why: Stabilisation measures are short-term steps to correct balance-of-payments problems and control inflation.

questions.q: GST was introduced in:
questions.why: GST was introduced in India in 2017.

questions.q: Assertion: Outsourcing grew rapidly in India after 1991. Reason: India had a large pool of skilled, English-speaking, low-cost workers and improving IT.
questions.why: Both are true. India's pool of skilled, English-speaking, low-cost workers and improving IT services made it a good outsourcing destination.

questions.q: Which industry still requires a licence after 1991?
questions.why: Hazardous chemicals still need a licence after 1991 for reasons of safety and environment.

questions.q: Case: RBI allows banks freedom to set many interest rates. Reform type:
questions.why: Freeing banks to set many interest rates is a financial sector reform, part of the reforms in banking and capital markets.

questions.q: Case: The government sold 5% shares of a PSU via the stock exchange. This is:
questions.why: Selling some of the government's shares in a public sector company is disinvestment.

questions.q: Case: Reserves fell to cover only about two weeks of imports and inflation was high. Year:
questions.why: Reserves covering only two weeks of imports, together with high inflation, mark the 1991 balance of payments crisis.

questions.q: Case: An Indian firm edits films for a Hollywood studio. Concept:
questions.why: Doing work such as film editing for a foreign firm is outsourcing, where services are bought from outside sources.

questions.q: Case: Farmers shifted from food crops to export crops and food prices rose. Criticism:
questions.why: Critics say reforms neglected agriculture and food security, as a shift to export crops raised food prices.

questions.q: Which is a structural reform?
questions.why: Removing industrial licensing changes the structure of the economy for the long term, so it is a structural reform. The others are short-term fixes.

questions.q: Case: Tax rates were cut, but tax revenue did not rise as expected and social spending was squeezed. Criticism area:
questions.why: If tax cuts did not raise revenue, the government had less money for social spending, which is a criticism of the reform in fiscal policy.

questions.q: Assertion: Reduction of import tariffs can hurt some domestic industries. Reason: Cheaper imports increase competition for domestic producers.
questions.why: Both are true. Cutting import tariffs makes imports cheaper, so domestic producers face stronger competition and some may lose sales, which is why the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: India borrowed about ___ from the IMF/World Bank in 1991.
questions.why: In 1991 India took loans of about $7 billion from the IMF and World Bank to meet its balance of payments crisis.

questions.q: Navratna status relates to:
questions.why: Navratna status gave profitable public sector units more financial and managerial autonomy.

courses.title: Human Capital Formation in India
courses.summary: Meaning and sources of human capital, its role in economic growth, human capital vs human development, and the state of education in India — spending, policies and achievements.
outcomes: Learners can define human capital and list its sources
Learners can compare human capital and physical capital
Learners can explain the link between human capital and growth, and human capital vs human development
Learners can describe the growth of the education sector in India

lessons.title: Meaning and sources of human capital

scenes.text: Riya's parents spend on her engineering degree.
Years later, her higher earnings repay the cost.
Education is an investment — human capital.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Human capital** = the stock of skill and expertise of a nation at a point of time (doctors, engineers, teachers, skilled workers). **Human capital formation** = the process of adding to it over time. Just as physical capital increases output, so does human capital.

steps.title: Sources
steps.body:
- **Expenditure on education** (raises future income)
- **Expenditure on health** (preventive, curative, social medicine, clean water, sanitation) — a healthy person works better
- **On-the-job training** (firms train workers; returns in higher productivity)
- **Migration** (people move for better jobs — costs of transport, higher cost of living; but higher earnings)
- **Expenditure on information** (about labour markets, education, health)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A company sends workers for a 3-month skill course in a new technology → **on-the-job training**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A nurse from Kerala moves to Gulf countries for higher pay → **migration** as a source of human capital (in terms of earnings and productivity).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing human capital (stock) with human capital formation (process).
- Leaving out health as a source.

activity.prompt: Match the example to the source of human capital
pairs: Moving to a city for a better job

quiz.why: Human capital is the stock of skill, knowledge and health embodied in people, which makes them more productive.

quiz.q: Which is a source of human capital?
quiz.why: Spending on health keeps people fit and productive, so it builds human capital. Roads, machinery and oil imports are physical or other investments.

quiz.q: Migration is a source because it:
options: Raises earnings and use of skills
quiz.why: People who migrate for better jobs earn more and use their skills more fully, so migration is a source of human capital formation.
Human capital formation is a continuing process of adding to people's skills and knowledge over time.

quiz.q: Information about job markets is a source because it:
quiz.why: Good information on jobs and wages helps people choose better, so it is a source of human capital formation.

lessons.title: Human capital vs physical capital; role in growth

scenes.text: A machine can be bought and sold.
Skills cannot be separated from their owner.
Both drive growth — differently.

steps.title: Differences
steps.body:
- **Tangibility:** physical capital is tangible; human capital is intangible
- **Separation:** physical capital can be separated from its owner; human capital is inseparable from the person
- **Mobility:** physical capital is fairly mobile between countries (except buildings); human capital mobility is limited by nationality and culture
- **Depreciation:** physical capital depreciates with use; human capital depreciates with ageing but can be reduced by continuous investment in education and health
- **Benefits:** physical capital benefits mainly the owner; human capital also benefits society (social benefits/externalities)

steps.title: Human capital and economic growth
steps.body: Educated, healthy workers are more productive, innovate and absorb new technology. Human capital raises GDP; growth in turn finances more education and health — a two-way relationship. Evidence: countries that invested heavily in education often grew faster.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: An educated farmer reads soil-test reports and uses fertilisers efficiently → higher output; his neighbours copy him → **social benefit** of human capital.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: India's IT boom drew on a large pool of engineers → human capital as a driver of growth (and of exports).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying human capital never depreciates.
- Saying physical capital benefits society more than human capital.

activity.prompt: Human capital or physical capital?

items.text: Can be sold separately from its owner

options: Intangible and inseparable from its owner
quiz.why: Human capital is intangible and cannot be separated from the person who has it, unlike physical capital, which can be sold separately.

quiz.q: Human capital depreciation can be reduced by:
options: Continuous investment in education and health
quiz.why: Human capital loses value as skills become outdated and people age. Continuous education, training and health care can slow this.

quiz.q: Social benefits of human capital mean:
options: Others also gain from an educated person
quiz.why: Social benefits means that others, not just the person, gain from an educated or healthy person, for example through better citizenship and spread of ideas.

quiz.q: Relationship between human capital and growth:
quiz.why: Human capital raises growth, and a richer economy can invest more in education and health, so the link runs both ways.

quiz.q: Physical capital mobility across countries is:
quiz.why: Physical capital, such as machines and funds, moves between countries more easily than people, so its mobility is relatively high.

scenes.text: Human capital view: education is valuable because it raises productivity.
Human development view: education and health are valuable in themselves.
Both matter for policy.

steps.title: Difference
steps.body:
**Human capital** treats education and health as **means** to increase labour productivity (and thus output).
**Human development** treats education and health as integral to human **well-being** — they are ends in themselves, because they expand people's choices and freedoms. Even if an investment does not raise output, it is valuable if it improves well-being.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Teaching reading to an elderly person who will not join the workforce — useless from a narrow human capital view but valuable from the **human development** view.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A government expands primary health centres to reduce suffering, not to raise GDP → human development approach.

steps.title: Policy implication
steps.body: Basic education and health are seen as human rights; governments must provide them to all, especially the poor, regardless of immediate economic returns.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying human development ignores productivity — it includes it but goes beyond.

statements.s: Human capital views education as a means to higher productivity.
Human development views education only as a way to raise GDP.
statements.why: It sees it as an end in itself.

statements.s: Basic education and health are seen as human rights in the human development view.

quiz.why: The human development view treats education as valuable in itself, because it widens people's choices and freedom, not only as a means of earning.
In the human capital view, health matters as a means to productivity and higher output.

quiz.q: Which view values literacy for the elderly?
quiz.why: Human development values literacy for its own sake, even for the elderly. The narrow human capital view values only what raises production.

quiz.q: Human development is ___ than human capital.
quiz.why: Human development is broader, since it covers wellbeing and freedom, while human capital looks only at the productive value of people.

quiz.q: Basic education as a right is part of:
quiz.why: Treating basic education as a right of every person is part of the human development view.

scenes.text: The RTE Act guarantees free schooling from 6 to 14.
Governments spend on schools, colleges and research.
Literacy has risen, but gaps remain.

steps.title: Spending and policy
steps.body:
- The **Education Commission (Kothari Commission, 1964–66)** recommended spending **6% of GDP** on education; the **National Education Policy 2020** reiterates the 6% goal. Actual public spending has generally been below this level.
- **Right to Education (RTE) Act, 2009:** free and compulsory education for children aged **6–14** (in force from 2010).
- An **education cess** (now a combined Health and Education Cess) is levied on income tax to fund education.
- Regulatory/academic bodies: Ministry of Education, **NCERT** (school curriculum), **UGC** (university grants), **AICTE** (technical education), **ICMR** (medical research).

steps.title: Achievements and challenges
steps.body:
Literacy rose sharply after independence (Census 2011: about **74%**); gender gap narrowing; huge expansion of schools and higher education institutions.
Challenges: quality of learning, dropouts, regional and gender gaps, low spending relative to targets, unemployment of educated youth, need for vocational skills.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A 9-year-old child from a poor family is refused admission because of fees in a government school. Which law protects her? → **RTE Act 2009** (free and compulsory education for 6–14).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Why does the government fund education instead of leaving it to markets? → Education has large **social benefits** and is a right; the poor may under-invest if left to the market.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the RTE covers ages 3–18 — it covers 6–14.
- Confusing UGC (universities) with AICTE (technical education).

activity.prompt: Match the body/policy to its role
pairs: Free and compulsory education for ages 6–14

quiz.why: The Right to Education Act covers free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14.
The Kothari Commission (1964–66) recommended spending 6% of GDP on education.
India's literacy rate in Census 2011 was about 74%.
The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) regulates technical education. UGC deals with universities.
India still struggles with poor learning outcomes and school dropouts, even where schools exist.

questions.q: Human capital means:
questions.why: Human capital means the skills, knowledge and expertise of people, which raise their productivity.

questions.q: RTE Act year:
questions.why: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act was passed in 2009 (in force from 2010).

questions.q: Which is NOT a source of human capital?
questions.why: Buying a tractor adds physical capital. Education, health and migration build human capital.

questions.q: Human capital is ___ from its owner.
questions.why: Human capital is inseparable from its owner, as skills cannot be detached from the person and sold.

questions.q: Human development sees education as:
questions.why: The human development approach sees education as an end in itself, as it enriches life and widens choices.

questions.q: Assertion: Government must invest in education. Reason: Education has social benefits beyond the individual.
questions.why: Both are true. Education benefits society beyond the individual, so private spending alone is not enough, and the government should invest.

questions.q: Case: A firm sends staff to learn data analytics at company cost. Source:
questions.why: Training employees at the firm's expense is on-the-job training, a source of human capital formation.

questions.q: Case: An engineer moves from Bihar to Bengaluru for a better job, paying higher rent. Source and cost:
questions.why: Moving for a better job is migration, which builds human capital through higher earnings, but it carries costs such as higher living expenses.

questions.q: Case: A child labourer aged 12 is not attending school. Which law applies?
questions.why: The Right to Education Act guarantees free and compulsory schooling for ages 6–14, so a 12-year-old should be in school.

questions.q: Which is TRUE?
options: Human capital can be sold separately
Physical capital is tangible; human capital is intangible
questions.why: Physical capital such as machines is tangible and can be sold separately. Human capital is intangible and inseparable from the person.

questions.q: Case: An educated farmer adopts drip irrigation; neighbours learn and copy. Concept:
questions.why: Neighbours copying the educated farmer's method shows a benefit that spreads to others, a social benefit (positive externality) of human capital.

questions.q: Case: Public spending on education stays near 3–4% of GDP while the target is 6%. Implication:
questions.why: Actual spending of 3–4% of GDP against a 6% target means public spending on education falls short of the goal.

questions.q: Assertion: Human capital depreciates with age. Reason: Continuous education and health spending can slow this depreciation.
options: Both true; R doesn't explain A (R is a remedy, not the cause)
questions.why: Both are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. Human capital depreciates as skills age and health declines; education and health spending is the remedy, not the cause.

questions.q: Case: A state funds adult literacy classes for elderly women not in the workforce. Which approach justifies it?
questions.why: Literacy classes for elderly women outside the workforce add no production, so only the human development view, which values education for itself, can justify them.

questions.q: UGC deals with:
questions.why: The University Grants Commission (UGC) looks after university education standards and funding.

questions.q: Health is a source of human capital because:
questions.why: Healthy people work harder and longer and lose fewer days to illness, so health raises productivity.

courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

courses.title: Rural Development
courses.summary: Meaning of rural development, rural credit and microcredit, agricultural marketing and alternative channels, diversification into productive activities, and sustainable development through organic farming.
outcomes: Learners can explain key issues in rural development
Learners can describe sources of rural credit and the role of NABARD and SHGs
Learners can explain agricultural marketing measures and alternative channels
Learners can explain diversification and organic farming

scenes.text: A small farmer borrows from a moneylender at very high interest.
A bad harvest traps him in debt.
A women's self-help group offers a cheaper loan.

steps.title: Rural development
steps.body: A comprehensive term focusing on action for the development of areas lagging behind in socio-economic development: human resources (literacy, skills, health, sanitation), land reforms, infrastructure (electricity, irrigation, credit, marketing, roads, research), and poverty alleviation.

steps.title: Rural credit
steps.body:
Farmers need credit for seeds, fertilisers, tools and family needs; the gestation period between sowing and income is long.
**Institutional sources:** commercial banks, **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)**, cooperatives and land development banks, coordinated by **NABARD** (set up in **1982**). **Kisan Credit Card** scheme gives farmers flexible credit.
**Non-institutional:** moneylenders, traders, landlords — often exploitative interest rates.
**Self-Help Groups (SHGs):** small groups (often of women) pool savings and give small loans to members — **microcredit**; linked to banks.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Twenty women in a village save ₹100 each monthly and lend to a member to buy a sewing machine → **SHG / microcredit**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A body set up in 1982 as the apex institution for rural finance → **NABARD**.

steps.title: Problems
steps.body: Inadequate institutional credit for small and marginal farmers, wilful defaults, poor recovery, loan waivers affecting bank health, continued dependence on moneylenders.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling NABARD a commercial bank — it is the apex development bank for rural credit.
- Saying moneylenders are an institutional source.

activity.prompt: Institutional or non-institutional source of rural credit?

items.text: Commercial bank via Kisan Credit Card

quiz.why: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) was set up in 1982.
Self-help groups pool the savings of members and give small loans, which is microcredit.
Regional Rural Banks are institutional sources of credit. Traders, moneylenders and landlords are non-institutional.

options: Long gestation between sowing and income
quiz.why: There is a long gap between sowing and harvest income, so farmers must borrow for inputs and living costs in between.

quiz.q: Kisan Credit Card helps farmers get:
quiz.why: The Kisan Credit Card gives farmers flexible, timely credit for farm needs.

scenes.text: A farmer sells tomatoes to a trader at a low price.
The trader uses faulty weights.
A regulated market and farmers' market help.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Agricultural marketing** = process of assembling, storing, processing, transporting, packaging, grading and distributing agricultural commodities. Problems: faulty weights and manipulation of accounts, lack of market information, poor storage, distress sales.

steps.title: Government measures
steps.body:
1. **Regulated markets** — orderly and transparent marketing conditions
2. **Physical infrastructure** — roads, railways, warehouses, cold storage, processing units
3. **Cooperative marketing** — farmers get fair prices (e.g. milk cooperatives in Gujarat)
4. **Policy instruments** — **minimum support price (MSP)**, **buffer stocks** by the Food Corporation of India, **Public Distribution System (PDS)**

steps.title: Alternative marketing channels
steps.body: Farmers sell directly to consumers: **Apni Mandi** (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan), **Hadaspar Mandi** (Pune), **Rythu Bazars** (Andhra Pradesh and Telangana), **Uzhavar Sandies** (Tamil Nadu). Also contracts with national/international fast-food chains and retailers.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: The government announces a price of ₹2,275 per quintal at which it will buy wheat to protect farmers from price falls → **MSP** (the figure is only illustrative).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A farmers' market in Tamil Nadu where farmers sell vegetables directly to consumers → **Uzhavar Sandies**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing buffer stock (government stock of grains) with PDS (distribution to consumers).
- Mixing up states for alternative channels.

activity.prompt: Match the farmers' market to its state/city

quiz.why: The minimum support price guarantees a floor price, protecting farmers from a fall in crop prices.
The Food Corporation of India buys foodgrains at MSP and maintains the buffer stocks.
Regulated markets set rules for trading, such as fair weighing and open auctions, so marketing is orderly and transparent.
Uzhavar Sandies, farmers' markets where farmers sell directly to consumers, are in Tamil Nadu.
Problems in marketing include faulty weighing and poor information on prices, which cheat farmers.

scenes.text: A family keeps two cows and sells milk to a cooperative.
Another runs a fish pond.
A third grows fruit for city markets.

steps.title: Why diversify?
steps.body: Diversification of crop production (from food crops to cash crops/horticulture) and of employment (from farming to animal husbandry, fisheries, poultry, food processing, rural industries) reduces risk, uses idle time (seasonal unemployment) and raises incomes.

steps.title: Key activities
steps.body:
- **Animal husbandry:** cattle, goats, poultry; **Operation Flood** (launched 1970) — dairy cooperatives (pooling milk, processing, marketing) made India a leading milk producer
- **Fisheries:** inland and marine; women play a large role in fish marketing
- **Horticulture:** fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices, medicinal plants — the period 1991–2003 is sometimes called the "golden revolution" in horticulture
- **Information technology:** e-governance, market information, weather and price alerts for farmers
- Non-farm activities: agro-processing, food processing, handicrafts, tourism

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A landless family earns from selling milk through a village cooperative → **animal husbandry/dairy (Operation Flood model)**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A farmer gets weather and price alerts on his phone and sells at the best mandi → role of **IT** in rural development.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Calling Operation Flood a Green Revolution programme — it is a dairy programme ("White Revolution").

activity.prompt: Match the activity to the revolution/programme
pairs: HYV seeds for wheat and rice

quiz.why: Operation Flood was the programme that built the dairy cooperative network and boosted milk production.
Spreading income over several activities means one failure hurts less, so diversification reduces risk.
The golden revolution refers to the growth of horticulture, meaning fruits, vegetables and flowers.
Food processing is a non-farm activity that gives rural people employment away from crop farming.
IT gives farmers information about weather and prices, helping them make better decisions.

scenes.text: Years of chemical use have hurt the soil.
A farmer switches to compost and natural pest control.
City buyers pay more for organic produce.

steps.title: Organic farming
steps.body: A system of farming that restores, maintains and enhances ecological balance — using organic manure, compost, crop rotation and biological pest control instead of chemical fertilisers and pesticides.

steps.title: Benefits
steps.body:
- Substitutes costlier agricultural inputs with locally produced organic inputs (cheaper)
- Generates income through exports (demand for organic food is high)
- Healthier food with more nutrients and no chemical residue
- Generates more employment (labour-intensive)
- Environment-friendly

steps.title: Challenges
steps.body: Needs awareness and willingness of farmers; inadequate infrastructure and marketing; yields may be lower initially; certification needed; shorter shelf life of organic produce; limited choice in off-season.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A farmer uses vermicompost made from farm waste instead of buying urea → **lower input cost** and better soil health.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Why do some farmers hesitate? → Yields may fall in the first years and they need assured markets/certification.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying organic farming always gives higher yields from the first year.

activity.prompt: Benefit or challenge of organic farming?

items.text: Lower yields in the initial years

quiz.why: Organic farming avoids chemical fertilisers and pesticides, and uses natural inputs like compost and manure.
Without chemical residues, organic produce is healthier food, and it also protects soil and water.
Yields are often lower in the initial years after switching to organic farming, which is a challenge for farmers.
Organic farming needs more manual work for composting, weeding and pest control, so it is labour-intensive.
By protecting soil, water and biodiversity, organic farming supports sustainable development.

questions.q: NABARD was set up in:
questions.why: NABARD was set up in 1982 to support agriculture and rural development.

questions.q: SHGs mainly promote:
questions.why: SHGs pool members' savings and give small loans, so they mainly promote microcredit.

questions.q: Operation Flood is linked with:
questions.why: Operation Flood was India's dairy programme, also called the White Revolution, which raised milk output.

questions.q: MSP is announced to:
questions.why: The minimum support price is announced to guarantee farmers a minimum price and protect them from price falls.

questions.q: Rythu Bazars are in:
questions.why: Rythu Bazars are farmers' markets in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana where farmers sell directly to consumers.

questions.q: Assertion: Farmers often depend on moneylenders. Reason: Institutional credit does not adequately reach small and marginal farmers.
questions.why: Both are true. Small and marginal farmers often cannot get enough institutional credit, so they turn to moneylenders.

questions.q: Case: The government holds wheat stocks to release in times of shortage. Policy tool:
questions.why: Holding stocks of grain to release in times of shortage is a buffer stock, kept by the government.

questions.q: Case: Women in a village pool savings and lend to members at low interest. Concept:
questions.why: Women pooling savings and lending to members at low interest are functioning as a self-help group.

questions.q: Case: A farmer adds a poultry unit to earn during the off-season. Concept:
questions.why: Adding a poultry unit to earn in the off-season is diversification of income sources.

questions.q: Case: A farmer finds traders cheating with faulty weights. Which measure addresses this?
questions.why: Regulated markets set rules for fair weights, fair auctions and transparent trading, so they address cheating by traders.

questions.q: Case: After switching to organic methods, a farmer's yield drops for two years but costs also fall. Assessment:
options: Initial yield fall is a challenge; lower input cost is a benefit
questions.why: A yield drop in the early years is a challenge, while lower costs from fewer chemical inputs are a benefit.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: Hadaspar Mandi is in Pune, Maharashtra. Apni Mandi is in Punjab, Uzhavar Sandies in Tamil Nadu and Rythu Bazars in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

questions.q: Case: Loan waivers are announced repeatedly; banks report rising defaults. Problem:
options: Weak recovery and wilful default affecting rural credit system
questions.why: Repeated loan waivers weaken the habit of repayment and lead to wilful default, which damages the rural credit system.

questions.q: Assertion: Diversification helps reduce rural unemployment. Reason: Activities like dairy and food processing provide work beyond the crop season.
questions.why: Both are true. Activities such as dairy and food processing give work beyond the crop season, so they reduce rural unemployment.

questions.q: PDS is related to:
options: Distribution of food at subsidised prices
questions.why: The Public Distribution System supplies foodgrains at subsidised prices through ration shops.

questions.q: Which is NOT an institutional source of credit?
questions.why: Moneylenders are non-institutional sources. Commercial banks, cooperatives and RRBs are institutional.

courses.title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues
courses.summary: Who is a worker, workforce participation, self-employed, regular and casual workers, distribution across sectors, formal and informal sectors, jobless growth and informalisation, kinds of unemployment and government employment programmes.
outcomes: Learners can define worker and workforce participation rate
Learners can classify workers by status and sector
Learners can distinguish formal and informal sectors
Learners can explain jobless growth, casualisation and informalisation
Learners can explain types of unemployment and government programmes

scenes.text: A woman helps on the family farm without a wage.
Her son works in an IT office.
Both are workers — they contribute to GDP.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
A **worker** is anyone engaged in an economic activity that contributes to the gross domestic product — including the self-employed and unpaid family helpers on farms or family enterprises.
**Workforce participation rate (WPR)** = (Total workers ÷ Total population) × 100.
WPR is higher in rural areas than urban (many rural people work on farms; urban youth study longer). Women's WPR is lower than men's (much of women's unpaid domestic work is not counted).

steps.title: Status of workers
steps.body:
- **Self-employed:** own and run an enterprise (farmer on own land, shop owner) — the largest category
- **Regular salaried employees:** hired and paid wages/salaries regularly
- **Casual wage labourers:** not hired regularly; paid daily; no social security
Rural areas: more self-employed and casual; urban areas: more regular salaried.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Population 10 crore; workers 4 crore → WPR = **40%**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A construction worker hired daily at a site → **casual wage labourer**. A teacher in a government school → **regular salaried**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Excluding unpaid family helpers from workers.
- Calculating WPR as workers ÷ labour force (that is a different ratio).

activity.prompt: Population of a district: 25 lakh; workers: 9 lakh. Workforce participation rate (%)?

quiz.why: The worker population ratio is workers divided by total population, multiplied by 100.

quiz.q: Largest category of workers in India:
quiz.why: Self-employed people, such as farmers and small shopkeepers, are the largest category of workers in India.
A daily-wage construction worker is hired by others on a day-to-day basis, so is a casual wage labourer.

quiz.q: Unpaid helper on family farm is:
quiz.why: An unpaid helper on a family farm contributes to output, so is counted as a worker.

quiz.q: Regular salaried jobs are more common in:
quiz.why: Regular salaried jobs are concentrated in urban areas, in offices, factories and services.

lessons.title: Distribution across sectors; formal and informal sectors

scenes.text: Most workers are still in agriculture.
Industry absorbs fewer.
Services are growing fast.

steps.title: Sectors
steps.body:
- **Primary:** agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining
- **Secondary:** manufacturing, construction, electricity/gas/water supply
- **Tertiary (services):** trade, transport, finance, real estate, public administration, other services
Agriculture still employs the largest share, though its share has been falling; services' share has been rising.

steps.title: Formal and informal sectors
steps.body:
**Formal (organised) sector:** all public sector establishments and private establishments employing **10 or more hired workers**; workers get social security (provident fund, gratuity, pension), paid leave, regulated hours, can form unions.
**Informal sector:** all other enterprises and workers — farmers, agricultural labourers, small shop owners, own-account workers; little or no social security, irregular income.
A large majority of Indian workers are in the informal sector.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A private factory employing 25 hired workers → **formal sector**. A tea stall run by its owner with one helper → **informal sector**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A worker in a private firm with 8 employees has no PF or paid leave → **informal sector** (below 10 hired workers).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all private sector jobs are informal.
- Using 20 instead of 10 workers as the cutoff (follow the NCERT definition: 10 or more hired workers).

activity.prompt: Formal or informal sector?

items.text: Worker in a private factory with 50 hired workers

quiz.q: Formal sector includes private units with at least ___ hired workers.
quiz.why: The formal (organised) sector includes private units hiring 10 or more workers, along with the public sector.

quiz.q: Social security benefits are mainly available in:
quiz.why: Formal sector workers get social security, such as PF, pensions and insurance. Informal workers mostly do not.
Construction is a secondary sector activity, as it builds things. It is often organised informally too.

quiz.q: Largest employer by sector in India:
quiz.why: Agriculture, the primary sector, employs the largest share of India's workers.

quiz.q: Most Indian workers are in the:
quiz.why: Most Indian workers are in the informal (unorganised) sector.

scenes.text: GDP grew fast in the 1990s and 2000s.
But regular jobs did not grow as fast.
More workers became casual and informal.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Jobless growth:** GDP grows without a proportionate increase in employment (e.g. through capital-intensive technology)
- **Casualisation of workforce:** rising share of casual wage labourers relative to self-employed and regular salaried workers
- **Informalisation:** rising share of workers in the informal sector, even within formal enterprises (contract workers without social security)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A car plant doubles output using robots and adds only 50 jobs → **jobless growth** (capital-intensive growth).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A factory replaces permanent workers with contract workers without PF → **informalisation** of the workforce.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Casual and informal workers face low and uncertain incomes, no social security, poor working conditions — making them vulnerable during shocks (illness, crop failure, lockdowns). Policies: skill development, MSME support, social security for unorganised workers, labour law reforms balancing flexibility and protection.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying jobless growth means no growth — output grows, jobs do not keep pace.

statements.s: Jobless growth means GDP falls.
Hiring contract workers without benefits is informalisation.
Casualisation means more casual wage labourers in the workforce.
Capital-intensive technology can contribute to jobless growth.

quiz.why: Jobless growth means output rises faster than employment, so growth does not create enough jobs.
Casualisation is the rising share of casual workers, who are hired without regular contracts.
Informalisation means more workers are in jobs with no formal contract or social security protections.
Capital-intensive technology uses machines in place of labour, so output can grow without new jobs.
Informal workers typically lack social security, such as PF, pension, paid leave and health insurance.

scenes.text: Five family members work on a farm that needs only three.
After harvest, there is no work for months.
MGNREGA offers 100 days of wage work.

steps.title: Types of unemployment
steps.body:
- **Open unemployment:** people willing and able to work have no job (common among urban educated and landless)
- **Disguised unemployment:** more people are engaged than needed; their **marginal productivity is zero** (common in family farms)
- **Seasonal unemployment:** no work during certain months (agriculture off-season)
- **Educated unemployment:** educated people unable to find suitable jobs

steps.title: Government programmes
steps.body: Direct job creation (government departments, public works) and indirect (via growth of output). Poverty alleviation and employment programmes provide wage employment and self-employment. The **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005** guarantees **100 days** of wage employment per rural household per year to adult members willing to do unskilled manual work.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A farm needs 4 workers; 7 family members work on it. Removing 3 does not reduce output → **disguised unemployment** of 3.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A rural labourer gets work building a village pond under a government guarantee scheme → **MGNREGA**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling seasonal unemployment "disguised".
- Saying MGNREGA guarantees 365 days of work.

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the type of unemployment
pairs: Graduate unable to find a suitable job
Seven people on a farm that needs four
No farm work for four months after harvest
Landless labourer searching for any work

quiz.q: MGNREGA guarantees ___ days of work per rural household per year.
quiz.why: MGNREGA guarantees up to 100 days of wage employment a year to each rural household that asks for it.
The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was enacted in 2005.

quiz.q: Disguised unemployment means marginal productivity is:
quiz.why: In disguised unemployment extra workers are not needed, so removing them does not change output; their marginal productivity is zero.
Seasonal unemployment is common in agriculture, where work is available only in some seasons such as sowing and harvest.

options: People willing to work have no work
quiz.why: Open unemployment means people who are willing and able to work at the going wage have no work.

questions.q: A worker contributes to:
questions.why: A worker produces goods or services, which adds to the country's GDP.

questions.q: MGNREGA year:
questions.why: MGNREGA was enacted in 2005.

questions.q: Most common status of workers in India:
questions.why: Self-employed workers are the biggest group, ahead of casual and regular salaried workers.

questions.q: Formal sector includes private units with ___ or more hired workers.
questions.why: The formal sector includes private units with 10 or more hired workers.

questions.q: Disguised unemployment is common in:
questions.why: Disguised unemployment is common on small family farms where more people work than are needed.

questions.q: Assertion: WPR is lower for women. Reason: Much of women's unpaid domestic work is not counted as economic activity.
questions.why: Both are true. A lot of women's unpaid household work is not counted as economic activity, which lowers their measured workforce participation.

questions.q: Population 50 lakh; workers 20 lakh. WPR:
questions.why: WPR = workers ÷ population × 100 = 20 ÷ 50 × 100 = 40%.

questions.q: Case: A daily-wage loader at a mandi without fixed employer. Status:
questions.why: A loader paid by the day with no fixed employer is a casual wage labourer.

questions.q: Case: A tailor runs her own shop at home. Status:
questions.why: A tailor with her own shop earns by running her own work, so she is self-employed.

questions.q: Case: GDP grew 7% but employment grew only 1%. Concept:
questions.why: Output grew 7% but jobs only 1%, so growth did not create jobs in proportion: jobless growth.

questions.q: Case: A company employing 200 people outsources security to contractors who don't give PF. Concept:
questions.why: Outsourcing security to contractors who give no PF shifts work from the formal to the informal sector, which is informalisation.

questions.q: Case: After removing 2 of 6 workers from a family farm, output is unchanged. Disguised unemployment:
questions.why: Output stays the same after removing 2 of 6 workers, so those 2 added nothing. Disguised unemployment is 2 workers.

questions.q: Assertion: Casualisation increases vulnerability of workers. Reason: Casual workers have irregular work and little social security.
questions.why: Both are true. Casual workers have irregular work and little social security, so they are more vulnerable, as the reason explains.

questions.q: Case: A village labourer gets 100 days of paid work digging a canal under a legal guarantee. Programme and type:
questions.why: A legal guarantee of 100 days of paid work is MGNREGA, which gives direct wage employment.

questions.q: Service sector is also called:
questions.why: The service sector is the tertiary sector, after primary (farming) and secondary (industry).

questions.q: Urban areas have a higher share of:
questions.why: Regular salaried jobs are more common in urban areas, while rural areas have more self-employed and casual workers.
