courses.title: Environment and Sustainable Development
courses.summary: Functions of the environment, carrying and absorptive capacity, global environmental issues, the state of India's environment, the meaning of sustainable development and strategies to achieve it.
outcomes: Learners can explain the four functions of the environment
Learners can explain carrying and absorptive capacity and why crises arise
Learners can describe India's environmental challenges
Learners can define sustainable development and list strategies to achieve it

scenes.text: Forests give timber; rivers give water.
Air and water absorb our wastes.
Mountains and rivers delight us.

steps.title: Environment
steps.body: The **environment** is the total planetary inheritance and all resources — **biotic** (living: plants, animals, birds) and **abiotic** (non-living: air, water, land).

steps.title: Four functions
steps.body:
1. **Supplies resources** — renewable (trees, fish — can be used without depletion if managed) and non-renewable (fossil fuels, minerals)
2. **Assimilates waste**
3. **Sustains life** — provides genetic and biodiversity
4. **Provides aesthetic services** — scenery, recreation

steps.title: Carrying and absorptive capacity
steps.body: The environment can perform these functions only within its **carrying capacity**: (a) **extraction of resources must not exceed their regeneration**, and (b) **wastes must be within the absorptive capacity** (the ability of the environment to absorb degradation). When these are violated, an **environmental crisis** results — e.g. rising demand for resources beyond regeneration rate.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A lake can clean itself of a limited amount of sewage. When a city doubles sewage inflow, fish die → **absorptive capacity exceeded**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Groundwater pumped faster than recharge by rain → **extraction exceeds regeneration**; water table falls.

steps.title: Global issues
steps.body:
**Global warming:** gradual rise in average surface temperature due to increase in greenhouse gases (from fossil-fuel burning and deforestation) — melting ice, rising sea levels.
**Ozone depletion:** thinning of the stratospheric ozone layer, largely by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) — more UV radiation. The **Montreal Protocol (1987)** phased out ozone-depleting substances.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling all natural resources renewable.
- Confusing global warming (greenhouse gases) with ozone depletion (CFCs).

activity.prompt: Match the example to the function of the environment
pairs: River dilutes and breaks down waste

quiz.why: Biotic elements are living things, such as plants and animals. Air, water and rocks are abiotic.

quiz.q: Absorptive capacity is the ability to:
quiz.why: Absorptive capacity is the environment's ability to take in degradation (waste and pollution) without damage.
An environmental crisis occurs when resources are extracted faster than they regenerate, and wastes exceed the absorptive capacity.

quiz.q: Ozone depletion is mainly caused by:
quiz.why: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) release chlorine in the stratosphere, which destroys ozone.
The Montreal Protocol (1987) is the international agreement to phase out ozone-depleting substances.

scenes.text: Cities are crowded; vehicles multiply.
Land is overused; forests shrink.
Air quality falls in winter.

steps.title: Main concerns
steps.body:
India has rich natural resources — fertile soils, rivers, forests, minerals (iron ore, coal, bauxite) — but faces:
- **Land degradation** (deforestation, soil erosion, shifting cultivation, overgrazing, improper irrigation, mining)
- **Loss of biodiversity**
- **Air pollution** (urban vehicles, industry, crop-residue burning)
- **Water contamination and scarcity**
- **Management of fresh water and solid waste**
Pressures come from both **poverty** (dependence on natural resources for survival) and **affluence** (high consumption, pollution).

steps.title: Institutions
steps.body: The **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)**, set up in **1974**, along with State Pollution Control Boards, monitors air and water quality and enforces pollution laws.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Farmers burn crop stubble after harvest; smog spreads to cities → **air pollution** from agricultural practice.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Excessive canal irrigation without drainage leads to waterlogging and salinity → **land degradation**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Blaming only poverty — affluent consumption also degrades the environment.

activity.prompt: Tick the causes of land degradation in India
items: Deforestation
Shifting cultivation
Overgrazing
Improper crop rotation
Soil erosion
Improper irrigation (waterlogging, salinity)
Mining and quarrying

quiz.why: The Central Pollution Control Board was set up in 1974 under the Water Act.
Overgrazing strips the plant cover and degrades land, causing erosion.
The poor depend directly on natural resources, and the rich consume more and pollute more, so both put pressure on the environment.

quiz.q: Urban air pollution is mainly from:
quiz.why: Vehicle exhaust and industrial emissions are the main sources of urban air pollution.
Over-irrigation without drainage raises the water table and causes waterlogging.

scenes.text: Grandmother used the river for drinking water.
Will her granddaughter be able to?
Sustainable development asks that question.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: The **Brundtland Commission** (UN World Commission on Environment and Development, report 1987) defined sustainable development as development that **meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs**. It requires that we pass on to the next generation a stock of capital (including natural capital) at least as large as we inherited.

steps.title: Herman Daly's guidelines (summary)
steps.body:
- Limit human population to a level within the carrying capacity
- Technological progress should be input-efficient, not input-consuming
- Renewable resources should be extracted on a sustainable basis (rate of extraction ≤ rate of regeneration)
- For non-renewable resources, rate of depletion should not exceed the rate of creation of renewable substitutes
- Inefficiencies from pollution should be corrected

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A fishing village limits its catch so fish populations can recover each season → renewable resource used **sustainably**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A country invests coal revenues in building solar capacity → depletion of a non-renewable resource matched by creation of a **renewable substitute**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying sustainable development means "no development".
- Attributing the Brundtland definition to the Montreal Protocol.

statements.s: Sustainable development means stopping all growth.
statements.why: It means growth that does not compromise future generations.

statements.s: The Brundtland Commission report appeared in 1987.
Renewable resources should be used no faster than they regenerate.
Pollution never needs correction if GDP rises.
statements.why: Inefficiencies from pollution must be corrected.

quiz.q: Sustainable development meets present needs without:
quiz.why: Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
This definition comes from the Brundtland Commission report, Our Common Future.
Herman Daly said technological progress should be input-efficient, using fewer resources per unit of output, not input-consuming.

quiz.q: Extraction of renewables should not exceed:
quiz.why: Renewable resources should be extracted no faster than they regenerate, so the stock is not depleted.
The Brundtland report was published in 1987.

scenes.text: A village gets solar lamps.
Gobar gas plants replace firewood.
Delhi's buses switched to CNG.

steps.title: Strategies
steps.body:
- **Use of non-conventional sources of energy:** wind power, solar power through photovoltaic cells
- **LPG and gobar gas in rural areas** (cleaner than firewood and dung cakes; reduce indoor air pollution)
- **CNG in urban areas** — e.g. Delhi's public transport switched to CNG, reducing air pollution
- **Mini-hydel plants** in mountainous regions
- **Traditional knowledge and practices** (Ayurveda, Unani, Tibetan medicine; traditional water harvesting; agriculture)
- **Biocomposting** (organic manure, earthworms)
- **Biopest control** (neem-based pesticides, natural predators like birds, cattle-friendly practices)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A village uses cattle dung in a biogas plant for cooking and uses the slurry as manure → **gobar gas** (energy + organic manure).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A farmer encourages birds and uses neem-based spray instead of chemical pesticides → **biopest control**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Calling LPG a renewable resource — it is a cleaner fossil fuel; gobar gas is renewable.

activity.prompt: Which strategy is each example?

quiz.why: Delhi switched its public transport to CNG, a cleaner fuel, to reduce air pollution.
Gobar gas (biogas) is produced from cattle dung.
Mini-hydel plants use fast-flowing streams, which are found in mountainous regions.
Biopest control uses natural predators and plant-based pesticides, such as neem, in place of harmful chemicals.
Solar power is a non-conventional (renewable) energy source. Coal, diesel and natural gas are conventional fossil fuels.

questions.q: Abiotic elements include:
questions.why: Abiotic elements are non-living, such as air, water and soil. Plants and animals are biotic.

questions.q: CPCB was established in:
questions.why: The Central Pollution Control Board was established in 1974.

questions.q: Sustainable development definition comes from:
questions.why: The widely used definition of sustainable development comes from the Brundtland Commission.

questions.q: Ozone depletion is caused mainly by:
questions.why: Chlorofluorocarbons are the main cause of ozone depletion.

questions.q: An environmental crisis results when:
options: Extraction exceeds regeneration and wastes exceed absorptive capacity
questions.why: An environmental crisis arises when resources are extracted faster than they regenerate and wastes exceed the environment's absorptive capacity.

questions.q: Assertion: Rural use of gobar gas supports sustainable development. Reason: It replaces firewood and provides manure.
questions.why: Both are true. Gobar gas replaces firewood, so it saves forests, and the slurry gives manure, so it supports sustainable development.

questions.q: Case: A river is used by a factory to dump effluents; fish die. Which capacity is exceeded?
questions.why: Dumping effluents beyond what the river can absorb kills fish, so the river's absorptive capacity has been exceeded.

questions.q: Case: Earthworms convert farm waste into manure. Strategy:
questions.why: Using earthworms to turn farm waste into manure is biocomposting.

questions.q: Case: Groundwater in Punjab falls as pumping exceeds recharge. Concept:
questions.why: Pumping groundwater faster than it is recharged is extraction exceeding regeneration.

questions.q: Case: A country earns from oil exports and invests the money in solar and wind. Daly's guideline:
options: Depletion of non-renewables matched by creation of renewable substitutes
questions.why: Daly said depletion of non-renewables should be matched by creating renewable substitutes. Investing oil earnings in solar and wind does this.

questions.q: Case: Smoke from wood stoves causes eye and lung problems in village homes; LPG is supplied. Benefit:
questions.why: LPG burns without the smoke that wood stoves give out, so it reduces indoor air pollution and the related health problems.

questions.q: Global warming is mainly caused by:
options: Greenhouse gases from fossil fuels and deforestation
questions.why: Global warming mainly results from greenhouse gases released by burning fossil fuels and clearing forests.

questions.q: Assertion: Both poverty and affluence harm the environment. Reason: The poor depend on natural resources for survival, while the affluent consume and pollute more.
questions.why: Both are true. The poor depend on resources for survival, which can degrade them, and the affluent consume and pollute more. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A tourist resort clears mangroves; later storms flood the area and tourists stop coming. Functions lost:
options: Sustaining life and aesthetic services (and resource protection)
questions.why: Mangroves protect coasts and give a pleasant landscape. Clearing them removes life-sustaining and aesthetic services, and lets storms flood the area.

questions.q: Montreal Protocol year:
questions.why: The Montreal Protocol was adopted in 1987.

questions.q: Renewable resource:
questions.why: Forests, if managed so they regrow, are a renewable resource. Coal, iron ore and petroleum are exhaustible.

courses.title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours
courses.summary: Development paths of India, China and Pakistan; comparison of demographic indicators, GDP growth and sectoral structure, and human development; and an appraisal of their strategies.
outcomes: Learners can describe the development paths of India, China and Pakistan
Learners can compare demographic indicators
Learners can compare growth and sectoral structure
Learners can compare human development and appraise strategies

scenes.text: India (1947) chose planned mixed economy.
China (1949) chose a command economy, then reformed in 1978.
Pakistan (1947) chose a mixed economy with frequent policy shifts.

steps.title: India
steps.body: Independent in 1947; mixed economy with planning (First Five Year Plan 1951–56); reforms from 1991.

steps.title: China
steps.body:
People's Republic of China established in **1949**; command economy; first Five Year Plan from 1953.
- **Great Leap Forward (1958):** aimed at rapid industrialisation, including backyard furnaces and commune farming; suffered serious problems (drought, famine)
- **Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution (1966–76):** students and professionals sent to work and learn from the countryside
- **Reforms from 1978:** first in agriculture (land to households — responsibility system), then industry; private firms and township and village enterprises; **dual pricing** (fixed quotas at government prices, surplus at market prices); **Special Economic Zones** to attract foreign investment

steps.title: Pakistan
steps.body: Mixed economy; public and private sectors coexist. In the late 1950s and 1960s, regulated policy (import substitution, tariffs); Green Revolution in agriculture; in the 1970s nationalisation of capital goods industries; late 1970s–80s shift to denationalisation and private sector; **reforms initiated in 1988**. Relied heavily on foreign remittances and foreign aid.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A policy allowing Chinese farmers to sell surplus output in the market after meeting state quotas → **dual pricing** (post-1978 reform).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Which country began reforms first? → **China (1978)**, then Pakistan (1988), then India (1991).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dating the Great Leap Forward to 1978 — it was 1958.
- Saying Pakistan had a command economy — it had a mixed economy.

activity.prompt: Arrange in chronological order

events.text: India's First Five Year Plan begins

quiz.why: China began its economic reforms in 1978.

quiz.q: Great Leap Forward was launched in:
quiz.why: China's Great Leap Forward was launched in 1958.
Pakistan began its reforms in 1988.

quiz.q: Special Economic Zones were set up by China to:
quiz.why: Special Economic Zones give foreign investors tax and other benefits to attract investment, and boost exports.

options: Quota at government price, surplus at market price
quiz.why: Under dual pricing in China, farmers sold a fixed quota to the state at a government price and sold the rest at market price.

scenes.text: China introduced a one-child norm in the late 1970s.
Population growth slowed sharply.
Later, the share of elderly rose.

steps.title: Comparisons (broad patterns)
steps.body:
- **Population:** China is the world's most populous country for decades (India's population has now become comparable/larger); Pakistan's is much smaller
- **Population growth:** lowest in China (due to the one-child policy introduced around **1979**), highest in Pakistan
- **Density:** China's population density is lower than India's (larger land area)
- **Sex ratio:** low in China and Pakistan (son preference is cited as a reason); India also has a low ratio
- **Fertility rate:** low in China, high in Pakistan
- **Urbanisation:** higher in China than India and Pakistan
(Exact figures change every year — use the latest official data where your exam requires numbers.)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Why is China's population growth low? → The **one-child policy** (from about 1979) reduced fertility; side effects include an ageing population and a skewed sex ratio.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A country has high fertility and fast population growth among the three → **Pakistan**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying China has the highest population density — India's is higher.
- Ignoring the side effects of the one-child policy.

activity.prompt: Match the indicator to the country it best describes (among India, China, Pakistan)

quiz.why: The one-child policy was introduced in China in 1979.
Pakistan has the highest population growth rate of the three.

quiz.q: A side effect of the one-child policy:
quiz.why: The one-child policy cut fertility, but it led to an ageing population as there are fewer young people.
India has the highest population density among India, China and Pakistan.
China has the highest share of urban population among the three.

scenes.text: China's manufacturing exports boomed after 1978.
India's growth came more from services.
Pakistan grew more slowly with frequent shocks.

steps.title: Growth
steps.body: China achieved the fastest and most sustained GDP growth among the three after 1978 (double-digit in many years). India's growth picked up after 1980 and especially after 1991. Pakistan's growth was relatively high in the 1980s but slowed and fluctuated in later decades.

steps.title: Sectoral structure
steps.body:
- **China:** large shift of workers from agriculture to manufacturing and services; manufacturing contributes a large share of GDP (export-led industrialisation)
- **India and Pakistan:** shift directly from agriculture to **services** (services contribute the largest share of GDP), while a large share of workers remain in agriculture
- Agriculture's share of output is lowest in China

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A country where manufacturing contributes the largest share of output among the three → **China**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A country whose services sector grew fastest while agriculture still employs about two-fifths or more of the workforce → **India** (also Pakistan).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying India followed China's manufacturing-led path — India's was more services-led.

activity.prompt: Which country best fits each statement?

items.text: Reforms in 1991 led to services-led growth
Heavy reliance on remittances and foreign aid; slowed growth

quiz.q: Fastest growth among the three after 1978:
quiz.why: After 1978 China grew fastest, at very high rates for many years.

quiz.q: India's growth has been led mainly by:
quiz.why: India's growth has been led mainly by the services sector, unlike China's manufacturing-led growth.

quiz.q: In China, workers shifted from agriculture mainly to:
quiz.why: In China, workers moved from agriculture mainly into manufacturing and services.

quiz.q: Pakistan's growth in later decades was:
quiz.why: Pakistan's growth was slower and fluctuated, compared with China and India.

quiz.q: Agriculture's share of output is lowest in:
quiz.why: China has the lowest share of agriculture in output, since manufacturing grew fast.

scenes.text: Life expectancy, literacy, health.
China ranks ahead on most indicators.
What lessons for India?

steps.title: Human development comparison (broad patterns)
steps.body: China performs better than India and Pakistan on most human development indicators — life expectancy, adult literacy, lower infant and maternal mortality, lower proportion of people below the poverty line, better access to sanitation and drinking water. India and Pakistan are closer to each other; Pakistan lags India on some indicators (e.g. literacy) but has done better on some others in certain years. Liberty indicators (democratic rights) are a different dimension: India's democratic institutions are a strength.

steps.title: Appraisal
steps.body:
- **China:** state-led reforms built on earlier investments in health, education and land reforms; rapid growth and poverty reduction; concerns include political freedoms, inequality, environment
- **Pakistan:** growth limited by political instability, dependence on remittances and foreign aid, low agricultural productivity and weak industrial base
- **India:** democratic set-up; services-led growth; needs faster manufacturing, better human development and employment growth

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Why could China grow fast after 1978? → It already had good social infrastructure (health, education) and land reforms; reforms then unleashed productivity.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A key reason for Pakistan's slowdown according to many analysts → **political instability and over-dependence on remittances/foreign aid**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Ranking countries only on GDP — human development and freedoms matter too.

activity.prompt: Which ONE lesson from China's or Pakistan's experience would you suggest for India's next decade, and why?
activity.hint: Think about health and education foundations, manufacturing jobs, stability, and democratic freedoms.

quiz.q: Which country leads on most human development indicators among the three?
quiz.why: China leads on most human development indicators among the three, such as life expectancy.

quiz.q: A reason for China's success after 1978:
options: Earlier investment in health, education and land reforms
quiz.why: Before reforms China had invested in health, education and land reform, which gave it a healthy, skilled workforce when markets opened.

options: Political instability and dependence on remittances/aid
quiz.why: Political instability and reliance on remittances and aid made Pakistan's growth unsteady.

quiz.q: A strength of India often highlighted:
quiz.why: India's democratic institutions are often counted among its strengths.
Human development covers outcomes such as life expectancy and literacy, not just income or output.

questions.q: PRC was established in:
questions.why: The People's Republic of China was established in 1949.

questions.q: China's reforms began in:
questions.why: China began reforms in 1978.

questions.q: Pakistan's reforms began in:
questions.why: Pakistan started economic reforms in 1988.

questions.q: Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution period:
questions.why: China's Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution took place from 1966 to 1976.

questions.q: One-child policy affected:
questions.why: The one-child policy was introduced in China.

questions.q: Assertion: China's population growth is the lowest of the three. Reason: The one-child policy reduced fertility.
questions.why: Both are true. China's one-child policy sharply reduced fertility, so its population growth rate is the lowest of the three.

questions.q: Which country's growth is most manufacturing-led?
questions.why: China's growth was led by manufacturing, while India's was led by services.

questions.q: Case: Farmers deliver a fixed quota to the state at fixed prices and sell the rest at market prices. Policy:
questions.why: A fixed quota at a government price with the rest sold at the market price is dual pricing, used in China.

questions.q: Case: A country's workers moved mostly from agriculture to services, skipping a big manufacturing phase. Likely:
questions.why: India's workers moved from agriculture mainly to services, skipping a large manufacturing phase. China had a big manufacturing phase.

questions.q: Case: Rural communes and backyard furnaces were part of:
questions.why: Rural communes and backyard furnaces were features of China's Great Leap Forward.

questions.q: Case: A country depends heavily on remittances and foreign aid; growth fluctuates with political changes. Country:
questions.why: Heavy reliance on remittances and aid, with growth swinging with politics, describes Pakistan.

questions.q: Which order of reforms is correct?
questions.why: China began reforms in 1978, Pakistan in 1988 and India in 1991.

questions.q: Assertion: China's later rapid growth built on earlier social investments. Reason: Good health and education raise productivity when markets open.
questions.why: Both are true. Earlier health and education spending gave China a productive workforce, so growth was fast once markets opened.

questions.q: Case: An analyst compares three countries on GDP only and ranks China first. What is missing?
questions.why: GDP alone leaves out human development (health, education) and freedom indicators, which are needed for a full comparison.

questions.q: Population density is highest in:
questions.why: India has the highest population density of the three countries.

questions.q: SEZs were first developed at scale by:
questions.why: China developed Special Economic Zones at a large scale.

lessons.title: Formula sheet: national income and money

scenes.text: National income questions are guaranteed marks.
Money multiplier is a quick win.

steps.title: Conversions
steps.body: Net = Gross − Depreciation · FC = MP − NIT (NIT = indirect taxes − subsidies) · National = Domestic + NFIA · NNP FC = GDP MP − Dep − NIT + NFIA

steps.title: Three methods
steps.body: Value added = Output − Intermediate consumption (Output = Sales + ΔStock) · Expenditure: GDP MP = C + I + G + (X − M) · Income: NDP FC = CoE + OS (rent + interest + profit) + mixed income

steps.title: Real GDP
steps.body: Real = Nominal × 100 / Deflator · Deflator = Nominal/Real × 100

steps.title: Money
steps.body: M1 = CU + DD + other deposits with RBI · M3 = M1 + net time deposits · H = CU + R · Money multiplier = 1/CRR · Credit created = Total deposits − Initial deposit

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body: Write the formula, substitute values with units, and box the answer. Show conversions step by step for partial credit.

steps.title: Top mistakes to avoid
steps.body: Wrong sign of NFIA; adding imports; including transfer payments; forgetting change in stock.

cards.back: Excluded
Part of compensation of employees
Only commission counts
Money supply falls
Rate at which RBI lends short-term to banks

quiz.why: Subtracting net indirect taxes from a market price value gives the factor cost value, so NDP at MP − NIT = NDP at FC.
Money multiplier = 1/CRR = 1/0.05 = 20.
In the expenditure method imports are subtracted, since they are spending on foreign output: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M).
M3 = M1 + net time deposits, so M3 − M1 = net time deposits of banks.

lessons.title: Formula sheet: income determination, budget, BoP

scenes.text: Equilibrium and multiplier.
Deficits.
BoP and exchange rate.

steps.title: Income determination
steps.body: C = C̄ + cY · S = −C̄ + (1 − c)Y · APC + APS = 1 · MPC + MPS = 1 · Y* = (C̄ + Ī)/(1 − c) · k = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS · ΔY = k × ΔI · inflationary gap: AD > AS at full employment; deflationary gap: AD < AS

steps.title: Budget
steps.body: RD = RE − RR · FD = TE − (RR + non-debt capital receipts) = borrowings · PD = FD − interest payments · capital receipts create liability or reduce assets

steps.title: BoP and forex
steps.body: Trade balance = X(goods) − M(goods) · CAB = trade balance + net invisibles · reserves change = CAB + capital account balance · ₹ per $ rises = rupee depreciates · India: managed floating

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body: For deficits, list RR, RE, CE, non-debt capital receipts and interest first; then compute RD, FD, PD.

steps.title: Top mistakes to avoid
steps.body: Subtracting borrowings again in FD; using 1/MPC for the multiplier; confusing depreciation with devaluation.

cards.back: Capital receipt (non-debt)
Borrowing only for interest
Current account (transfers)
To slow rupee depreciation

quiz.why: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest = 500 − 200 = 300.
Multiplier = 1/MPS = 1/0.25 = 4, so ΔY = 4 × 40 = 160.
Foreign direct investment is a capital flow, so it is in the capital account.
Fewer rupees are needed per dollar (₹78 against ₹80), so the rupee has appreciated.

Group them by chapter.

steps.title: Colonial economy
steps.body: Growth < 2%; per capita ~0.5% · estimates: Naoroji, Digby, Shirras, V.K.R.V. Rao, R.C. Desai · zamindari / Permanent Settlement · commercialisation · de-industrialisation · TISCO 1907 · Suez Canal 1869 · first census 1881 · 1921 "great divide" · literacy < 16%, IMR ~218, life expectancy ~32 · agriculture 70–75% of workforce

Three categories of industries
GATT

questions.why: National income is another name for NNP at factor cost, the total of factor incomes of normal residents.

questions.why: A sharp fall in fertility after a one-child norm and a move of workers into export manufacturing fits China.

school-c12-english-a.description: Every Flamingo prose chapter: summary, themes, character sketches, board-style Q&A and answer-writing labs.

courses.title: Flamingo · The Last Lesson
courses.summary: Franz, a young boy, is late for school and hasn't learnt participles. He thinks of skipping school but goes. He finds the class unusually quiet; M. Hamel wears his fine Sunday clothes, and village elders, including old Hauser, sit at the…
outcomes: Learners can summarise the text in their own words
Learners can explain its central themes with evidence
Learners can write character sketches
Learners can answer board-style short and long questions

scenes.text: Franz is late for school and fears a scolding on participles.
M. Hamel announces an order from Berlin: only German will be taught in Alsace and Lorraine.
He writes 'Vive La France!' on the blackboard.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A story by **Alphonse Daudet**, set in 1870 during the Franco-Prussian War when Prussia conquered the French districts of Alsace and Lorraine. It highlights the value of one's mother tongue (linguistic chauvinism of conquerors) and the regret of procrastination.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: Franz, a young boy, is late for school and hasn't learnt participles. He thinks of skipping school but goes. He finds the class unusually quiet; M. Hamel wears his fine Sunday clothes, and village elders, including old Hauser, sit at the back.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: M. Hamel announces that an order has come from Berlin to teach only German in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine; this is their last French lesson. Franz feels regret for wasting time. M. Hamel says everyone — parents, pupils and he himself — was to blame for putting off learning.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: M. Hamel calls French the most beautiful language in the world, 'clearest, most logical', and says that as long as people hold fast to their language, it is as if they had the key to their prison. He teaches grammar, writing and history; at noon, overcome, he writes 'Vive La France!' on the board and dismisses the class.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the story without linking it to the question asked.
- Mixing up who says or does what — reread the key scene.
- Writing the theme as a one-word label without evidence from the text.

activity.prompt: Put these moments of the text in the correct order
items: Franz is late and fears a scolding
He notices the strange quiet and village elders
M. Hamel announces the order from Berlin
Franz regrets neglecting his lessons
M. Hamel praises French as the key to their prison
He writes 'Vive La France!' and ends the class

quiz.why: Daudet.
Berlin.

quiz.q: Franz was afraid of being questioned on
quiz.why: Participles.
Forty years.

scenes.text: A student asks: what is this text really about, beyond what happens?
Themes and characters answer that question — and they carry the most marks in long answers.

steps.title: Theme: Mother tongue and identity
steps.body: Language is part of a people's freedom and identity.

steps.title: Theme: Procrastination
steps.body: 'Plenty of time to learn tomorrow' costs everyone.

steps.title: Theme: Linguistic imperialism
steps.body: Conquerors impose their language to control people.

steps.title: Character sketch: Franz
steps.body: Transforms from carefree to regretful and patriotic.

steps.title: Character sketch: M. Hamel
steps.body: Dignified, patriotic; teaches the last lesson with great patience.

steps.title: Character sketch: Old Hauser
steps.body: Attends with his primer to honour the teacher and language.

steps.title: Style & literary devices
steps.body:
- First-person narration by Franz; irony and pathos.

courses.summary: Saheb-e-Alam, whose family came from Dhaka after storms swept away their fields, scavenges in garbage in Seemapuri. He says there's no school nearby; the author jokingly promises to start one. For ragpickers, garbage is 'gold' — survival.…

scenes.text: Saheb scrounges for gold in Seemapuri's garbage dumps.
Mukesh, in Firozabad, works in a bangle industry near hot furnaces.
Yet Mukesh dares to dream of being a motor mechanic.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: Excerpts by **Anees Jung** from *Lost Spring*. She describes child ragpickers in Seemapuri (Delhi) and bangle-making children in Firozabad, exposing poverty, exploitation and lost childhood.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: Saheb-e-Alam, whose family came from Dhaka after storms swept away their fields, scavenges in garbage in Seemapuri. He says there's no school nearby; the author jokingly promises to start one. For ragpickers, garbage is 'gold' — survival. Later Saheb works at a tea stall for Rs 800 a month and a meal, but he is no longer his own master; his steel canister is heavier than the plastic bag.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: In Firozabad, famous for glass bangles, about 20,000 children work near furnaces with high temperatures, often losing their eyesight. Families are trapped by the 'vicious circle' of sahukars, middlemen, policemen, politicians and the bureaucracy. They accept their fate as 'karam' (destiny).

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: Mukesh, unlike others, wants to be a motor mechanic and will learn to drive a car. The author sees hope in his dream, though the road ahead is hard.

scenes.text: As a child, William Douglas was knocked down by a wave at California beach.
At the YMCA pool a big boy throws him into the deep end; he nearly drowns.
Years later he hires an instructor and conquers his fear.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: An extract from *Of Men and Mountains* by **William O. Douglas**, later a US Supreme Court judge. It describes his terror of water and how he overcame it.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: At three or four, a wave knocked him down at a California beach, frightening him. At ten or eleven he decided to learn swimming at the YMCA pool in Yakima, which was relatively safe.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: A burly eighteen-year-old picked him up and threw him into the deep end. He sank, struggled, came up three times, and finally lost consciousness; he was rescued. Afterwards he feared water for years, missing canoeing, fishing and swimming.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: He hired an instructor who taught him piece by piece — exhaling under water, kicking — with a rope and pulley. To test himself he swam at Lake Wentworth in New Hampshire and Warm Lake, finally conquering fear. He realised 'all we have to fear is fear itself' and that there is peace in death; terror only is to fear.

steps.body:

scenes.text: A poor peddler sells rattraps and thinks the whole world is a rattrap.
He steals 30 kronor from a kind crofter and gets lost in a forest.
Edla Willmansson's kindness changes him.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A story by Swedish Nobel laureate **Selma Lagerlöf**, set in the mining region of Värmland. It shows that kindness can awaken goodness in anyone.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: A vagabond peddler sells rattraps and begs or steals to survive. He believes the world is a rattrap that tempts people with bait — riches, joy, food — and then traps them. A lonely old crofter gives him shelter, porridge and shows him thirty kronor; the peddler later steals the money.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: Lost in the forest, he realises he is trapped. At Ramsjö ironworks the ironmaster mistakes him for an old regimental comrade, Captain von Stahle, and invites him home; he refuses but the ironmaster's daughter Edla persuades him. Next day, cleaned and dressed, he is recognised as a stranger; the ironmaster wants to call the sheriff, but Edla insists he spend Christmas with them.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: He leaves on Christmas Day. He leaves a rattrap gift for Edla, with the thirty kronor to be returned to the crofter, and a letter signed 'Captain von Stahle' — because she treated him like a captain, he wants to be nice in return.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: An extract from *The Life of Mahatma Gandhi* by **Louis Fischer**, about the Champaran episode (1917) in Bihar, where Gandhi helped indigo sharecroppers against British landlords.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: Rajkumar Shukla, an illiterate sharecropper from Champaran, met Gandhi at the 1916 Lucknow Congress session and followed him until Gandhi agreed to visit. Under the long-term contract, peasants had to plant 15% of their land with indigo and give the harvest as rent. When synthetic indigo arrived from Germany, landlords demanded compensation instead.

steps.title: Summary — part 2

steps.title: Summary — part 3

story.title: Is an interview art or invasion?

scenes.text: Journalists interview the famous every day.
Some celebrities call interviews an invasion; others value them.
Umberto Eco talks about writing novels on Sundays.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: Part I is an extract from **Christopher Silvester**'s introduction to *The Penguin Book of Interviews*: views on the interview as a form. Part II is an interview of **Umberto Eco** by Mukund Padmanabhan (The Hindu).

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: Part I: The interview was invented over 130 years ago and is now commonplace. Opinions differ: some see it as 'an art', a source of truth; others dislike it. V.S. Naipaul felt people are 'wounded' by interviews; Lewis Carroll avoided interviewers; Rudyard Kipling called it immoral, 'a crime'; H.G. Wells called it an 'ordeal'. Still, the interview is a supremely serviceable medium of communication.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: Part II: Umberto Eco, Italian scholar of semiotics and novelist (*The Name of the Rose*), explains he uses 'interstices' — empty spaces in time — to write. He says his scholarly work has a narrative style; he only wrote novels by chance. His novel sold 10–15 million copies, surprising him since it was serious and set in the Middle Ages.
